cirneco-cons-ampd2-study-2024.name: Murgiano et al. (2024) - Frameshift Variant in AMPD2 in Cirneco dell'Etna Dogs with Retinopathy and Tremors (Genes)

nsdtr-immune-mediated-disease-patterns-2.name: Disease Patterns and Incidence of Immune-Mediated Disease in Insured Swedish Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers
nsdtr-immune-mediated-disease-patterns-2.note: Bremer HD, Vilson Å, Bonnett BN, Hansson-Hamlin H (Veterinary Record 2015;177(3):74). Epidemiological cohort study of 2,890 insured Swedish Tollers (2002–2007) reporting elevated relative risk and incidence rates for SRMA (20 per 10,000 DYAR; RR 12) and IMRD (6.8 per 10,000 DYAR; RR 18), higher lymphoma risk, and lower ear and heart disease rates compared with other breeds.

nsdtr-immune-mediated-health-survey-2024.name: In Sickness and Health - A Questionnaire-Based Study of Immune-Mediated Diseases and Neoplasia in Swedish Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers
nsdtr-immune-mediated-health-survey-2024.note: Nilsson K et al. / Hansson-Hamlin H (Acta Veterinaria Scandinavica 2024;66:39). Questionnaire study of 935 living and 177 deceased Swedish Tollers reporting living lifetime prevalence of 3.0% for IMRD and 3.5% for SRMA, owner-reported neoplasia of any type in 14% of living dogs (mammary 22%, mast cell 15%), and neoplasia as cause of death in 38.4% of deceased dogs.

nsdtr-resf1-jadd-study-2026.name: A Variant in RESF1 Is Associated with Addison's Disease and Multiple Autoimmune Syndrome in Young Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers
nsdtr-resf1-jadd-study-2026.note: Brown EA, Cullen JN et al. / Bannasch DL (Scientific Reports 2026;16:13194). Identifies an autosomal recessive missense variant in RESF1 (Chr27:29,736,795, c.3170C>T, p.Pro1057Leu) associated with juvenile-onset Addison's disease (~75% penetrance by 1 year, median onset 5 months) and multiple autoimmune syndrome (41.7%–70.8% concurrent immune disorders; median survival 2.0 years).

uc-davis-vgl-jadd-nsdtr.name: UC Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory - Juvenile Addison's Disease in Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers
uc-davis-vgl-jadd-nsdtr.note: UC Davis VGL test page for the RESF1 c.3170C>T (p.Pro1057Leu) juvenile Addison's disease (JADD) variant, documenting autosomal recessive inheritance with incomplete (~75.9%) penetrance, ~20%–23% carrier frequency, concurrent ocular/immunologic comorbidities, and breeding guidance.

overview.summary: The Alpine Dachsbracke is a sturdy, short-legged Austrian scent hound developed for demanding work in mountainous hunting country. It has a strong, elongated body, a dense double coat, pendant ears, and a confident, alert expression. Traditionally, it follows scent trails to locate wounded deer and is also used to hunt hare and fox. Its compact build should not be mistaken for low exercise needs: this is a working hound with a strong nose and a drive to investigate scents. As a companion, it benefits from daily outdoor activity, nose-led enrichment, patient training, and secure handling wherever wildlife or traffic may be present.
overview.description: The Alpine Dachsbracke is a compact but powerfully built hound whose short legs and long body give it a distinctive outline. Its body is muscular and elongated, with strong bone, a broad and deep chest, and firm feet suited to working over challenging terrain. The head is slightly arched through the skull, with a pronounced stop, strong muzzle, dark-brown eyes, and smooth, pendant ears with rounded tips. Its double coat has a dense undercoat beneath a thick outer coat that lies close to the body. Common standard colours are dark deer red, sometimes interspersed with black hairs, or black with clearly defined red-brown markings; a white chest star is permitted. The breed was developed as a practical hunting dog rather than as a purely decorative companion. It can be affectionate and friendly, but its scenting instincts, stamina, and need for meaningful activity should be part of any ownership decision.
overview.history: The Alpine Dachsbracke has a long association with hunting in the Alpine region. Historical accounts describe dogs of similar appearance being used for hunting long before the modern breed was formally recognised. In the late nineteenth century, Crown Prince Rudolf of Habsburg took these hounds on hunting expeditions. Austrian canine organisations recognised the Alpine-Erzgebirge Dachsbracke in 1932; the breed name was later changed to Alpenländische Dachsbracke, and Austria was designated its country of origin. It was subsequently placed in the scent-hound section of the international classification.
overview.originalPurpose: A robust mountain hunting dog used to track wounded deer and to hunt hare and fox by scent.
currentRoles: Hunting and trailing work where lawful
Active companion for owners able to meet working-hound needs

physical.sizeCategory: Small to medium, short-legged working hound
physical.coatType: Dense double coat with a thick outer coat and dense undercoat.
physical.coatLength: Short to medium, close-fitting, with longer hair beneath the tail.
coatColors: Dark deer red, with or without lightly interspersed black hairs
Black with clearly defined red-brown markings on the head, chest, legs, feet, and underside of the tail
A white star on the chest is permitted
distinctiveFeatures: Short legs and a strong, elongated body
Robust bone structure and firm musculature
Deep, broad chest
Dark-brown eyes with close-fitting, dark-pigmented eyelids
Smooth, pendant ears with rounded tips
Dense double coat suited to working outdoors
Thick tail root with longer hair on the underside
Strong scenting instinct and a working-hound outline

traits: The breed standard describes an intelligent, friendly expression and a fearless personality
Bred for persistence and concentration while following a scent trail
Likely to investigate interesting scents during walks
Benefits from consistent, reward-based training
Needs safe boundaries because scent-driven exploration may compete with recall
Its behaviour around children, unfamiliar people, and other animals depends on the individual dog and its experiences
Working instincts can be channelled into scent games and structured nose work

exercise.level: Moderate to high. The Alpine Dachsbracke was developed for sustained scent work and outdoor hunting. Provide daily walks, opportunities to sniff, and structured activities matched to the dog's age, fitness, and health. Secure areas are preferable for off-leash activity unless recall is reliable and the location is safe.
activities: Daily walks with time for controlled sniffing
Scent trails and beginner nose-work games
Reward-based recall and handler check-in practice
Tracking games in safe, legal environments
Food puzzles and scent-based enrichment
Hikes or outdoor exploration suited to the individual dog's fitness
Short, positive obedience sessions

grooming.level: Low to moderate. The double coat is designed for practical outdoor work, but routine brushing and checks help keep it in good condition.
grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a suitable grooming brush or mitt to remove loose hair and debris. Increase brushing during heavier shedding periods if needed.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when the dog is dirty or has developed an odour, using a dog-formulated shampoo. Avoid frequent unnecessary bathing that could dry the skin or disrupt coat condition.
notes: Inspect the coat and skin after outdoor activity for ticks, burrs, cuts, and irritation.
Check the pendant ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, or persistent scratching.
Dry the ears gently if they become wet and ask a veterinarian about recurring ear problems.
Trim nails as needed to maintain comfortable movement.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.
Check the paws and pads after walks on rough or rocky ground.

training.difficulty: Moderate. This is a working scent hound, so interesting trails can be more rewarding than handler cues. Use consistent reward-based methods, practise recall in secure places, and give the dog suitable outlets for scenting behaviour.
tips: Start recall and name-response training early, beginning in low-distraction environments.
Reward voluntary check-ins and returning promptly to the handler.
Use scent games to provide a structured outlet for natural tracking behaviour.
Train loose-leash walking before pulling becomes habitual.
Keep sessions positive and short enough to maintain engagement.
Avoid relying on off-leash recall in unsecured areas near roads or wildlife.
Introduce handling for grooming, nail care, and veterinary examinations gradually.
training.socialization: Provide gradual, positive exposure to people, friendly dogs, household sounds, transport, and varied walking environments. Practise calm responses around wildlife and scent distractions while maintaining secure physical control. Keep introductions age-appropriate and do not force interactions when the dog is frightened or overwhelmed.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity, and health. Working dogs may need different energy intake from less active companions.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Use a complete puppy diet appropriate for growth and follow its feeding guidance. Monitor growth and body condition with veterinary advice rather than increasing portions solely because the puppy seems hungry.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured portions of a complete adult diet and adjust them according to body condition, activity, and health. Account for training treats in the daily allowance.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose portions and food according to body condition, mobility, dental health, activity, and any medical conditions. Discuss persistent appetite or weight changes with a veterinarian.

nutrition.guidelines: Provide a complete and balanced diet, clean drinking water, and portions suited to the individual dog. Monitor body condition regularly and adjust intake when activity or weight changes. Avoid unbalanced homemade diets and unnecessary supplements; ask a veterinarian for a tailored plan when the dog has medical needs or performs substantial working activity.
considerations: Measure meals and adjust portions to maintain a healthy body condition.
Provide fresh, clean water at all times.
Include training treats in the daily food allowance.
Transition gradually when changing foods where practical.
Avoid giving supplements without a clear need and appropriate veterinary guidance.
Seek veterinary advice for persistent digestive changes, appetite loss, or unexplained weight change.
nutrition.note: The consulted breed standard does not provide a breed-specific weight range or calorie requirement. Feeding quantities should be individualised rather than inferred from the breed name alone.

preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary wellness examinations and maintain vaccination and parasite prevention appropriate to local risks.
Monitor body condition, mobility, appetite, drinking, and changes in activity.
Inspect ears, paws, skin, and coat after outdoor work.
Maintain routine dental care and seek veterinary assessment for pain, persistent bad breath, or eating changes.
Use secure leads and fencing in areas where scent-following could lead the dog toward roads or wildlife.
Seek prompt veterinary attention for serious injury, collapse, breathing difficulty, sudden weakness, or other acute concerning signs.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly using dog-safe toothpaste. Dental chews may provide supplementary help but do not replace brushing or veterinary examinations. Ask a veterinarian about professional dental cleaning if there is significant tartar, persistent bad breath, pain, or a change in eating.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, discomfort, or head shaking. Clean only with a product appropriate for dogs and seek veterinary advice for recurring or painful symptoms.
health.skinCare: Check the coat and skin during grooming and after outdoor activity. Look for ticks, plant material, scratches, rashes, or persistent itching. Seek veterinary advice for sores, unexplained hair loss, or recurring skin irritation.

idealFor: Owners who enjoy regular outdoor activity and scent-based games
People interested in tracking, nose work, or lawful hunting-related activities
Households able to provide secure exercise and consistent training
Owners willing to manage a dog that may follow interesting scents
People who understand the needs of a working hound rather than expecting a low-activity companion
notIdealFor: People seeking a dog with minimal exercise and enrichment needs
Owners who expect dependable off-leash recall without training
Households unable to provide safe outdoor management
People who cannot accommodate the individual dog's activity and scenting needs

Its name reflects its distinctive low-legged, elongated outline.
The breed has been used to track wounded deer and to hunt hare and fox by scent.
The standard recognises deer-red coats and black coats with red-brown markings.
The breed's double coat has a dense undercoat beneath a thick outer coat.

faq.question: Where does the Alpine Dachsbracke originate?
faq.answer: The Alpine Dachsbracke originates from Austria and is associated with hunting traditions in the Alpine region.

faq.question: How tall is an Alpine Dachsbracke?
faq.answer: The breed standard gives a height at the withers of 34–42 cm. Ideal heights are listed as 37–38 cm for males and 36–37 cm for females.

faq.question: How much does an Alpine Dachsbracke weigh?
faq.answer: The consulted official breed standard does not specify a weight range, so a reliable breed-specific figure cannot be provided from that source.

faq.question: What colours does the Alpine Dachsbracke come in?
faq.answer: Recognised colours include dark deer red, sometimes with lightly interspersed black hairs, and black with clearly defined red-brown markings. A white star on the chest is permitted.

faq.question: What was the Alpine Dachsbracke bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a robust hunting dog, especially for tracking wounded deer and hunting hare and fox by scent.

faq.question: Is the Alpine Dachsbracke easy to train?
faq.answer: Training is usually most effective when it is consistent and rewarding. Because the breed was developed for scent work, recall and attention around interesting trails need deliberate practice.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Alpine Dachsbracke need?
faq.answer: It needs regular outdoor activity and opportunities to use its nose. There is no verified universal daily minute target for every dog, so exercise should be adjusted to age, health, fitness, and behaviour.

faq.question: What health problems are common in the Alpine Dachsbracke?
faq.answer: The sources consulted did not establish a reliable breed-specific list of common conditions or screening tests. Routine veterinary care and individual assessment are more appropriate than assuming a disease list without evidence.

faq.question: How long does an Alpine Dachsbracke live?
faq.answer: A reliable lifespan range was not established from the sources consulted. Individual lifespan depends on many factors, including genetics, health, environment, and care.

overview.summary: An athletic American scent hound bred to track raccoons and other quarry, the American English Coonhound is energetic outdoors, sociable with people and dogs, and known for its ringing voice.
overview.description: The American English Coonhound is a lean, muscular hunting dog built for speed, stamina and sustained scent work. Bred to follow trails across varied terrain and locate game in trees, it has a strong nose, considerable endurance and a distinctive bay or howl that can carry over long distances. Many are friendly and relaxed with familiar people when their exercise needs are met, but their hunting drive can make recall unreliable around wildlife and fresh scent. Prospective owners should plan for daily outdoor activity, patient reward-based training, secure exercise arrangements and a voice that may be challenging in close urban housing.
overview.history: The breed descends from English Foxhounds and related hounds brought to North America by settlers. In the colonies and later the United States, breeders selected dogs that could work efficiently over rough terrain and pursue foxes by day and raccoons at night. The type was historically known as the English Fox and Coonhound. As coonhound varieties became distinct, the Treeing Walker and Bluetick lines separated from the broader English hound population. The American Kennel Club adopted the name American English Coonhound when it recognised the breed in 2011.
overview.originalPurpose: Scent-trailing and treeing raccoons, as well as hunting foxes and other quarry where traditional hound work is practised.
currentRoles: Coon hunting and other lawful scent-hunting work
Family companion in a home able to meet its exercise and vocalisation needs

physical.coatType: Short to medium-short, dense and protective, lying close to an athletic body.
physical.coatLength: Short
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; weekly grooming helps remove loose hair.
distinctiveFeatures: Lean, muscular and deep-chested frame built for endurance
Broad head with a slightly domed skull and a square, substantial muzzle
Long, low-set, soft ears that can reach nearly to the nose when drawn forward
Dark-brown eyes and a friendly, hound-like expression
Medium-coarse, close-lying coat with varied ticking and patch patterns
Long legs and strong feet suited to covering rough ground
A tail usually carried up while moving
A strong, carrying bay or howl used during trailing and hunting

traits: Sociable and generally friendly with people
Alert, confident and usually comfortable working with other dogs
Highly energetic and enduring outdoors
Persistent and focused when following a scent
Independent-minded, especially when hunting
Often affectionate with familiar family members
Vocal, with a distinctive bay or howl
Needs purposeful activity and patient training to channel its hunting instincts

exercise.level: High. This is an endurance hunting hound that needs substantial daily movement and scent-based enrichment. The exact workload depends on age, health, fitness and whether the dog works in the field.
activities: Brisk, sustained leash walks
Hikes on safe trails with opportunities for controlled sniffing
Scent-work games and tracking exercises
Structured play in a secure, fenced area
Reward-based obedience and recall practice around gradually increasing distractions
Suitable field or hunting activities where legal and responsibly supervised

grooming.brushing: Brush about once a week with a grooming mitt or soft brush to remove loose hair and distribute coat oils. Check the ears and skin at the same time, and increase brushing if shedding becomes more noticeable.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty or when the coat needs freshening, using a dog-safe shampoo and rinsing thoroughly. Avoid unnecessary frequent bathing that may dry the skin.
notes: Inspect the long ears regularly for redness, odour, excess wax or discharge.
Dry the ears and coat after swimming or getting thoroughly wet.
Check paws, pads and nails after long walks over rough ground.
Trim nails as needed and build calm handling into the dog's routine.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.
If the dog spends time in brush or tall grass, check for ticks, burrs and small injuries after outings.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for novice owners. The breed can learn well, but a strong scent drive and persistence on trail can compete with handler focus.
tips: Start reward-based training and socialisation early.
Teach recall in secure areas first; do not rely on off-leash recall around wildlife or fresh scent trails.
Use high-value rewards and gradually increase distractions during training.
Provide scent games and tracking activities so natural hunting behaviours have an appropriate outlet.
Train loose-leash walking because the dog may pull when it catches a scent.
Introduce calm routines around neighbours and visitors, and plan how to manage baying or howling.
Use a secure fence or leash for outdoor exercise rather than assuming the dog will stay nearby.
training.socialization: Give the puppy positive, gradual exposure to people, dogs, sounds, handling and everyday settings. Continue socialisation in adulthood. Train calm behaviour around wildlife and unfamiliar dogs while keeping the hound securely managed when its prey drive might take over.

climates: Temperate conditions
Warm weather with shade, fresh water and exercise during cooler hours
Cool weather when the dog has a dry, sheltered resting place

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to life stage, body condition, activity level and veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.adult: Use measured portions and a consistent meal routine. Meal count should be adjusted to the dog's age, activity, appetite and veterinary advice rather than assumed from breed alone.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose nutritionally complete food for the dog's life stage and adjust portions to maintain a lean body condition. A working hound may need more calories than a sedentary companion, so account for actual activity rather than feeding a fixed breed-wide amount. Keep fresh water available, count treats as part of the daily ration and introduce diet changes gradually.
considerations: Monitor body condition because adult coonhounds can gain excess weight when activity decreases.
Use a diet suited to growth for puppies and discuss growth needs with a veterinarian.
Avoid adding supplements unless a veterinarian recommends them.
Provide fresh water during and after exercise.
Ask a veterinarian about bloat risk and suitable feeding/exercise routines for the individual dog.
Adjust portions when hunting workload, exercise, age or medical status changes.
nutrition.note: The reviewed sources do not establish a universal breed-specific puppy or senior meal schedule. This section gives general nutrition guidance, not an individual feeding prescription.

health.overview: The American English Coonhound is described as generally healthy in breed-profile guidance, but that does not mean an individual dog is free of disease. Breed guidance identifies hip and elbow dysplasia, eye disorders including progressive retinal atrophy and cataracts, and bloat as potential concerns. The American Kennel Club currently lists no recommended national breed-club health tests specifically for this breed, so screening decisions should be discussed with a veterinarian and breeder rather than represented as a formal universal requirement. Hanging ears also deserve routine inspection because moisture and debris can contribute to irritation or infection.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — a developmental joint condition that can affect comfort and mobility; individual risk varies.
Elbow dysplasia — a group of developmental elbow conditions that may cause lameness or arthritis.
Eye disorders, including progressive retinal atrophy or cataracts — potential concerns in breed-care guidance, but a breed-wide prevalence was not established.

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) — a life-threatening emergency that can affect large or deep-chested dogs; abdominal swelling, unproductive retching, marked restlessness or collapse require immediate veterinary attention.
Ear inflammation or infection — long hanging ears can retain moisture or debris; persistent odour, discharge, redness or head-shaking warrants veterinary attention.
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary wellness examinations and follow vaccination and parasite-prevention advice appropriate to your region.
Keep the dog at a healthy body condition and discuss persistent lameness or reduced stamina with a veterinarian.
Check the ears regularly and seek advice for repeated irritation or infections.
Learn bloat warning signs and identify an emergency veterinary clinic in advance.
Discuss any family history of hip, elbow or eye disease with the breeder and veterinarian.
Maintain dental care, nail trimming and post-outing checks for ticks, burrs or paw injuries.
recommendedScreenings: The American Kennel Club's current breed-club recommendation list does not specify health tests for American English Coonhounds.
Ask the breeder what veterinary evaluations have been performed on the parents, especially if there is a family history of hip, elbow or eye disease.
A veterinarian may recommend orthopaedic or ophthalmic assessment based on family history, symptoms or breeding plans; these should not be treated as universal breed-club mandates.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with a dog-specific toothbrush and toothpaste. Schedule veterinary oral examinations and professional cleaning as recommended, and ask for advice if there is persistent bad breath, oral pain or a change in eating.
health.earCare: Inspect the long ears routinely for redness, excess wax, odour, discharge or repeated head-shaking. Clean only as needed with a veterinarian-approved product, and seek veterinary advice if symptoms persist or infections recur.
health.skinCare: Check the short coat and skin while brushing, especially after outdoor activity. Look for ticks, burrs, cuts, irritation or unusual lumps. Contact a veterinarian for persistent itching, hair loss or skin changes.

funFacts: The breed is sometimes called the Redtick Coonhound because red ticking is a familiar coat pattern.
The American English Coonhound developed from English hounds brought to North America and adapted for hunting across rough terrain.
This hound was traditionally used to hunt foxes by day and raccoons at night.
Its carrying bay or howl helps hunters follow the dog during trailing work.
The breed combines endurance and speed with a strong instinct to follow scent.

faq.question: What is another name for the American English Coonhound?
faq.answer: It is often called the English Coonhound or Redtick Coonhound. Historically, the type was also known as the English Fox and Coonhound.

faq.question: How large does an American English Coonhound get?
faq.answer: The AKC standard lists males at 24–26 inches (about 61–66 cm) and females at 23–25 inches (about 58–64 cm). The AKC profile gives a typical weight of 45–65 pounds (about 20–29.5 kg). The UKC English Coonhound standard allows different height limits, so measurements depend on the registry standard being used.

faq.question: How long does an American English Coonhound live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club breed profile lists an expected lifespan of about 11–12 years. This is a population-level estimate, not a promise for an individual dog.

faq.question: What colours can an American English Coonhound have?
faq.answer: Recognised patterns include red-and-white ticking, blue-and-white ticking, tri-colour with ticking, red and white, and white and black. The UKC standard gives its own permitted colour descriptions, so registration rules can differ between organisations.

faq.question: Is the American English Coonhound a good apartment dog?
faq.answer: It is usually a difficult fit for apartment living because it has high exercise needs and a loud bay or howl. A secure outdoor area, regular activity and a realistic plan for managing vocalisation are important.

faq.question: What health problems should owners know about?
faq.answer: Potential concerns include hip and elbow dysplasia, eye disorders and bloat, although reliable breed-wide prevalence figures were not established in the reviewed sources. Discuss family history and any screening with a veterinarian; suspected bloat is an emergency.

faq.question: How much grooming does an American English Coonhound need?
faq.answer: Its short coat generally needs only weekly brushing. The long ears need more regular attention: check for wax, redness, odour or discharge, and consult a veterinarian if irritation recurs.

faq.question: Can an American English Coonhound be trusted off leash?
faq.answer: Not reliably around wildlife or interesting scent trails. Its hunting instinct can draw it away from the handler, so practise recall in secure areas and use a leash where the surroundings are not safely enclosed.

overview.summary: A sturdy, medium-sized French scent hound developed for persistent hunting, known for its strong nose, pack-working ability and distinctive tricolour coat.
overview.description: The Artois Hound is a compact yet powerful scent hound built for stamina rather than extreme speed. Its broad head, long drooping ears, muscular body and short, dense coat give it a recognisable hound appearance. The breed was developed for hunting with people and other hounds, using scent to follow game over sustained periods. Its working background means that nose-led exploration, substantial daily activity and secure outdoor management are important considerations. The breed standard describes a balanced and affectionate dog that works well in a pack; individual behaviour still depends on genetics, early experience, health and training.
overview.history: The Artois Hound, historically also called the Picard, is an old French hunting breed associated with the Artois and Picardy regions. Historical accounts describe it as valued for hare hunting and other scent-hunting work. Crossbreeding and declining numbers weakened the traditional type, and after the Second World War the breed was feared lost. A reconstruction effort begun in the early 1970s, associated with M. Audrechy and Mme Pilat, helped re-establish it among French scenthounds. The FCI recognises the breed definitively and lists France as its country of origin.
overview.originalPurpose: Scent hunting with a human hunting party and in packs, especially following hare; the official standard also describes work on deer and wild boar in suitable terrain.
currentRoles: Scent-hunting and tracking in appropriate working settings

faq.question: Where does the Artois Hound come from?
faq.answer: It comes from France and is historically associated with the Artois and Picardy regions of the country's north.

faq.question: What was the Artois Hound bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a scent hound for hunting with people and in packs, particularly tracking hare and other game.

faq.question: How large is an Artois Hound?
faq.answer: The FCI standard lists 53–58 cm at the withers for both sexes, with an average weight of 28–30 kg.

faq.question: What coat does an Artois Hound have?
faq.answer: The standard describes a short, dense, fairly flat coat, typically dark-fawn tricolour with a mantle or large patches.

faq.question: Is the Artois Hound suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: A breed-specific yes-or-no recommendation is not recorded because reliable evidence was not found. Its stamina, scenting drive and vocal working style mean that daily activity, enrichment and the individual dog's behaviour should be assessed carefully.

faq.question: Which inherited diseases affect the Artois Hound?
faq.answer: The sources reviewed did not establish a dependable breed-specific list or prevalence estimates. Ask a veterinarian and a responsible breeder about the health history of the individual dog's family and any screening appropriate to the line.

overview.summary: A powerful, elegant, medium-to-large Swiss herding breed with a pure white double coat, erect ears, and a calm, attentive, deeply loyal character suited to active families and versatile canine sports.
overview.description: The Berger Blanc Suisse (White Swiss Shepherd Dog) is a well-muscled, medium-to-large shepherd dog combining athletic power with an elegant, harmonious outline. Slightly rectangular in proportions—with a body length to withers height ratio of 12:10—it features a level, firm topline, a finely sculpted wedge-shaped head, erect triangular ears, and a bushy sabre tail reaching at least to the hock. The weather-resistant double coat is pure white and occurs in two varieties: a dense medium-length coat (Stockhaar) and a longer coat (Langstockhaar) with a distinct neck mane and leg breeches. Lively, attentive, and socially adaptable, it bonds deeply with its household and remains watchful without unprovoked aggression, thriving on daily outdoor activity, positive training, and close human companionship.
overview.history: The breed shares ancestral roots with the German Shepherd Dog, in which white-coated individuals were recorded in the late nineteenth century. After white colouring was struck from European shepherd standards in 1933, white shepherd dogs were preserved and selectively bred in the United States and Canada as an independent population. In the early 1970s, dogs from North America were imported to Switzerland; an American-bred male named Lobo (whelped 5 March 1966) was brought by Agatha Burch and became the foundational progenitor of the Swiss lines. The breed multiplied across Europe and was registered in the Swiss Stud Book appendix from June 1991. Demonstrating eight independent ancestral maternal lines, Switzerland achieved definitive international recognition for the breed in 2011 as its official country of origin.

nutrition.guidelines: Provide measured portions of a nutritionally balanced diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. health.overview: The Berger Blanc Suisse is fundamentally a robust and athletic breed with an average lifespan of 10 to 14 years. Because it shares ancestral genetic roots with the German Shepherd Dog while having been bred independently for decades, primary health management and pre-breeding screening focus on orthopedic health (hip and elbow dysplasia), hereditary spinal neuropathy (degenerative myelopathy, DM), and the multi-drug resistance 1 (MDR1) gene mutation. Official breed clubs in Switzerland, Europe, and North America mandate or strongly recommend pre-breeding radiographic screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA testing for DM and MDR1, veterinary eye examinations, and cardiac evaluations.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: a developmental orthopedic malformation evaluated prior to breeding via radiographic scoring; health registry data indicates hips average tighter than ancestral German Shepherd stock
Elbow dysplasia: developmental elbow joint disease (fragmented medial coronoid process, ununited anconeal process, or osteochondritis dissecans), monitored through pre-breeding radiographic clearance

Multi-Drug Resistance 1 (MDR1 / ABCB1 gene mutation): a transport protein defect causing sensitivity and neurotoxicity to certain antiparasitic agents (such as high-dose ivermectin), loperamide, acepromazine, and chemotherapy drugs
Degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1 mutation): a late-onset, progressive spinal cord neuropathy causing hind-limb ataxia and weakness in older dogs, monitored via DNA screening

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat): an acute, life-threatening emergency in deep-chested dogs where the stomach distends with gas and twists; manageable through divided meals and resting around exercise
Cardiac abnormalities: subaortic stenosis, aortic stenosis, and heart murmurs have been detected in some lines, warranting veterinary cardiac auscultation and optional echocardiography
Ophthalmic and dental conditions: occasional cataracts or eyelid abnormalities, as well as missing premolars (PM1) or bite irregularities evaluated in conformation
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents hold documented health clearances for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA test certificates for MDR1 and DM, and current veterinary eye and cardiac examinations.
Determine the dog's MDR1 status before administering certain prescription drugs, or inform your veterinarian to avoid known neurotoxic medications (such as high-dose ivermectin and loperamide).
Raise puppies on non-slip surfaces and avoid forced high-impact jumping or prolonged stair climbing until growth plates have closed.
Feed multiple smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous running immediately before or after eating to reduce bloat risk.
Maintain a lean body condition and keep vaccinations, dental hygiene, and routine veterinary wellness visits up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic certification via recognized national or international veterinary scoring schemes prior to breeding)
Elbow dysplasia evaluation (radiographic screening via recognized veterinary scoring schemes prior to breeding)
Multi-Drug Resistance 1 (MDR1 / ABCB1 mutation) DNA test
Degenerative Myelopathy (DM / SOD1 mutation) DNA test
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (specialist eye registry scheme)
Basic or advanced cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist
Optional dentition evaluation and screening for inherited bleeding disorders (Von Willebrand's disease and Hemophilia A)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule veterinary dental checks. The breed standard calls for a strong, complete scissor bite of 42 teeth set square to the jaws (missing more than two PM1 is a severe fault; over- or undershot bites and wry mouth are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Inspect the erect triangular ears regularly for wax accumulation, dirt, redness, or odour, and clean gently only as needed using a veterinarian-approved ear cleaner.
health.skinCare: The dense double coat naturally repels dried dirt and protects the skin. Brush weekly (daily during shedding season) to remove loose undercoat, inspect the skin for parasites, cuts, or hot spots, and never shave the coat for routine convenience.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who spend significant daily time outdoors and include their dog in activities
Owners interested in obedience, rally, agility, tracking, mantrailing, or search-and-rescue training
Handlers who appreciate a sensitive, intelligent companion that responds to gentle, positive reinforcement
Households prepared for regular brushing and heavy twice-yearly seasonal undercoat shedding
Homes where someone is present for much of the day to provide companionship
notIdealFor: Sedentary households unable to provide substantial daily physical exercise and mental engagement
Homes where the dog would be left isolated outdoors, confined in a kennel, or alone for long workdays
Handlers who rely on harsh, forceful, or punitive training methods
People intolerant of dog hair indoors during seasonal coat blows

funFacts: Although the breed's historical roots trace to white-coated herding dogs in North America and Europe, Switzerland proved eight independent breeding lines to become recognized as its official country of origin.
A white male puppy named Lobo, whelped in the United States on 5 March 1966, was imported to Switzerland by Agatha Burch and became the foundational ancestor of the modern European population.
Despite its striking pure white coat, the breed is not an albino; official standards call for dark skin pigmentation with black eye rims, lips, and nose leather.

White coats were originally disqualified from the German Shepherd standard in Europe in 1933, leading North American fanciers to preserve the white lineage before it was reintroduced to Switzerland in the 1970s.

The breed exists in two distinct double-coat varieties—medium-length (Stockhaar) and long-coat (Langstockhaar, featuring an elegant neck mane and bushy tail)—both of which naturally shed dried dirt once dry.
Known for high social competence and versatility, the breed excels across a wide spectrum of canine sports, including agility, mantrailing, obedience, and search-and-rescue.

faq.question: What is a Berger Blanc Suisse?
faq.answer: The Berger Blanc Suisse (White Swiss Shepherd Dog) is a medium-to-large, white-coated herding breed that originated from North American white shepherd bloodlines and was formally developed and recognized in Switzerland as an independent companion and family dog.

faq.question: How big does a Berger Blanc Suisse get?
faq.answer: Conformation standards specify a withers height of 58 to 66 cm (about 23 to 26 inches) and an approximate weight of 30 to 40 kg (66 to 88 pounds) for males, and 53 to 61 cm (about 21 to 24 inches) and an approximate weight of 25 to 35 kg (55 to 77 pounds) for females.

faq.question: How does the Berger Blanc Suisse differ from the German Shepherd?
faq.answer: While sharing ancestral origins, the Berger Blanc Suisse has been recognized as a distinct breed for decades with its own closed studbooks and standard. Conformationally, it requires a pure white coat, a level backline without an exaggerated slope, and more moderate angulation. Temperamentally, it was bred specifically as a gentle, socially adaptable family companion rather than for bite work.

faq.question: What coat varieties does the breed have?
faq.answer: The breed has two accepted double-coat varieties: a dense medium-length coat (Stockhaar) and a long coat (Langstockhaar), the latter featuring a distinct neck mane, leg feathering ('trousers'), and a very bushy tail. Both varieties possess an abundant undercoat.

faq.question: What is the temperament of the Berger Blanc Suisse?
faq.answer: The breed is known for its balanced, attentive, and lively disposition. It is deeply devoted to its family, gentle with children, highly trainable, and alert without unprovoked aggression, though it can be sensitive to harsh handling.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Berger Blanc Suisse need?
faq.answer: As an active and intelligent shepherd breed, it requires substantial daily physical activity—such as brisk walks, hiking, and off-leash running in secure areas—combined with mental enrichment through obedience, agility, or scent tracking.

faq.question: Can a Berger Blanc Suisse live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes, provided it receives sufficient daily outdoor exercise, mental stimulation, and close companionship with its family, as it is generally calm and quiet indoors.

faq.question: Does the Berger Blanc Suisse shed a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. The dense double coat sheds moderately year-round and blows its entire undercoat heavily roughly twice a year over several weeks, during which daily brushing is recommended.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Parent-club health guidelines recommend radiographic screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA testing for the multi-drug resistance 1 (MDR1) mutation and degenerative myelopathy (DM), veterinary eye examinations, and cardiac evaluations.

faq.question: How long does a Berger Blanc Suisse live?
faq.answer: The average life expectancy is 10 to 14 years when provided with appropriate nutrition, regular exercise, weight management, and preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: Is the Berger Blanc Suisse easy to train?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed is exceptionally intelligent, eager to please, and responsive to positive reinforcement and food rewards. However, because of its sensitive nature, training must be patient and encouraging rather than punitive.

overview.summary: The Bernese Mountain Dog is a large, long-coated Swiss working breed known for its striking black, white and rust markings, steady nature and close bond with its family. Developed for practical farm work, it can be a devoted companion when its size, coat care, exercise and health needs are well managed.
overview.description: Powerful but balanced in build, the Bernese Mountain Dog has a long, dense coat, dark eyes, pendant ears and distinctive tricolour markings. The ground colour is black, with rich rust markings and clear white areas arranged in a characteristic pattern. Historically associated with farms around the Swiss canton of Bern, the breed helped guard property, move cattle and pull loads. Many individuals are affectionate and calm with familiar people, but they are still large, strong dogs that benefit from early training, sensible exercise and thoughtful socialisation. Their thick coat needs regular care, and prospective owners should be prepared for a relatively short expected lifespan compared with many smaller breeds.
overview.history: The Bernese Mountain Dog developed as an all-purpose farm dog in the pre-Alpine and lowland areas around Bern, Switzerland. It was historically known as the Dürrbächler, a name associated with the Dürrbach area where dogs of this type were numerous. Dogs of the breed appeared at shows in the early 1900s, and enthusiasts formed a club in 1907 to promote consistent breeding. The name Bernese Mountain Dog became established as the breed gained recognition beyond its original region.
overview.originalPurpose: Farm guarding, cattle driving, and draft work such as pulling carts or loads.
currentRoles: Therapy or community work for suitable, trained individuals

physical.coatType: Long, dense double coat with a moderately long outer coat and a woolly undercoat.
physical.coatLength: Long, moderately soft, straight or slightly wavy.
coatColors: White markings on the head, chest, feet and tail tip in the characteristic tricolour pattern
physical.sheddingLevel: High, with heavier seasonal shedding.
distinctiveFeatures: Large, strong, well-balanced working-dog build
Long, dense coat with a black, rust and white tricolour pattern
White facial blaze and chest markings are characteristic
Dark brown, almond-shaped eyes
Medium-sized, high-set triangular ears that hang close to the head when relaxed
Broad, deep chest and strong limbs
Bushy tail reaching at least to the hocks
A compact body proportion, with the body slightly longer than the height at the withers

traits: Affectionate and devoted to familiar people
Generally calm and steady when appropriately socialised
Attentive and watchful
Confident in ordinary situations
Often friendly and gentle with family members
May be reserved or composed around unfamiliar people
Intelligent and usually responsive to reward-based training
People-oriented and often happiest when included in family activities

exercise.level: Moderate. Regular daily movement and family activities are important, but exercise should be adjusted for age, health, weather and individual fitness. Growing puppies should not be pushed into strenuous repetitive exercise.
activities: Daily walks at a comfortable pace
Sniffing and exploration in safe areas
Hiking on suitable routes once the dog is physically mature and conditioned
Reward-based obedience and training games
Carting or draft activities with appropriate training and equipment
Low-impact play and enrichment adapted to age and joint health

grooming.level: Moderate to high, especially during seasonal shedding.
grooming.brushing: Brush at least weekly to remove loose hair and help prevent tangles. Brush more frequently during heavy shedding periods, paying attention to areas where the coat can mat, such as behind the ears, around the hindquarters and under the legs.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using a dog-formulated shampoo and rinse the dense coat thoroughly. Make sure the undercoat dries fully, particularly in cool or humid conditions.
notes: Expect substantial hair around the home, with heavier shedding periods during the year.
Check the skin and coat during brushing for mats, irritation, ticks or unusual lumps.
Trim nails regularly and inspect paw pads after outdoor activities.
Check ears for redness, odour, discharge or persistent scratching.
Brush teeth regularly with dog toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental care as needed.
Avoid shaving the double coat for routine cooling; ask a veterinarian or qualified groomer about coat problems or medical exceptions.

training.difficulty: Moderate. The breed is often eager to work with its people, but its large adult size makes early manners, leash skills and calm behaviour especially important.
tips: Start reward-based training and positive socialisation early, before the dog becomes physically powerful.
Teach loose-leash walking, recall, settling and polite greetings in manageable steps.
Avoid harsh corrections; use consistent cues, rewards and short, successful sessions.
Introduce handling for brushing, nail care, ear checks and veterinary examinations gradually.
Manage jumping and pulling before they become difficult habits in a large adult dog.
Keep activity appropriate to growth and health; ask a veterinarian for guidance on strenuous exercise during development.
training.socialization: Introduce puppies and young dogs to people, surfaces, sounds, transport, handling and suitable dogs in a gradual, positive way. Supervise interactions with children because even a friendly large dog can accidentally knock a child over. Give the dog space and reward calm behaviour rather than forcing contact.

climates: Generally better suited to cool or temperate conditions than prolonged hot weather because of the dense double coat.
In hot weather, provide shade, ventilation, fresh water and exercise during cooler periods.
Avoid leaving the dog in a hot vehicle or exposed outdoor space during high temperatures.
Provide a comfortable indoor resting area and monitor the individual dog's comfort in both hot and cold conditions.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: This is a people-oriented breed. Build time alone gradually, provide a safe resting space and suitable enrichment, and avoid routinely leaving the dog isolated for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity and veterinary needs. Large-breed puppy food is generally appropriate during growth when recommended for the individual puppy.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Use an age-appropriate complete puppy diet and follow its feeding guidance with veterinary advice. Divide the daily amount into suitable meals for the puppy's age and appetite.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured meals on a consistent schedule and adjust the total amount to maintain a healthy body condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a diet and feeding routine based on age, activity, body condition and any health conditions, with veterinary advice when needed.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure portions rather than feeding by guesswork, keep fresh water available, and monitor body condition as the dog grows. Avoid excessive calorie intake during growth and adulthood. Make dietary changes gradually and consult a veterinarian for individual calorie targets, persistent weight changes or special dietary needs.
considerations: Account for training treats and chews in the daily calorie intake.
Monitor growth and body condition rather than trying to maximise a puppy's growth rate.
Ask a veterinarian about feeding routines around vigorous exercise, particularly if the dog has digestive or other health concerns.
Do not add supplements or use restrictive diets without an appropriate reason and veterinary guidance.
Keep foods that are unsafe for dogs out of reach.
nutrition.note: These are general canine nutrition recommendations, not a breed-specific veterinary diet or calorie prescription.

health.overview: Bernese Mountain Dogs have several documented breed health concerns, including orthopaedic disease and certain cancers. Hip and elbow dysplasia, some eye and cardiac disorders, degenerative myelopathy and histiocytic sarcoma are among the conditions considered in breed health programmes. These risks do not mean that every dog will develop a condition, and individual risk depends on genetics and other factors. Prospective owners should seek health-test information from responsible breeders and discuss preventive care with a veterinarian.

Elbow dysplasia

preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations appropriate to local veterinary guidance.
Discuss breed-relevant health testing and family health history when selecting a puppy or planning breeding.
Maintain a healthy body condition and use age-appropriate exercise to support joint health.
Seek prompt veterinary advice for persistent lameness, unusual lumps, unexplained weight loss, exercise intolerance or changes in behaviour.

Learn the emergency signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus, including a swollen abdomen, repeated unproductive retching, restlessness or sudden weakness, and seek emergency veterinary care if suspected.
Use parasite prevention appropriate to local risks and the dog's activities.

health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog toothpaste. Arrange veterinary dental checks and seek advice for persistent bad breath, gum inflammation, oral pain or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge or persistent scratching. Seek veterinary advice if signs of irritation or infection appear.
health.skinCare: Inspect the dense coat and skin during grooming for mats, parasites, irritation or unusual lumps. Contact a veterinarian about persistent skin changes or new or growing masses.

It is one of the four Swiss Mountain Dog breeds and is distinguished by its long coat.
Its original farm duties included guarding, driving cattle and pulling loads.
The breed's characteristic appearance combines a black ground colour with rust and white markings.
Its working background is reflected in activities such as carting, tracking and obedience.

faq.question: Where did the Bernese Mountain Dog originate?
faq.answer: It originated in Switzerland, particularly the farming areas around the canton of Bern, where it was used for practical farm work.

faq.question: How large does a Bernese Mountain Dog get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 64–70 cm for males and 58–66 cm for females. Published weight ranges vary by registry; the figures in this record are converted from an American Kennel Club profile.

faq.question: What colours does a Bernese Mountain Dog have?
faq.answer: The breed has a characteristic tricolour coat: black, with rust markings and white areas on the head, chest, feet and tail tip.

faq.question: How long does a Bernese Mountain Dog live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists an expected lifespan of 7–10 years. This is a population-level estimate, not a prediction for an individual dog.

faq.question: Does a Bernese Mountain Dog shed a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. Its dense double coat sheds noticeably, with heavier seasonal shedding. Regular brushing and more frequent grooming during shedding periods help manage loose hair and tangles.

faq.question: Is a Bernese Mountain Dog good with children?
faq.answer: Many are affectionate and gentle with family, including children, but temperament varies. Because the breed is large and strong, supervise interactions and teach children how to interact respectfully with dogs.

faq.question: Which health tests are relevant to the breed?
faq.answer: Breed-club guidance includes hip and elbow evaluations, eye and cardiac examinations, and degenerative myelopathy testing. Additional testing may be considered with veterinary guidance. Screening helps inform decisions but cannot guarantee that a dog will remain healthy.

faq.question: Can a Bernese Mountain Dog live in a hot climate?
faq.answer: It can be challenging because the breed has a dense double coat. In warm weather, provide shade, water, good ventilation and exercise during cooler hours, and watch carefully for signs of overheating.

overview.summary: The Black Mouth Cur is a muscular, agile American working dog known for its hunting ability, stamina, loyalty, and protective instincts. It generally suits an active home that can provide purposeful exercise, training, and clear boundaries.
overview.description: This medium-sized, short-coated working dog has a sturdy, athletic build, a broad head, drop ears, and a muzzle that is often darkly pigmented. Coat colours vary and can include shades of red, yellow, fawn, brown, black, buckskin, and brindle. The black muzzle is characteristic but is not present in every accepted colour pattern. Bred for practical work rather than an exaggerated appearance, the Black Mouth Cur is valued for stamina, courage, scenting ability, and versatility. Individual dogs can differ substantially in size, appearance, and working style, particularly across established bloodlines.
overview.history: The breed developed in the southern United States, where families used versatile cur-type dogs for practical work on farms and homesteads. Its precise origin is uncertain: accounts have associated its development with more than one southern state. Historically, these dogs helped track and hunt game and guard people, property, and livestock. The breed was recognised by the United Kennel Club in 1998.

faq.question: Is every Black Mouth Cur's muzzle black?
faq.answer: No. Dark muzzle pigmentation is characteristic, but accepted coat colours and markings vary, and not every dog has a solid black mask.

faq.question: Where did the Black Mouth Cur originate?
faq.answer: It developed in the southern United States. Its exact origin is uncertain, and historical accounts differ about the state where it first developed.

faq.question: Is the Black Mouth Cur a good choice for a low-activity home?
faq.answer: Usually not the easiest match. It is a working-type dog that generally benefits from regular physical activity, training, and mental enrichment.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Black Mouth Cur need each day?
faq.answer: A reliable breed-specific minute range is not established in this record. Needs vary with age, health, fitness, and working drive, so build a routine around the individual dog and consult a veterinarian when necessary.

faq.answer: The sources checked for this profile did not establish a sufficiently reliable list of breed-specific common conditions. Routine preventive veterinary care is still important.

overview.summary: A large, powerful scent hound recognised for its exceptional tracking ability, long drooping ears, loose facial skin and calm, affectionate temperament.
overview.description: The Bloodhound is a large, substantial dog with a long head, deeply hanging ears, loose skin and a short, weather-resistant coat. Its exceptional ability to follow human and animal scent trails over long distances has made it valuable in tracking, search and recovery work. At home, it is often gentle and affectionate with people, but its independent scent-driven nature can make it difficult to recall when an interesting trail is found. Bloodhounds benefit from patient reward-based training, regular walks that allow safe sniffing, and a securely enclosed outdoor area. Owners should also be prepared for considerable drooling, vocal baying, large-dog food and care requirements, and daily hygiene around the ears and facial folds.
overview.history: The modern Bloodhound is closely associated with the Saint-Hubert hounds developed in the Ardennes region of Belgium. Historical accounts describe these dogs as scent hounds maintained by monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert for tracking and hunting. Hounds of this type later became established in England, where the breed developed further and became known for its ability to follow difficult scent trails. Bloodhounds have been used to track wounded game and to search for missing people. Although the breed has ancient historical roots, claims about its exact early ancestry are not fully documented.
overview.originalPurpose: A scent hound for following game trails and tracking wounded animals, with a long-established role in human scent trailing and search work.

grooming.brushing: Brush approximately weekly using a rubber grooming mitt, hound glove or suitable soft-to-medium bristle brush. Increase brushing during seasonal shedding. Grooming should also include regular checks of the ears, eyes, skin folds, paws and nails.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed to remove dirt and manage coat odour. Use a dog-safe shampoo and rinse thoroughly. Clean facial and neck folds as appropriate and dry them carefully so moisture does not remain trapped against the skin.
notes: The short coat is relatively easy to maintain, but seasonal shedding can require more frequent brushing.
Inspect the long, hanging ears regularly for redness, odour, wax build-up or discharge.
Check the facial and neck folds frequently, gently clean soiled areas and dry thoroughly.
Pay attention to damp skin around the lips, jowls and loose facial folds.
Trim nails when needed and check the paws after outdoor exercise.
Keep fresh water and suitable clean-up materials available because many Bloodhounds drool heavily.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.
Introduce grooming and handling calmly from an early age.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Bloodhounds can learn well with patient reward-based training, but scent-driven independence may compete with recall and obedience.
tips: Use positive reinforcement, food rewards and praise.
Start puppy socialisation and basic training early.
Practise recall consistently, but do not rely on it alone near wildlife or interesting scent trails.
Use a secure leash and enclosed areas for exercise.
Include scent games and tracking activities to channel natural abilities.
Keep training sessions patient, clear and consistent.
Reward attention to the handler before introducing stronger distractions.
Teach calm behaviour and settling routines at home.
Avoid harsh corrections; sensitive dogs may respond poorly to intimidating methods.
Prepare for baying and howling by managing triggers and reinforcing appropriate quiet behaviours.
training.socialization: Provide gradual, positive exposure to different people, dogs, places, sounds and everyday handling. Supervise introductions to unfamiliar animals and children. Continue socialisation throughout adulthood while respecting the dog's individual response to new experiences.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate, but many Bloodhounds prefer companionship. Teach alone-time skills gradually, ensure the dog has appropriate activity and enrichment, and avoid routinely leaving it isolated for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced dog food suited to a large-breed dog's life stage, body condition, activity level and individual health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several smaller meals daily, with frequency adjusted to the puppy's age, growth and veterinary guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two or three smaller meals daily may be preferable to one large meal, particularly because deep-chested dogs are at risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus.
feedingFrequency.senior: Individualise meal frequency and portion size according to appetite, weight, activity, dental health and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions and use the food's feeding guidance as a starting point. Adjust the amount to maintain a healthy body condition, taking age, activity, food energy density and medical needs into account. Keep fresh water available. Because Bloodhounds are large and deep-chested, discuss ways to reduce gastric dilatation-volvulus risk with a veterinarian; avoid vigorous exercise around meals.
considerations: Avoid overfeeding and monitor body condition regularly.
Use a nutritionally appropriate large-breed puppy diet during growth.
Divide adult food into smaller meals rather than feeding one very large meal.
Avoid vigorous exercise immediately before or after meals.
Ask a veterinarian about gastric dilatation-volvulus risk and whether preventive gastropexy is appropriate for the individual dog.
Count training treats as part of the daily food allowance.
Prevent access to rubbish, unsafe food and objects the dog might swallow.
Do not add supplements or change diets for joint health without veterinary advice.
Adjust nutrition to the dog's actual body condition and health rather than relying only on a breed-average weight.
nutrition.note: No universal daily food quantity is given because calorie needs vary by age, body condition, food energy density, activity and medical history. A veterinarian can help individualise portions and feeding practices.

health.overview: Bloodhounds can be affected by several health concerns associated with large size, deep chest, loose facial skin and hanging ears. Important issues include gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat), hip and elbow dysplasia, ear infections and irritation within skin folds. Breed-club health surveys have also identified cancer among reported causes of death, although exact risks vary and some surveys involve limited numbers of dogs. Eye problems related to eyelid shape can occur as well. Health screening of breeding dogs and appropriate daily care help manage some risks, but neither guarantees that an individual dog will remain free of disease. GDV is a life-threatening emergency: a swollen abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness or sudden abdominal discomfort requires immediate veterinary care.
commonConditions: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat) — a life-threatening emergency in which the stomach expands and may twist. Large, deep-chested dogs are at risk.
Hip dysplasia — a developmental abnormality of the hip joint that can contribute to pain, arthritis and impaired mobility.
Elbow dysplasia — a group of developmental elbow-joint abnormalities that can cause pain, lameness and arthritis.
Recurrent ear infections (otitis) — the hanging ears can reduce ventilation and retain moisture, creating conditions that favour inflammation and infection.
Skin-fold dermatitis — moisture, friction and debris around the facial folds, lips and neck can contribute to irritation or infection.
Eyelid abnormalities, including entropion or ectropion — eyelid position and loose surrounding skin can cause irritation or expose the eye surface.
Cancer or neoplasia — reported in Bloodhound health surveys among important causes of death, but specific tumour types and the population-wide prevalence are not established by this record.
Eye disorders associated with the structure of the eyelids and surrounding tissues; the exact condition and treatment depend on veterinary examination.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary wellness checks and ask about the individual dog's joint, heart, eye and body-condition needs.
Learn the warning signs of GDV, including abdominal enlargement, unproductive retching, restlessness and abdominal pain; seek emergency veterinary help immediately if suspected.
Discuss feeding practices and preventive gastropexy with a veterinarian when appropriate for the individual dog.
Maintain a healthy body weight to reduce avoidable stress on joints.
Keep the ears clean and dry as advised by a veterinarian, especially after bathing or swimming.
Inspect and gently clean facial and neck folds as needed, drying them thoroughly.
Seek veterinary care for persistent ear odour, discharge, redness, squinting, eye discharge, skin irritation or lameness.
Provide regular physical activity suited to age and health and avoid pushing an overweight or unfit dog into strenuous exercise.
Keep vaccinations, parasite prevention and dental care appropriate to the dog's location, age and veterinary advice.
Ask breeders for documented hip, elbow and cardiac evaluation results rather than relying only on verbal assurances.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation for breeding dogs through an accepted programme such as OFA or an appropriate national equivalent.
Elbow dysplasia evaluation for breeding dogs.
Cardiac examination for breeding dogs, with the examiner and method selected according to current programme requirements and veterinary advice.
Veterinary ophthalmic examination of breeding stock is encouraged in some national breed-health guidance; confirm the current local recommendation.
Optional eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist where indicated by breeding plans, family history or current guidance.
Optional patellar luxation evaluation where indicated by the breeding-health programme.

Optional degenerative myelopathy (DM) DNA testing may be considered within an appropriate breeding programme; discuss interpretation and relevance with a veterinarian or veterinary genetic counsellor.
Screening recommendations differ by country and programme. Confirm the latest requirements with the relevant breed club or health-testing organisation before making breeding decisions.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and an appropriate toothbrush. Large dogs still need routine oral care. Ask a veterinarian to assess persistent bad breath, gum inflammation, tartar, oral discomfort or changes in eating. Home brushing does not replace professional dental examinations.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, discharge, excess wax, odour or discomfort. Keep the ears clean and dry using a suitable veterinary-approved product when appropriate. Ask a veterinarian for guidance if infections recur, and do not insert cotton swabs or other objects deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Inspect facial folds, the lips, jowls and neck routinely. Gently remove dirt or moisture with an appropriate soft cloth or pet-safe product, then dry the area thoroughly. Look for redness, odour, sores or persistent irritation and seek veterinary advice if changes continue. Check the rest of the short coat for parasites, lumps or unusual hair loss.

funFacts: The Bloodhound is also known as the Chien de Saint-Hubert.
Its long ears and loose facial skin are among its most recognisable physical features.
The breed is known for methodically following scent trails over long distances.
Bloodhounds have been used for both animal tracking and human scent-trailing.
Their deep voice can be expressed as baying or howling, not only ordinary barking.
The coat is short, dense and weather-resistant rather than long or heavily feathered.
Although commonly calm with familiar people, Bloodhounds can become highly persistent when following a scent.
Its distinctive head and neck folds require regular attention to cleanliness and dryness.

faq.question: Where does the Bloodhound originate?
faq.answer: The breed is associated with Belgium, particularly the Ardennes region and the historic hounds linked with the Abbey of Saint-Hubert.

faq.question: Why is the Bloodhound famous?
faq.answer: The breed is known for its exceptional sense of smell and ability to follow scent trails over long distances. It has been used to track animals and people and in properly trained search work.

faq.question: How big does a Bloodhound get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives ideal heights of 68 cm for males and 62 cm for females, with a tolerance of 4 cm in either direction. It lists male weight at about 46–54 kg and female weight at 40–48 kg. Other kennel-club standards may give somewhat different ranges.

faq.question: How long does a Bloodhound live?
faq.answer: A commonly published breed-level estimate is 10–12 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, environment and veterinary care.

faq.question: Is a Bloodhound a good family dog?
faq.answer: Bloodhounds are often gentle and affectionate with familiar people and can live successfully with children when well socialised. Because they are very large and powerful, interactions with children should always be supervised.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Bloodhound need?
faq.answer: It needs daily walks and opportunities to use its nose, explore safely and receive mental enrichment. Exercise should be adapted to age, fitness and medical condition; no single daily minute target is suitable for every Bloodhound.

faq.question: Does a Bloodhound drool a lot?
faq.answer: Yes, heavy drooling is common for this breed. Owners should be prepared for saliva around the mouth, bedding, furniture and after drinking or eating.

faq.question: Does a Bloodhound need a lot of grooming?
faq.answer: The short coat is relatively easy to maintain with regular brushing, but the ears and facial folds need frequent inspection and cleaning. Areas that become damp should be dried thoroughly.

faq.question: Can a Bloodhound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment living can be challenging because of the dog's size, vocal baying, drooling and exercise needs. A secure outdoor area and a household prepared for these requirements are generally a better fit.

faq.question: What health conditions should owners know about?
faq.answer: Important concerns include bloat or GDV, hip and elbow dysplasia, ear infections, skin-fold irritation and some eye disorders. Cancer has also been reported among important causes of death in breed surveys. These are risks to discuss with a veterinarian, not predictions that an individual dog will develop a disease.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip, elbow and cardiac evaluation results for breeding dogs. Depending on the programme, eye evaluations, patellar checks or degenerative myelopathy DNA testing may also be considered. Confirm current recommendations with the relevant breed club and veterinarian.

faq.question: How can I reduce the risk of bloat?
faq.answer: Discuss feeding routines and risk-reduction options with a veterinarian. Smaller meals, avoiding vigorous exercise around mealtimes and learning the emergency signs can be helpful. If GDV is suspected, seek emergency veterinary care immediately.

faq.question: Can a Bloodhound be trained to walk off-leash?
faq.answer: A Bloodhound may follow an interesting scent instead of responding to recall, even after training. Use a leash in unsecured areas and reserve off-leash activity for safely enclosed places.

faq.question: What kind of food is suitable for a Bloodhound?
faq.answer: Choose complete and balanced food appropriate for a large-breed dog and its life stage. Portion size should be adapted to body condition, activity and health. Ask a veterinarian about feeding routine and GDV risk.

breeds.name: Boykin Spaniel
breeds.group: AKC Sporting Group; UKC Gun Dog Group. Developed as a flushing and retrieving spaniel.

origin.region: South Carolina, especially the Camden and Wateree River area

overview.summary: A compact, athletic brown sporting spaniel from South Carolina, bred to flush and retrieve game on land and in water.
overview.description: The Boykin Spaniel is a medium-sized, energetic sporting dog developed in South Carolina for practical hunting work. Its manageable size, webbed feet, water confidence and enthusiasm for retrieving made it useful to hunters working from small boats and through marshes and wooded cover. Boykins are typically sociable, eager to work and responsive to reward-based training, but they need regular exercise, companionship and activities that engage their nose and retrieving instincts. Their wavy or curly brown coat is usually straightforward to maintain with routine brushing, while their pendant ears deserve regular checks, especially after swimming.
overview.history: The breed took shape in the early twentieth century around the Boykin community near Camden, South Carolina. A small stray dog found in Spartanburg was given to hunter Whitaker Boykin, whose work with the dog and later breeding helped establish a compact flushing and retrieving spaniel suited to local hunting and small boats. The Boykin Spaniel became South Carolina's official state dog in 1985. The breed was recognised by the United Kennel Club in 1985 and by the American Kennel Club in 2009.
overview.originalPurpose: Flushing upland game and retrieving waterfowl and other game in marshes, rivers, wooded cover and from small hunting boats.
currentRoles: Active family companion for households that provide exercise and training
Scent games, retrieving games and outdoor activities

grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty or after muddy or smelly outings, using a dog-safe shampoo and rinsing well. Dry the coat and ears thoroughly after swimming.

Brush out burrs and plant material after walks in long grass or woodland.
Trim nails as needed and check paws after running on rough ground.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.
Introduce grooming and ear handling positively from puppyhood.
Avoid removing protective coat unnecessarily.
