overview.summary: An ancient, agile, and sure-footed Sicilian hunting hound built on a square, long-limbed frame, prized for its rigid upright ears, monochromatic fawn coat, keen triple-sense hunting skill on volcanic rock, and affectionate bond with its household.
overview.description: The Cirneco dell'Etna (plural: Cirnechi) is a medium-sized primitive-type hunting dog from Sicily whose slender, chiseled elegance conceals remarkable physical hardiness and stamina. Built on a square outline where body length equals height at the withers, it stands high on lean, muscular legs because its upper arm is relatively short compared with its shoulder blade and forearm, leaving the brisket just above or level with the elbows. Its narrow, almost flat-topped head carries high-set, rigid triangular ears and small oval ochre, amber, or hazel eyes, while the coat, skin, nose, eye rims, lips, pads, and nails share a harmonious monochromatic fawn-to-flesh palette. In the field—especially across the jagged lava slopes of Mount Etna—the Cirneco is a tenacious wild-rabbit specialist that scans terrain by sight, pinpoints underground movement by hearing, and trails quarry by a powerful sense of smell, traditionally working in partnership with a ferret. Indoors, a well-exercised Cirneco is gentle, clean, playful, and deeply devoted to its people, often burrowing under blankets for warmth, though its intense prey drive requires secure fencing, leashed walks in open areas, and patient, reward-based training.
overview.history: Present in Sicily since antiquity, the Cirneco dell'Etna belongs to the ancient Mediterranean warren-hound group. Traditional cynological accounts proposed that prick-eared hunting dogs from pharaonic Egypt spread across the Mediterranean with Phoenician traders, while Greek coins minted across Sicilian cities between the fifth and second centuries BC, a dog skeleton dated to roughly 1500 BC near the Simeto River, and fourth-century AD Roman mosaics at Villa Romana del Casale in Piazza Armerina attest to hounds of this type on the island for millennia. Even the name Cirneco has been linked either to ancient Cyrene in North Africa (Kyrenaikos, mentioned by Aristotle) or to the Latin verb cernere / cirniri ('to sift' or 'search'). Modern genomic and phylogeographic studies confirm that the Cirneco dell'Etna is an autochthonous Sicilian population closely related to Malta's Kelb tal-Fenek (Pharaoh Hound) and the Segugio Italiano rather than modern Egyptian dogs. By 1932, the breed had grown scarce until Dr. Maurizio Migneco, a veterinarian in Adrano, published an urgent appeal in Il Cacciatore Italiano. Sicilian noblewoman Baroness Agata Paternò Castello dei Duchi di Carcaci ('Donna Aga') answered the call, gathering surviving working dogs from around Mount Etna and breeding selectively under the Aetnensis affix for 26 years. Working with zoologist Prof. Giuseppe Solaro, she established the first official breed standard in 1939—when the suffix dell'Etna was formally added—followed by the first Italian conformation champion (Aetnensis Pupa) in 1952, formation of a dedicated preservation society in Catania in 1951, definitive international recognition on 9 March 1956, and mandatory working trials for Italian championship titles from 1994. Introduced to North America in the late 1990s (with organized preservation and a dedicated studbook established in 1997–1998), the breed gained national recognitions in 2006 and 2015.
overview.originalPurpose: Searching for, scent-trailing, flushing, and pursuing wild rabbits and small furred or feathered game across jagged volcanic lava fields, dry-stone walls, and dense brush in Sicily (traditionally worked alongside a ferret).
currentRoles: Working wild-rabbit hunting dog in Sicily and field-trial competitor
Lure coursing and precision coursing competitor
Agility, rally, and reward-based obedience competitor
Active walking and hiking partner in securely managed settings

physical.coatType: Vitreous (glassy, stiff like horsehair) and dense single coat lying sleek and close to the body without feathering; short and smooth on the head, ears, and legs, and semi-long (approximately 2 to 2.5 cm / 1 inch) on the trunk and tail.
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Self-coloured fawn / tan in shades from light (wheaten, sand, or isabella dilutions) to dark (wheaten and honey-golden shades are traditionally prized, while deep mahogany is less desirable), optionally with a mixture of slightly lighter and darker hairs

Fawn / tan with white markings restricted to a white head blaze or mark, chest and/or throat mark, white feet/toes, tail tip, or belly (a white collar is less appreciated; solid brown/liver, black, brindle, or any black hairs or patches are disqualifying faults)
distinctiveFeatures: Square body outline in which body length from point of shoulder to buttock equals height at the withers, standing high on lean, muscular limbs with chest depth (~43% of withers height) slightly less than elbow-to-ground height

Dolichocephalic, lean, well-chiselled head measuring 4/10 of withers height (cephalic index under 50%), with an almost flat oval skull, parallel or slightly divergent craniofacial planes, a slight stop (~150°), and a pointed muzzle equal to (or at least 80% of) skull length

Very high-set, close-together, rigid triangular ears with thick basal cartilage, narrow tips tilting slightly backward, frontal openings, and parallel vertical axes when alert, measuring no more than half the total head length
Small, semi-laterally set oval eyes (~25° palpebral angle) in ochre, amber, or hazel harmonizing with the coat (never grey, brown, yellow, or blue/walleye)

Monochromatic pigment harmony across coat, fine taut skin, mucous membranes, rectangular flesh-to-brown nose, tight lips, oval eye rims, hard paw pads, and strong curved brown or flesh-coloured nails (any black pigment or total depigmentation is a disqualifying fault)
Slightly oval, well-knuckled, arched feet with hard pads and no hind dewclaws (foreleg dewclaws are retained in North American standards)

Low-set tail of nearly uniform thickness reaching to or slightly below the hock, carried sabre-fashion at rest and raised in a high scythe or trumpet curve over the back when alert (never curled into a ring over the back)
Characteristic springy, rapid trot and agile, sure-footed bounding gallop built for leaping across sharp volcanic lava rock

Withers height of 46–50 cm for males and 44–48 cm for females (with a ±2 cm tolerance to 44–52 cm and 42–50 cm internationally, and 18–20 inches [45.7–50.8 cm] for males and 17–19 inches [43.2–48.3 cm] for females in North America) and adult weight of 10–13 kg for males and 8–11 kg for females (20–28 lbs and 19–25 lbs in North American profiles)

traits: Affectionate, gentle, and deeply attached to its owner and family
Alert, vigilant, and observant
Lively, playful, and spirited
Strong-willed, resolute, and independent-minded
Keen, tenacious hunter driven by scent, hearing, and sight
Agile, athletic, and sure-footed on rough terrain
Inquisitive and mentally active
Responsive to patient, gentle, reward-based training
Can be reserved with strangers if not well socialized early
Warmth-seeking indoors (often burrowing under blankets)

exercise.level: Moderate to high
activities: Daily brisk leashed walks and hikes tailored to the dog's age, fitness, and weather
Free sprinting and interactive play with its owner in a securely fenced enclosure
Lure coursing and precision coursing trials
Scent work, nose work, and tracking exercises that engage the breed's primary hunting sense
Agility, rally, and reward-based obedience training
Interactive puzzle games and mental enrichment

grooming.brushing: Brush once a week with a soft-bristle brush or rubber hound glove to remove loose hair and dust and keep the short, vitreous coat sleek and gleaming.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally as needed using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, and dry thoroughly afterward so the thin-skinned, low-body-fat dog does not become chilled.
notes: The short, close-lying single coat has no feathering and requires minimal upkeep compared with long- or double-coated breeds.
During the seasonal molt, slightly lighter, undefined coat patches may temporarily appear on the shoulders, sides of the neck, or thighs.
Inspect the large, erect, open-fronted ears every week for dust, plant debris, excess wax, redness, or odour, and clean gently if needed with soft gauze and a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser.
Trim nails frequently if they do not wear down naturally on hard ground, as overly long nails cause foot discomfort and splaying.
Check the paw pads and interdigital spaces after runs over rocky, thorny, or hot terrain.
Brush teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm, reward-based handling.

training.difficulty: Moderate; quick to learn and often more biddable than many traditional sighthounds, yet independent-minded and powerfully motivated by hunting instincts
tips: Use patient, upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement; harsh physical or verbal corrections are counterproductive with this sensitive, primitive-type hound.
Give the dog a purposeful outlet—such as lure coursing, nose work, tracking, agility, rally, or obedience—to satisfy its inquisitive, working mind.
Practise recall in securely fenced enclosures, and never trust off-leash reliability near roads, highways, or open wildlife areas where a fleeting scent or movement can trigger an instant chase.
Provide secure physical fencing around yards, as Cirnechi are agile jumpers built to bound from rock to rock.
Supervise carefully and introduce household cats and small furry pets gradually, recognizing that high prey drive toward squirrels, rabbits, and outdoor cats is innate.
Start puppy training classes and broad socialization early so the dog develops confident manners around unfamiliar people and environments.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, positive exposure early in puppyhood to diverse people, friendly dogs, novel sights, sounds, and surfaces. Because primitive hunting hounds raised in isolation can become wary or diffident toward strangers, consistent early socialization is essential to nurture an outgoing, confident companion.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Despite its independent working drive in the field, the Cirneco bonds closely with its family, loves to stay alongside its people indoors, and should never be left isolated alone in a backyard or kennel for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), activity level, and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and workload. Monitor body condition so the dog maintains its lean, athletic silhouette with visible musculature and a gently rising underline without excess weight. Keep clean, fresh drinking water available at all times, and consult a veterinarian or breeder regarding individual portion sizes and diet questions.
considerations: Active coursing, hunting, or agility dogs require higher caloric intake than dogs in lighter companion routines.
Count training treats within the daily calorie allowance to prevent unwanted weight gain.
Avoid feeding unsafe human foods, cooked bones, or rich table scraps.
Transition between diets gradually over several days unless directed otherwise by a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian if unexplained weight loss, digestive upset, or changes in appetite occur.
nutrition.note: No universal numerical daily meal schedule is prescribed for puppies, adults, or seniors; determine meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian based on the individual dog and food.

health.overview: The Cirneco dell'Etna is widely regarded as a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 15 to 16 years and a historically low incidence of documented hereditary disease. In North America, no routine breed-wide health test requirements are currently mandated, while in Italy selected breeding registration (Riproduzione Selezionata) from 18 months of age requires radiographic hip dysplasia grading of HD A or B. However, because the global population derives from a relatively small gene pool—with genomic studies showing higher homozygosity in self-coloured fawn lines than in tan-and-white blazed lines—responsible breeders monitor genetic diversity and emerging research closely. In February 2024, a peer-reviewed genomic study identified an autosomal recessive frameshift deletion in exon 15 of the AMPD2 gene on chromosome 6 (c.2131delG / p.D711Mfs12Stop) as the likely cause of Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS) in two male littermates that developed episodic head tremors and forelimb dyskinesia/atypical seizures at 2 to 2.5 years of age followed by progressive retinal degeneration (PRA) and cerebral white-matter thinning by 4 years of age. Genotyping of 35 Cirnechi found the variant only in the two affected littermates and three related carriers (including their shared grandmother and a related European dog), indicating that the mutation likely originated within a specific bloodline rather than being widespread across the breed. A targeted AMPD2 DNA test is available to help breeders screen breeding stock, prevent carrier-to-carrier matings, and avoid creating a genetic bottleneck.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary wellness examinations and maintain appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention protocols (including vector protection against Leishmania infantum in endemic Mediterranean regions).
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and provide safe, enclosed exercise to prevent traffic trauma—one of the primary real-world hazards for high-prey-drive hounds.

Monitor adult dogs for any episodic head bobbing, tremors, forelimb cramping, cervical pain, or signs of dim-light vision loss, and discuss targeted AMPD2 genetic testing or specialist ophthalmic and neurological evaluation with a veterinarian if signs or family history warrant.

For breeders, utilize pedigree analysis, genomic diversity tools, hip evaluations (where required for selected breeding), and AMPD2 carrier testing thoughtfully so deleterious recessive variants are managed without narrowing the breed's small gene pool.
Inspect the upright ears weekly for dirt or wax buildup, brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste, and keep nails trimmed short.
Check paw pads, nails, and thin skin for cuts, thorns, or abrasions after running on rocky or brushy terrain, and provide a warm coat in cold or wet weather.
recommendedScreenings: No routine breed-wide mandatory health test panel is currently established in North American registration programs.
Hip dysplasia radiographic screening (graded HD A or B) is required from 18 months of age for dogs entering the Italian Selected Breeding Register (Riproduzione Selezionata).

Targeted DNA testing for the AMPD2 frameshift variant (c.2131delG on chromosome 6, associated with Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome / CONS) is recommended by veterinary geneticists and breed health foundations to monitor allele frequency and avoid carrier-to-carrier matings, particularly in related bloodlines.
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist and neurological assessment are advised for any dog displaying visual deficits, tremors, or paroxysmal movement episodes.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth frequently using dog-specific toothpaste and a soft canine toothbrush, and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require a complete, regular scissor bite with incisors set square to the jaws (absence of PM1 and M3 premolars/molars is permissible under international rules).
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, rigid upright ears every week for dust, plant awns, excess wax, redness, or unusual odour, especially after field runs. Clean gently when needed using soft gauze and a veterinarian-recommended ear-cleaning solution, and never insert cotton swabs deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Examine the fine, taut skin and short, vitreous coat during weekly brushing for scratches, ticks, or irritation, noting that minor honourable working scars are never penalized in conformation. Protect the paw pads on rough lava rock or hot pavement, and provide warm bedding and cold-weather clothing when temperatures drop.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who enjoy daily walks, hiking, lure coursing, scent work, or agility
Experienced hound or primitive-breed handlers who appreciate a lively, alert, independent-minded companion
Households with a securely fenced yard or consistent access to safe, enclosed running areas
Owners who want an affectionate, clean, low-odour indoor dog that loves cuddling under blankets after exercise
People committed to patient, gentle, reward-based training and careful management around wildlife
notIdealFor: Owners seeking reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas near roads or wildlife
Households with cats, rabbits, or small furry pets where strong chasing instincts cannot be safely managed
Sedentary homes unable to provide daily physical exercise and mental stimulation
People who plan to leave a dog isolated outdoors or alone for long workdays without companionship
Handlers who use harsh, forceful, or punitive training methods

funFacts: Between the fifth and second centuries BC, Greek cities across Sicily minted hundreds of coin varieties bearing the image of a prick-eared hound remarkably similar to the modern Cirneco dell'Etna.

The breed takes its name from Mount Etna, Europe's largest active volcano on the east coast of Sicily, where it leaps sure-footedly across jagged volcanic lava fields in pursuit of wild rabbits; the suffix 'dell'Etna' was officially added when the first breed standard was approved in 1939.

In 1932, after Adrano veterinarian Dr. Maurizio Migneco warned that the ancient Sicilian hound was nearing extinction, Baroness Agata Paternò Castello dei Duchi di Carcaci ('Donna Aga') spent 26 years reviving the breed under her Aetnensis kennel affix.

Unlike pure sighthounds that rely mainly on vision, the Cirneco is a triple-sense hunter: it scans the landscape by sight, listens through its rigid upright ears for rabbits moving underground, and relies primarily on its keen nose to track and flush quarry.

In traditional Sicilian rabbit hunting, the Cirneco works in a classic partnership with a ferret: once the dog locates a rabbit deep inside a lava crevice or burrow and signals with excited barks, it steps aside and waits silently while the handler releases the ferret to bolt the quarry.

Every part of a Cirneco dell'Etna is meant to be monochromatic: its coat, skin, nose leather, eyelid rims, lips, paw pads, nails, and amber-to-ochre irises all harmonize in shades of fawn, tan, and flesh, and any trace of black pigment is a disqualification.

A 2021 Italian genomic study found that the Cirneco dell'Etna is genetically closest to Malta's Kelb tal-Fenek (Pharaoh Hound) and the Segugio Italiano, and identified the MITF gene as the primary locus distinguishing tan-and-white blazed Cirnechi from self-coloured fawn dogs.

faq.question: Where does the Cirneco dell'Etna originate, and what does its name mean?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the island of Sicily in southern Italy, particularly the volcanic slopes around Mount Etna. The word 'Cirneco' (pronounced 'cheer-NEK-oh', plural 'Cirnechi') is thought to derive either from ancient Cyrene in North Africa (Kyrenaikos / Cyrenaecus) or from the Latin verb cernere / cirniri ('to sift' or 'search'), while 'dell'Etna' was added in 1939 to honour its volcanic homeland.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna a sighthound or a scent hound?
faq.answer: Although often informally called the 'Sicilian Greyhound' and eligible for sighthound lure coursing, the Cirneco is classified internationally as a primitive-type hunting dog that hunts primarily by scent, while also using its acute hearing to detect rabbits underground and its keen sight to scan rocky terrain and course flushed game.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Cirneco dell'Etna?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 46 to 50 cm for males and 44 to 48 cm for females (with a ±2 cm tolerance resulting in an overall range of 44 to 52 cm for males and 42 to 50 cm for females) and an adult weight of 10 to 13 kg for males and 8 to 11 kg for females. North American standards specify 18 to 20 inches (45.7–50.8 cm) and 20 to 28 pounds (9.1–12.7 kg) for males, and 17 to 19 inches (43.2–48.3 cm) and 19 to 25 pounds (8.6–11.3 kg) for females.

faq.question: How long does a Cirneco dell'Etna typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 15 to 16 years, making the Cirneco dell'Etna a notably long-lived medium-sized breed.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are allowed in the Cirneco dell'Etna?
faq.answer: Accepted colours are self-coloured fawn or tan ranging from light wheaten, sand, or isabella to dark tan (with wheaten and honey-golden shades traditionally prized and deep mahogany less desired), as well as fawn/tan with white markings on the head (blaze), chest, throat, feet, tail tip, or belly (a white collar is less appreciated). Nose, eye rims, lips, pads, and nails must be flesh-coloured to brown; any black pigment, solid brown/liver, or brindle coat is a disqualification.

faq.question: How does a Cirneco dell'Etna differ from a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The two breeds are close Mediterranean cousins from neighbouring islands—the Cirneco from Sicily and the Pharaoh Hound (Kelb tal-Fenek) from Malta—and share an upright-eared, amber-eyed, tan-coated appearance. However, the Cirneco dell'Etna is substantially smaller and lighter (standing 44–50 cm and weighing 8–13 kg, compared with 53–63.5 cm and 20–25 kg for the Pharaoh Hound) and is built on a square 1:1 outline rather than the Pharaoh Hound's slightly longer rectangular profile.

faq.question: Does the Cirneco dell'Etna require much grooming?
faq.answer: Very little. Its short, sleek, vitreous coat stays clean with a quick weekly brushing using a soft bristle brush or hound glove and an occasional bath as needed. Weekly ear checks, frequent nail trimming, and regular tooth brushing complete its routine care.

faq.question: Can a Cirneco dell'Etna be trusted off-leash in open areas?
faq.answer: No. Because the breed was selected for millennia to pursue rabbits independently across rugged terrain, a fleeing squirrel, rabbit, or cat can instantly override recall training. Off-leash running should be restricted to securely fenced enclosures far from road traffic.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna good with cats and small pets?
faq.answer: Caution is essential. While some Cirnechi raised from puppyhood with an indoor cat coexist peacefully under supervision, the breed's innate drive to chase small furry animals is very strong, and outdoor cats or small pets may be viewed as quarry.

faq.question: What is Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS), and what health tests exist for the breed?
faq.answer: Historically, the breed has had very few reported hereditary diseases and no mandatory North American screening panel (while Italian selected breeding requires HD A or B hip scores). In 2024, researchers identified an autosomal recessive frameshift deletion in the AMPD2 gene on chromosome 6 causing Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS) in two male littermates that developed episodic head tremors and forelimb movement episodes at 2 to 2.5 years of age and progressive retinal degeneration by 4 years of age. Genotyping showed the mutation was confined to the affected family and three related carriers rather than widespread across the breed, and a targeted AMPD2 DNA test is now available to help breeders avoid carrier-to-carrier matings.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes, provided its daily need for brisk leashed walks, enclosed running play, and mental enrichment is met. Indoors, a well-exercised Cirneco is calm, clean, affectionate, and fond of curling up under blankets next to its owners.

overview.summary: A cheerful, intelligent, and deeply affectionate small companion dog from southwestern Madagascar, distinguished by its soft, cotton-textured coat, expressive dark eyes, and devoted bond with its household.
overview.description: The Coton de Tulear is a sturdy, small, long-coated companion breed built on a rectangular outline where height at the withers is roughly two-thirds of the body length. Beneath its profuse, supple white coat—which has the dry, airy feel of a natural cotton boll rather than silky or woolly hair—lies a well-muscled frame with a slightly convex topline that arches gently over a short loin to a low-set tail. Round, dark, wide-set eyes and black-pigmented lips and eyelids give the face a bright, inquisitive expression. Lively, stable, and highly sociable with people and other dogs, Cotons are renowned for their clownish antics, habit of walking on their hind legs to please their owners, and repertoire of purr-like, grunting, and trilling vocalizations. While their compact size adapts well to apartments and houses alike, their coat requires committed brushing and their people-oriented nature calls for daily companionship, positive training, and interactive play.
overview.history: Originating on the island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa, the breed takes its name from the French word coton ('cotton') and the southwestern port city of Toliara, historically known as Tuléar. Around the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, small white European Bichon-type dogs travelled aboard merchant and pirate vessels sailing around the Cape of Good Hope into the Indian Ocean, serving both as shipboard ratters and as companions to passengers. Traditional island lore recounts that survivors of a shipwreck near Tuléar swam ashore, adapted in packs, and interbred with local island dogs, though exact early ancestry narratives remain undocumented in primary historical records. By the seventeenth century, these small white dogs had been adopted by the native Malagasy and the ruling Merina tribal monarchy, which restricted ownership to nobility and royalty—earning the breed the enduring title 'Royal Dog of Madagascar'. French colonists later brought specimens to France, leading to formal international breed recognition in 1970 (with the first international standard published in 1971), organized studbook preservation in North America beginning in 1976, introduction to the United Kingdom in 1987, and subsequent national recognitions in 1996 and 2014.
overview.originalPurpose: Companion dog of Malagasy royalty and nobility (with ancestral shipboard ratter and pack-foraging roots).
currentRoles: Canine sports competitor in agility, tracking, and freestyle dancing

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb gently all the way down to the skin 3 to 4 times per week—or daily when maintaining a full adult coat—using a quality pin brush (without balls on the pin tips, which can snag and tear the hair) and a metal comb. Mist the coat lightly with a leave-in spray conditioner before brushing to prevent hair breakage and mat formation next to the skin.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed using a gentle, dog-safe shampoo and conditioner formulated for long coats, rinse thoroughly, and dry the coat completely while brushing so damp hair does not felt or mat.
notes: Pay special attention to coat maintenance between 9 and 14 months of age, when the softer puppy coat transitions to the denser adult coat and matting risk is at its peak.
Inspect high-friction areas carefully during every brushing session, including behind the ears, under the collar or harness, around the elbows and armpits, in the groin, and down the legs.

Keep hair on the bottom of the feet and between the paw pads trimmed neat for traction and cleanliness; otherwise, the coat is traditionally kept in its natural, un-scissored state unless clipped into a shorter pet trim for easier upkeep.
Check the pendulous ears a couple of times each week for excess hair, wax, redness, odour, or debris to help prevent ear canal infections.
Trim nails regularly and accustom puppies early to gentle handling of their paws, face, ears, and tail.
Although low-shedding, no dog breed is completely non-allergenic; prospective owners with allergies should spend time around the breed before committing.

training.difficulty: Generally trainable and eager to please when taught with upbeat, reward-based methods
tips: Use positive reinforcement with small food rewards, play, and enthusiastic praise; Cotons are sensitive and shut down under harsh or negative corrections.
Keep training sessions short, lively, and varied so the dog stays mentally engaged and does not grow bored.
Channel their natural desire to entertain into trick training, rally, obedience, or agility.
Teach calm household manners and polite responses to doorway noises, as the breed is naturally alert and watchful of its home.
Condition puppies gradually to grooming brushes, combs, nail trims, tooth brushing, and baths as positive bonding routines.
Practice gradual alone-time conditioning early so the dog's close attachment to its people does not develop into separation distress.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to a wide variety of people, gentle children, friendly dogs, household sounds, travel, and novel environments so their naturally sociable, adaptable temperament flourishes.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Bred solely for human companionship, the Coton thrives as an indoor family member that follows its people from room to room; leaving the dog isolated for long workdays without gradual conditioning and enrichment can lead to boredom, vocalizing, or destructive behaviour.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), body size, and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. Because some individuals are prone to gaining excess weight, monitor body condition regularly, limit high-calorie table scraps, and account for training treats within the daily calorie allowance. Provide constant access to clean, fresh water.
considerations: Watch calorie intake and body condition closely to prevent overweight and unnecessary strain on the patellas, hips, and spine.
Keep training treats small and deduct them from the daily food ration.
Avoid feeding cooked bones or high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or pancreatitis.
Transition between foods gradually over several days unless directed otherwise by a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian promptly if sudden weight changes, picky eating, or excessive water consumption occur.
nutrition.note: A single universal meal schedule is not assigned because optimal feeding frequency depends on age, caloric density of the diet, activity level, and individual health; confirm portion sizes and daily meal counts with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Coton de Tulear is generally a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 15 to 19 years, and documented hereditary diseases occur at a relatively low incidence (often estimated at 1% to 5% in screened populations). Health management distinguishes between clinical orthopedic, ophthalmic, and cardiac conditions monitored through pre-breeding veterinary examinations—namely patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, inherited eye anomalies, and congenital cardiac murmurs—and specific autosomal recessive mutations for which validated DNA tests allow breeders to avoid carrier-to-carrier matings. Molecularly characterized recessive disorders in the breed include Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1 mutation), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (BEST1 mutation), and primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT mutation), alongside broader canine DNA tests for von Willebrand disease, degenerative myelopathy, hyperuricosuria, and FGF4 retrogene intervertebral disc disease predisposition.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation — a potential orthopedic issue in small breeds in which the kneecap slips out of its trochlear groove; veterinary patellar evaluation is a core pre-breeding requirement.
Hip dysplasia — reported occasionally in the breed and monitored through mandatory pre-breeding radiographic hip evaluation.

Ocular disorders and Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 2 (CMR2) — periodic veterinary ophthalmologist examinations screen for cataracts and retinal anomalies, while an autosomal recessive BEST1 gene mutation (c.482G>A) causes CMR2, producing discrete subretinal blisters around 15 weeks of age that typically stabilize by 1 year without causing blindness.

Cardiac abnormalities — congenital heart murmurs or valve defects are screened via pre-breeding veterinary cardiac evaluations; the screening requirement reflects preventive stewardship rather than high clinical prevalence.

Intervertebral disc disease (spinal disc disease) and FGF4 retrogene variants — back and disc problems are occasionally reported in the breed, and elective DNA testing is available for the chromosome 12 FGF4 retrogene (CDDY) associated with premature intervertebral disc degeneration as well as the chromosome 18 FGF4 retrogene (CDPA) associated with short-limbed chondrodysplasia.

Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (BNAt / NCA) — a severe autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia caused by a retrotransposon insertion in exon 8 of the GRM1 gene on chromosome 1; affected puppies exhibit intention tremors, head nodding, and inability to stand or walk from about 2 weeks of age, and a separate autosomal recessive juvenile cerebellar ataxia is also under genomic investigation.

Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH) — a rare, fatal neonatal autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a missense mutation (c.996G>A / p.Gly102Ser) in the AGXT gene, leading to calcium oxalate crystal accumulation and acute renal tubular necrosis at 3 to 4 weeks of age (identified with an 8.5% carrier rate in a Finnish study cohort).

Additional conditions included in elective pre-breeding genetic or clinical panels — type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), hyperuricosuria (HU / SLC2A9), autoimmune thyroiditis, elbow dysplasia, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
preventiveCare: Request documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents—covering veterinary ophthalmologist exams, patellar luxation, hip radiographs, cardiac evaluation, and relevant breed-appropriate DNA tests—before acquiring a puppy.
Maintain a lean body weight and healthy muscle tone through daily walks and portion control to minimize mechanical stress on the knees, hips, and spine.
Brush the coat thoroughly down to the skin several times a week to prevent painful mats that trap moisture and hide skin irritation.
Check and gently clean the drop ears a couple of times weekly to prevent wax accumulation and otitis externa.
Brush teeth regularly and schedule routine veterinary wellness and dental examinations throughout the dog's long lifespan.
Seek prompt veterinary evaluation for limping, skipping gaits, back pain, eye cloudiness or redness, coughing, or urinary changes.
recommendedScreenings: Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (core pre-breeding requirement, performed from 6 months of age and periodically thereafter).
Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement at 12 months of age or older).
Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement; preliminary radiographs before 24 months and final certification after 24 months of age).
Cardiac examination by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist (performed at 12 months of age or older prior to breeding).

Elective genetic and clinical evaluations based on lineage and breeding program requirements: DNA tests for Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (CMR2 / BEST1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH / AGXT), type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), hyperuricosuria (HU / SLC2A9), chondrodystrophy (CDDY / FGF4), and chondrodysplasia (CDPA / FGF4), as well as laboratory thyroid profiling, elbow radiographs, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes evaluation.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week—ideally daily—using dog-safe toothpaste and a small, soft canine toothbrush. Because small companion breeds are prone to plaque accumulation and periodontal disease over a 15- to 19-year lifespan, combine home brushing with regular veterinary dental assessments and professional cleanings when indicated.
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, pendulous triangular ears two to three times a week and after baths. Gently remove excess hair, wax, or debris as advised by a veterinarian, keep the ear canals dry, and seek veterinary care for redness, foul odour, discharge, or head shaking.
health.skinCare: Part the dense cottony coat down to the skin during brushing to check for hidden tangles, redness, parasites, or dry skin. Use a gentle dog shampoo and leave-in conditioning spray to keep the skin and hair supple, and ensure the coat is dried completely after bathing or rain.

funFacts: The breed's name combines the French word coton ('cotton'), referring to its soft, airy cotton-boll coat texture, with Tuléar (now Toliara), the southwestern Malagasy port city associated with its early history.
In seventeenth-century Madagascar, the ruling Merina monarchy restricted ownership of these small white dogs to royalty and nobility, earning the breed the title 'Royal Dog of Madagascar'.
Madagascar has honoured the Coton de Tulear as its Official National Dog and featured the breed on national postage stamps, including a well-known 1974 stamp issue.

Cotons are famous for two endearing habits when interacting with their families: rising up to walk or hop on their hind legs and conversing through unique purr-like, grunting, or trilling vocalizations.
Unlike several other Bichon-family breeds with flat backs, the Coton de Tulear has a distinctive slightly convex topline that rises gently over a short, muscular loin to a low-set tail.

Many Coton puppies are born with noticeable yellow, tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches on the head, ears, or body that gradually fade over their first 12 to 18 months, leaving an adult coat that is predominantly white or lightly shaded with champagne or grey on the ears.

faq.question: Where does the Coton de Tulear come from?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa. Its name refers to its cotton-like coat texture and the southwestern port city of Toliara, formerly called Tuléar.

faq.question: How big is an adult Coton de Tulear?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify an ideal withers height of 26 to 28 cm for males (with a tolerance of 25 to 30 cm) and 23 to 25 cm for females (with a tolerance of 22 to 27 cm), and an adult weight of 4 to 6 kg for males and 3.5 to 5 kg for females. North American standards list an ideal height of 10 to 11 inches (9–15 pounds) for males and 9 to 10 inches (8–13 pounds) for females, while some traditional Malagasy-type lines reach heights up to 12.5 or 13 inches (25–33 cm) and weights up to 14 or 18 pounds.

faq.question: How long does a Coton de Tulear typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 15 to 19 years, making the Coton de Tulear one of the longest-lived companion dog breeds.

faq.question: Does the Coton de Tulear shed, and is it hypoallergenic?
faq.answer: The breed sheds very little—primarily losing small amounts of hair during brushing or in springtime—and has hair rather than a typical fur undercoat. While many people with mild sensitivities tolerate the breed well, no dog is completely hypoallergenic because allergens are also carried in dander and saliva.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Coton de Tulear need?
faq.answer: Maintaining a full, flowing adult coat requires gentle brushing and combing all the way to the skin 3 to 4 times a week (or daily), misting lightly with a leave-in conditioner to prevent breakage and mats. Particular care is needed between 9 and 14 months of age when the puppy coat transitions to the adult coat. Owners who do not show their dogs often opt for a shorter 'puppy clip' to simplify daily maintenance.

faq.question: Is the Coton de Tulear suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes. Its small stature, moderate exercise needs, and polite indoor demeanor make it well suited to apartments as well as houses with yards, provided it receives daily walks, interactive play, and plenty of human companionship.

faq.question: Is the Coton de Tulear good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed is known for a stable, cheerful, and sociable temperament toward people, children, other dogs, and household cats. As with any small breed, interactions with young children should be supervised so the dog is handled gently.

faq.question: What health screenings and DNA tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Prospective buyers should ask for documented results of four core clinical evaluations—board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, patellar luxation evaluation, hip radiographs, and cardiac examination—along with relevant DNA tests used to prevent carrier-to-carrier matings, such as Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (CMR2 / BEST1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH / AGXT), von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM), and hyperuricosuria (HU).

faq.question: What colour is a Coton de Tulear, and why do puppies change colour?
faq.answer: In most conformation standards, the adult ground colour is white, with slight light-grey or light-tan/red-roan shading permitted on the ears and only minimal shading (up to 5% to 10%) tolerated on the body. Puppies are frequently born with darker tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches on the head and body controlled by colour-dilution genes; these markings progressively fade into white or pale champagne by 12 to 18 months of age. Some traditional Malagasy and North American lines also recognize black-and-white and tri-colour varieties.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Coton de Tulear need?
faq.answer: The breed is moderately active and thrives on daily leashed walks at a comfortable pace combined with indoor or backyard games such as fetching a ball, trick training, or agility. Rather than following a rigid daily minute quota, tailor the duration and pace of exercise to the individual dog's age, health, and conditioning.

overview.summary: The Drentsche Patrijshond is a medium-sized Dutch hunting dog developed to work closely with its handler in the field and retrieve game from land or water. It is known for its gentle character, intelligence, and close connection with its family. This breed generally suits people who can provide regular outdoor activity, kind training, and opportunities to use its natural scenting and retrieving abilities.
overview.description: This dog has a balanced, slightly elongated body, a moderately broad head, hanging feathered ears, and a bushy tail with long feathering. Its coat is dense and weather-resistant, with longer hair around the ears, chest, legs, and tail. The typical colour is white with brown markings, sometimes with ticking or spots. It was developed as a versatile hunting companion, and many individuals enjoy scent-based games, retrieving, and other activities that combine movement with cooperation.
overview.history: The breed traces its history to hunting dogs known in the Netherlands as partridge dogs, with roots described as far back as the sixteenth century. Dogs of this type were preserved in the eastern Netherlands, particularly in Drenthe, rather than being extensively mixed with other breeds. Formal recognition in the Netherlands followed in 1943, and the national breed association was established in 1948. The breed is related to other European hunting dogs, including the Small Münsterländer and the French Spaniel.
overview.originalPurpose: A versatile pointing and retrieving hunting dog designed to work within range of its handler, locate game, point, and retrieve from fields or water.
currentRoles: Outdoor activities with a closely involved handler

faq.question: What is a Drentsche Patrijshond?
faq.answer: It is a Dutch pointing and retrieving dog developed for versatile hunting work. It is also kept as a companion by people who can meet its exercise, training, and social needs.

faq.question: How large does a Drentsche Patrijshond get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 58–63 cm for males and 55–60 cm for females. Standard weights are 30–35 kg for males and 25–31 kg for females.

faq.question: What colour is the Drentsche Patrijshond?
faq.answer: The standard colour is white with brown markings, which may include spots or ticking. A brown mantle can occur but is less desired under the FCI standard.

faq.question: Is a Drentsche Patrijshond suitable for family life?
faq.answer: It can be a close family companion when its activity, training, and companionship needs are met. Individual temperament matters, and children should always be supervised around dogs.

faq.question: How much exercise does this breed need?
faq.answer: Many individuals benefit from substantial daily activity and mental enrichment. The 60–120 minute range in this record is an editorial estimate, not a verified breed-wide requirement. Adjust it to age, fitness, health, weather, and the individual dog.

faq.question: What grooming does it need?
faq.answer: Brush several times a week, especially around the ears, chest, legs, and tail where longer hair can collect debris or tangle. Check the coat and ears after outdoor work.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip and elbow assessments and an eye examination, including ECVO screening where applicable. Check the current breed-club requirements and discuss family history with your veterinarian.

faq.question: Is the Drentsche Patrijshond easy to train?
faq.answer: It is described as intelligent and gentle, but training still requires consistency and patience. Reward-based methods are a better fit than forceful handling, and recall should be trained carefully around wildlife.

overview.summary: An elegant, friendly sporting dog with a feathered coat, a gentle expression and a strong instinct for locating game birds.
overview.description: The English Setter is a medium-to-large sporting dog developed to search for game birds and indicate their location to a hunter. Its distinctive appearance combines a refined head, long silky feathering and a white coat patterned with fine flecks known as belton. At home, many English Setters are affectionate and sociable companions, while outdoors they can be energetic, curious and strongly interested in scents and birds. They usually do best with regular exercise, patient reward-based training, coat maintenance and close companionship. Their hunting instincts mean that a secure outdoor area and reliable recall training are especially important.
overview.history: The English Setter developed in England as a bird-finding dog. Earlier setters were trained to locate game and crouch or 'set' near it, allowing hunters to approach and use nets; later, the breed was adapted to work alongside firearms. Historical accounts describe the influence of older spaniel and pointer-type dogs, although the exact ancestry of the modern breed is not fully documented. Breeders in the nineteenth century helped establish recognisable lines for field work and exhibition. Today, English Setters continue to participate in hunting and field activities and are also kept as active companions.

faq.question: Is the English Setter a good family dog?
faq.answer: Many English Setters are affectionate and sociable companions. As with any breed, children and dogs should be supervised together, and the individual dog's temperament, training and needs matter.

faq.question: How much exercise does an English Setter need?
faq.answer: They are an active sporting breed and generally need substantial daily movement and mental enrichment. The 60–120 minutes listed here is a practical estimate, not a universal prescription; age, health and working activity change the amount needed.

faq.question: Does an English Setter shed?
faq.answer: Yes. Regular brushing helps remove loose hair and prevent tangles in the longer feathering.

faq.question: How often should an English Setter be brushed?
faq.answer: Brush several times a week as a starting point, checking the feathered areas for knots. Some coats need daily attention, especially after outdoor activity.

faq.question: What does belton mean?
faq.answer: Belton describes a flecked pattern on the coat, commonly seen as coloured speckling on a white ground.

faq.question: Are English Setters easy to train?
faq.answer: They can respond well to patient, reward-based training. Their interest in birds and scents can make recall and focus challenging outdoors, so practise gradually and use secure areas.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask about hip and elbow evaluation, thyroid evaluation and BAER hearing testing. Discuss the results and their relevance with a veterinarian; screening reduces uncertainty but cannot guarantee future health.

faq.question: Can an English Setter live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment living suitability depends on the individual dog, daily exercise, training, noise and time spent alone. The catalog does not assign a definitive breed-wide yes or no.

faq.question: What colours do English Setters have?
faq.answer: Common recognised patterns include blue, orange, lemon and liver belton, along with tricolour patterns. Exact wording and acceptance can vary by registry.

faq.question: Are English Setters prone to bloat?
faq.answer: Bloat is a serious risk discussed in general breed-care guidance. Sudden abdominal swelling, unproductive retching, collapse or severe distress needs emergency veterinary care.

overview.summary: A self-assured, calm, and even-tempered medium-sized German Spitz breed developed specifically as a devoted household companion.
overview.description: The Eurasier is a balanced, well-constructed medium-sized Spitz-type dog with prick ears, a wedge-shaped head, a dense double coat, and a bushy tail carried lying forward over the back, bent slightly sideways, or rolled up. The body is slightly longer than the height at the withers, with medium bone and a coat length that still reveals the dog's natural outline. Calm, poised, and watchful without being noisy, the Eurasier bonds to its entire family rather than a single person and displays a dignified reserve toward strangers without fear or aggression. To develop its characteristic even temperament, the breed requires close daily indoor contact with its household, gentle and consistent guidance, and regular outdoor walks.
overview.history: The breed originated in Weinheim, Germany, in 1960 when Julius Wipfel, joined by Charlotte Baldamus and other dedicated breeders, crossed Wolfspitz females with Chow Chow males to create a family-oriented Spitz with primitive canine traits. This initial cross was known as the Wolf-Chow. In 1972, Samoyed blood was introduced through the male Cito von Pol to broaden genetic diversity and enhance a friendly, cooperative disposition. In 1973, the breed was renamed Eurasier—reflecting its combined European and Asian heritage—and gained official national and international recognition. Ethologist Konrad Lorenz acquired a Eurasier in 1972 and praised the breed's character and devotion.

grooming.brushing: Thorough combing and brushing once a week to once every two weeks normally, increasing to daily brushing for roughly three weeks once or twice a year when the undercoat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Infrequent, only as needed; the coat has very little doggy odour and naturally sheds dirt.
notes: Use a pin brush and metal comb to reach through the dense undercoat, paying attention to feathering on the forelegs, hind-leg breeches, and behind the ears.
Daily brushing during the once- or twice-yearly coat blow prevents loose undercoat wool from matting or collecting indoors.
Spaying or neutering can cause the coat to become noticeably thicker, longer, softer, and more labour-intensive to groom.
Avoid shaving or clipping the double coat unless medically required, as it provides insulation and skin protection.
Check eyes, ears, paw pads, and nails (especially dewclaws) during weekly grooming sessions.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Intelligent and eager to please its family, though capable of independent thought and easily bored by repetitive drills.
tips: Rely on affectionate, reward-based positive reinforcement and calm, consistent leadership.
Avoid harsh corrections or heavy-handed pressure, which can shut down a sensitive dog.
Keep training sessions varied, purposeful, and engaging rather than repeating the same exercise.
Focus on chase games and interactive rewards rather than repetitive ball retrieving, which many individuals find tedious.
Practise reliable recall in enclosed spaces before allowing off-leash freedom.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, positive exposure to varied people, sights, sounds, and other animals early in puppyhood and continue into adulthood. Because the breed naturally assesses unfamiliar people at its own pace, allow the dog to approach strangers voluntarily rather than forcing physical contact.

climates: Cold and snowy climates
Cool climates
Temperate climates
Warm climates when provided with shade, air-conditioned or cool tile resting areas, fresh water, and exercise during cooler hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. The breed requires close indoor contact with its household and must never be kept in a kennel or isolated outdoors. Adult dogs can handle short periods alone after gradual training, but routine long hours of daily isolation cause distress and may lead to destructive behaviour.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced diet appropriate for the dog's life stage, activity level, and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Provide a high-quality commercial or veterinary-approved diet suited to the dog's age and activity level. Relative to their medium build, many Eurasiers are light or selective eaters that regulate their own intake and rarely overeat. Rotating flavours or incorporating safe variety can help keep picky eaters interested, and fresh water should always be available.
considerations: Many individuals have modest appetites for their size and may seem finicky if fed the same food indefinitely.
Introduce new foods or rotational variety gradually to avoid digestive upset.
Monitor body condition and adjust portions so the dog remains lean, supporting joint health.
Be aware of the signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) and discuss feeding routines with a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian if appetite changes suddenly or if digestive issues persist.
nutrition.note: Consulted breed sources do not prescribe a fixed daily meal count for puppies, adults, or seniors; portion sizes and feeding schedules should be tailored with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Eurasier is generally a sturdy, long-lived breed with an average lifespan of 12 to 14 years, supported by strict breed-club health screening protocols prior to breeding. The most frequently recorded hereditary concern in health registries is autoimmune thyroiditis (leading to hypothyroidism), followed by orthopedic conditions such as patellar luxation, elbow dysplasia, and hip dysplasia, as well as eyelid and eyelash abnormalities. A breed-specific autosomal recessive neurological disorder, Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM), has a validated genetic test (`VLDLR` gene) that enables breeders to prevent affected puppies. Other conditions such as exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, gastric dilatation-volvulus, primary ciliary dyskinesia, and rare pedigree-specific recessive disorders have been reported less frequently.
commonConditions: Autoimmune thyroiditis and resulting hypothyroidism, the most frequently recorded condition in breed health registries (reported in roughly 14%–20% of tested dogs, typically manifesting between 2 and 7 years of age)
Patellar luxation, the most common orthopedic finding in breed screening statistics (affecting about 7.6% of evaluated dogs)
Elbow dysplasia, an inherited joint abnormality recorded in approximately 5.2% of screened dogs
Hip dysplasia, an inherited joint malformation recorded in approximately 3.2% of screened dogs
Ophthalmic disorders including distichiasis (extra eyelashes), entropion, ectropion, glaucoma, and progressive retinal atrophy

Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM), an autosomal recessive congenital cerebellar hypoplasia caused by a VLDLR gene deletion (c.1713delC) that produces non-progressive cerebellar ataxia from puppyhood

Additional reported risks and isolated pedigree-specific conditions: gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI), primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), and rare autosomal recessive polioencephalopathy (PE) and epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EB)
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of a puppy have completed required pre-breeding screenings for hips, patellas, eyes, thyroid function, and Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM).
Consider periodic veterinary thyroid blood panels (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies) during adulthood, especially between 2 and 7 years of age.
Maintain a lean body condition and avoid excessive high-impact jumping during skeletal growth to protect hips, elbows, and patellas.
Monitor the eyes for tearing, squinting, or irritation caused by distichiasis or eyelid conformation.
Learn the emergency signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (unproductive retching, distended abdomen, restlessness) and seek immediate veterinary care if they occur.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation (radiographic screening at 24 months or older, or distraction-index evaluation)
Patella evaluation (veterinary examination at 12 months or older)
Ophthalmic evaluation by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Annual thyroid panel (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies, tested within 12 months before breeding)
Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM) DNA test (VLDLR c.1713delC mutation)
Optional additional screenings: radiographic elbow evaluation (at 24 months or older) and adult dentition count
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule veterinary dental checks. The breed standard requires a complete scissor or pincer bite of 42 teeth, and missing incisors, canines, third or fourth premolars, or first or second molars are disqualifying faults in conformation.
health.earCare: Inspect the erect triangular ears during weekly grooming for wax buildup, redness, parasites, or odour, and clean gently only when needed with a veterinarian-approved ear cleaner.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat during weekly brushing to check the skin for burrs, ticks, hot spots, or dryness, and check the hair between the paw pads for trapped debris or ice balls in winter.

idealFor: Families and households that include their dog in daily indoor life and activities
Owners seeking a calm, quiet indoor companion that enjoys daily outdoor walks and play
People who appreciate a dog that is polite and reserved rather than effusive with strangers
Households prepared to brush a thick double coat and manage heavy twice-yearly seasonal shedding
notIdealFor: People who leave a dog alone for long workdays or intend to keep a dog in a kennel or backyard
Owners looking for an aggressive guard dog or a dog that greets every stranger as an instant best friend
Those unwilling to deal with heavy seasonal undercoat shedding twice a year
Handlers who use harsh, repetitive, or forceful training methods

funFacts: The breed began in 1960 in Weinheim, Germany, as the 'Wolf-Chow' before Samoyed ancestry was added in 1972 and the name 'Eurasier' was adopted in 1973 to reflect its European and Asian roots.
Nobel Prize-winning ethologist Konrad Lorenz acquired a Eurasier female in 1972 and described her as one of the finest dogs he had ever owned.
Reflecting its Chow Chow heritage, a Eurasier's tongue can be solid blue-black, solid pink, or spotted with both colours.

From the beginning of the breeding program, founder Julius Wipfel prioritized sound temperament and health over coat colour, allowing almost all colours and combinations except pure white and piebald.
Many Eurasiers love games of chase and tag with their families or other dogs, but quickly lose interest in repetitive ball-fetching.

faq.question: Is the Eurasier a one-person dog or a family dog?
faq.answer: The Eurasier bonds with its entire household, including children and extended family members it knows well, rather than attaching exclusively to a single person. When raised with gentle guidance and supervision around young children, it is an affectionate, tolerant family companion.

faq.question: How much does an adult Eurasier weigh and measure?
faq.answer: Males stand 52 to 60 cm at the withers and weigh 22 to 30 kg, with an ideal of 56 cm and 26 kg. Females stand 48 to 56 cm and weigh 18 to 26 kg, with an ideal of 52 cm and 22 kg.

faq.question: Does the Eurasier shed heavily or require difficult grooming?
faq.answer: For most of the year, the coat is relatively low maintenance and needs only a thorough weekly or bi-weekly brushing, as it has little odour and sheds dirt easily. However, once or twice a year the breed blows its entire undercoat over about three weeks, requiring daily brushing during that period.

faq.question: How does a Eurasier behave around strangers and other dogs?
faq.answer: Toward strangers, the Eurasier is calm, discerning, and reserved without being fearful or aggressive, preferring to approach new people at its own pace. Around other dogs, it is typically polite and non-confrontational, backing away from conflict rather than initiating fights.

faq.question: Can a Eurasier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. Because it is calm indoors and barks only when warranted rather than incessantly, the Eurasier adapts well to apartments of sufficient size, provided it receives daily outdoor walks, mental enrichment, and close companionship with its family.

faq.question: What inherited health conditions and screenings are most important for Eurasiers?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should ask breeders for health clearances covering autoimmune thyroiditis (annual thyroid panel), patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, ophthalmic examinations, and the DNA test for Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM, caused by a VLDLR gene mutation). Elbow radiographs and dentition records are also commonly tracked.

faq.question: How does the Eurasier handle hot or cold weather?
faq.answer: With its thick double coat, the Eurasier thrives in cool and snowy weather. It can also live comfortably in warmer climates when given shade, cool indoor flooring or air conditioning, fresh water, and walks during the cooler hours of the day. The double coat should never be shaved.

overview.summary: The Gascon Saintongeois is a French scent hound bred for hunting, valued for its keen nose, stamina, pack-working instinct, and distinctive voice. It has two recognised varieties: the larger Grand and the smaller Petit. Both have a short, close coat, a mostly white ground colour with black patches, and characteristic tan markings. Although the breed standard describes a calm and affectionate temperament, its working instincts and need for purposeful activity make it best suited to owners who can provide regular exercise, scent-based enrichment, training, and secure outdoor management.
overview.description: The Gascon Saintongeois is a well-proportioned French hound combining strength with an elegant outline. Its head is long and refined, with a strong muzzle, brown oval eyes, black nose, and fine, curled ears that reach at least to the tip of the nose. The body is athletic, with a broad, deep chest and strong limbs; the tail tapers towards the tip and is carried in a sabre-like curve. The coat is short and close-fitting. The standard describes a white ground colour marked with black patches, sometimes lightly speckled, plus tan markings around the cheeks and above the eyes. The breed's two varieties differ substantially in height: the Grand is a large hound, while the Petit is medium-sized. They share a strong scenting instinct and were developed for hunting, often working with other hounds. Prospective owners should plan for regular activity and safe opportunities to sniff and explore rather than relying only on short neighbourhood walks.
overview.history: The Grand variety developed in the mid-19th century when Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour sought to revive the declining Hound of Saintonge. He crossed its remaining descendants with Bleu de Gascogne hounds associated with Baron de Ruble, creating the Gascon Saintongeois type while the original Hound of Saintonge disappeared. In the mid-20th century, hunters in southwestern France selected smaller dogs from Grand Gascon Saintongeois litters and established the Petit variety, initially with hare hunting in mind.
overview.originalPurpose: Hunting dog used to pursue hare and larger game, with the Grand variety often working in a pack or tracking independently and the Petit variety serving as a versatile hunting hound.
currentRoles: Hunting and tracking activities suited to the individual dog

physical.sizeCategory: Medium to large, depending on variety
physical.coatType: Short, close-fitting coat.
physical.coatLength: Short.
coatColors: White ground colour with black patches
White with light speckling in some individuals

Tan markings on the cheeks and above the eyes

Fine, curled ears that should reach at least the tip of the nose

Broad, deep chest and strong, athletic limbs
Short, close-fitting coat with a white ground colour and black patches
Tan facial markings, including markings above the eyes

traits: Described by the breed standard as calm and affectionate
Typically suited to scent-led work and outdoor exploration
Has a strong instinct to join and work with a pack
May follow interesting scents and become less responsive when tracking
Can be vocal, as expected of a working scent hound
Benefits from consistent, reward-based training
Needs safe boundaries and reliable handling around roads and wildlife
Individual behaviour depends on breeding, socialisation, health, and experience

exercise.level: High. This is an active scent hound developed for hunting. Plan for regular walks, opportunities to sniff, structured enrichment, and activity appropriate to the individual dog's fitness and health. A secure area is preferable for off-leash exploration because scent tracking can distract the dog from recall.
activities: Brisk walks adjusted to age, fitness, and health
Supervised scent games and nose-work activities
Tracking games using safe, controlled scent trails
Reward-based obedience and recall practice
Exploration in secure, dog-safe outdoor spaces
Appropriate pack or group activities with compatible, well-managed dogs
Food puzzles and other enrichment that engages the nose

grooming.level: Low to moderate. The short, close coat is relatively straightforward to maintain, but regular grooming still helps remove loose hair and identify skin or parasite problems.
grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a soft-bristled brush or grooming mitt. Check the coat and skin after outdoor walks, particularly after running through vegetation.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-formulated shampoo, such as after becoming muddy or unusually dirty. Avoid excessive bathing that may dry the skin.
notes: Check the long, pendant ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, or irritation.
Dry the ears gently if they become wet; ask a veterinarian for advice if irritation or recurring problems occur.
Inspect the coat and paws after walks for burrs, grass seeds, cuts, or parasites.
Trim nails as needed to maintain comfortable movement.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for owners unfamiliar with scent hounds. The breed's scenting motivation can compete with recall and handler focus, so training should be consistent, rewarding, and practised in gradually more distracting environments.
tips: Start recall training early and practise first in low-distraction, secure areas.
Reward voluntary check-ins and returning to the handler.
Use scent games as a structured outlet for natural tracking behaviour.
Train loose-leash walking before the dog develops strong pulling habits.
Keep sessions positive, clear, and short enough to maintain engagement.
Do not rely on off-leash recall in unsecured areas near roads or wildlife.
Teach calm handling for grooming, ear checks, veterinary visits, and transport.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to people, friendly dogs, sounds, transport, surfaces, and everyday environments. Practise calm behaviour around wildlife and other scent distractions, while maintaining safe physical control. Socialisation should be age-appropriate and should never force a frightened dog into an interaction.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity level, and health. Individual energy needs vary with exercise and working activity.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy diet suitable for growth and follow the product's age- and weight-based guidance. Ask a veterinarian to review growth, body condition, and portion sizes as the puppy develops.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured portions of a complete adult diet and adjust them according to body condition and activity. Dogs doing substantial hunting or endurance work may have different energy needs from less active companions.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose food and portions based on body condition, activity, dental health, and any medical conditions. Review diet changes with a veterinarian, especially if weight or appetite changes.

nutrition.guidelines: Use a complete and balanced diet rather than relying on unbalanced homemade meals or unneeded supplements. Measure portions, account for training treats, maintain access to clean water, and monitor body condition. Working activity, age, reproductive status, and health can all change an individual dog's energy needs. Consult a veterinarian for a tailored feeding plan or if weight, appetite, or digestion changes unexpectedly.
considerations: Adjust food portions to the dog's body condition and activity level.
Provide fresh, clean drinking water at all times.
Include training treats in the overall daily food allowance.
Avoid sudden diet changes; transition gradually when practical.
Do not give supplements unless there is a clear need and appropriate veterinary advice.
Seek veterinary guidance for persistent digestive problems or unexplained weight change.
nutrition.note: No breed-specific calorie target or weight range was established from the sources consulted. Portion sizes should be individualised rather than inferred from breed name alone.

preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary wellness examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local risk.
Monitor body condition, mobility, appetite, drinking, and changes in activity.
Check ears and paws after outdoor activity and seek veterinary advice for persistent irritation or injury.
Maintain routine dental care and professional assessment when indicated.
Use secure handling and fencing to reduce risks associated with scent-following and road traffic.
Seek prompt veterinary attention for significant injury, sudden weakness, breathing difficulty, collapse, or other acute concerning signs.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste. Dental chews and other products should be selected carefully and do not replace tooth brushing or veterinary assessment. Ask a veterinarian about professional dental cleaning if tartar, bad breath, pain, or eating changes develop.
health.earCare: The ears are long and pendant, so check them routinely for odour, redness, discharge, scratching, or head shaking. Clean only with a product recommended for dogs and use veterinary guidance for recurring or painful symptoms.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin and coat during brushing and after outdoor walks. Look for ticks, grass seeds, scratches, rashes, or persistent itching. Seek veterinary advice for recurring skin problems, sores, or unexplained hair loss.

idealFor: Owners who enjoy regular outdoor activity and scent-based enrichment
People experienced with, or willing to learn about, scent hound behaviour
Households able to provide secure outdoor exercise and reliable handling
Owners interested in tracking, hunting-related activities where legal, or structured nose work
Homes that can accommodate a vocal, active dog and meet its daily needs
notIdealFor: People seeking a low-exercise dog with minimal enrichment needs
Owners who expect dependable off-leash recall without sustained training
Households unable to manage a dog that may follow scents or vocalise
Homes without safe ways to exercise and contain an active hound

funFacts: The breed's history is linked to Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour's 19th-century effort to revive the Hound of Saintonge.
The Grand and Petit varieties were developed at different times; the smaller variety was established from smaller dogs in Grand litters.
The FCI standard places the Grand in the large-sized scenthound section and the Petit in the medium-sized scenthound section.
The standard describes a very sonorous voice and a strong instinct to join a pack.
The breed's characteristic coat has a white ground colour with black patches and tan facial markings.

faq.question: What is a Gascon Saintongeois?
faq.answer: It is a French scent hound developed for hunting. The breed has two recognised varieties, Grand and Petit, which differ mainly in size and historical selection.

faq.question: What is the difference between Grand and Petit Gascon Saintongeois?
faq.answer: The Grand is the larger variety, with standard heights of 65–72 cm for males and 62–68 cm for females. The Petit is medium-sized, with standard heights of 56–62 cm for males and 54–59 cm for females. The standard allows a tolerance of ±1 cm.

faq.question: What colours does the Gascon Saintongeois have?
faq.answer: The standard describes a white ground colour with black patches, sometimes lightly speckled, and tan markings around the cheeks and above the eyes. The precise placement and appearance of markings are part of the breed standard.

faq.question: Is the Gascon Saintongeois good with other dogs?
faq.answer: The breed was developed as a pack hound and has an instinct to work with other hounds. Compatibility still depends on the individual dog's socialisation and experience, so introductions and group activities should be supervised.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Gascon Saintongeois need?
faq.answer: It is an active scent hound that benefits from regular exercise and opportunities to use its nose. There is no verified universal daily minute target for every dog; exercise should be adjusted to age, fitness, health, and behaviour.

faq.question: Can a Gascon Saintongeois be walked off leash?
faq.answer: Scent hounds may become focused on a trail and less responsive to recall. Use secure areas unless the individual dog has reliable recall and the location is safe and legally suitable.

faq.question: What health problems are common in the Gascon Saintongeois?
faq.answer: The sources consulted did not establish a reliable, breed-specific list of common diseases or recommended genetic screening tests. Arrange routine veterinary care and ask a veterinarian about risks based on the individual dog's history and lifestyle.

faq.question: How long does a Gascon Saintongeois live?
faq.answer: A breed profile gives a typical life expectancy of about 12–14 years. This is an approximate reference, not a guarantee; individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, environment, and care.

overview.summary: The German Rough-haired Pointer, known in its country of origin as the Deutsch Stichelhaar, is a medium-to-large German pointing dog developed for practical gundog work. Its hallmark features are a firm, bristly coat, strong build, pronounced bushy eyebrows and a moderate beard.
overview.description: This robust, balanced pointing dog has a practical rather than ornamental appearance. The body coat is harsh, stiff and bristly, usually around four centimetres long, with somewhat longer hair beneath the body and light feathering on parts of the limbs. A moderate beard and strong, outward-arching eyebrows give the head a distinctive expression. The breed standard describes a calm, even temperament and a dog that should be courageous without being uncontrolled, and neither shy nor aggressive. As a working gundog, it is best matched with people who can provide consistent training, regular outdoor activity and appropriate opportunities for scent-led work.
overview.history: The Deutsch Stichelhaar is recognised as an old German rough-coated pointing-dog type. Historical accounts describe it as the rough-coated form of the German partridge dog, rather than a newly created variety of the short-haired pointing dog. In the late nineteenth century, the breed was documented and developed from the relatively small number of surviving dogs. The Club Stichelhaar was founded in 1892 and was renamed Verein Deutsch Stichelhaar in 1976. The breed remains a distinct FCI-recognised pointing dog, separate from the German Wirehaired Pointer.

Introduce scent games and appropriate gundog exercises to provide mental as well as physical activity.
Teach calm handling, settling and cooperative care alongside active skills.
