overview.summary: An imposing, elegant giant mountain guardian from the Pyrenees range, bred for centuries to protect flocks independently in harsh alpine weather and prized for its weatherproof white double coat, quiet composure, and steadfast devotion to its charges.
overview.description: The Great Pyrenees (also called the Pyrenean Mountain Dog or Patou) is a dog of immense size, balanced rectangular proportions, and noble bearing without heaviness or coarseness. Beneath a thick, dirt-shedding double coat—all white or white shaded on the head, ears, tail base, and a few body spots with badger, wolf-grey, pale yellow, orange, or tan—lies medium-to-strong bone and lean muscle built for tireless mountain patrols. Distinguishing anatomical traits include a blunt V-shaped head without a pronounced stop, almond-shaped dark amber-brown eyes with a contemplative expression, small triangular ears set at eye level, a plumed tail that curls into a circle ('making the wheel') over the loin when alert, and characteristic double dewclaws on each hind leg. Calm, patient, and gentle with its own household and animals, the breed retains the independent judgment, nocturnal vigilance, resonant warning bark, and territorial instinct of a true livestock guardian.
overview.history: Descended from ancient white flock-guarding dogs of Asia Minor that accompanied shepherds and domestic sheep into the Pyrenees around 3000 BC—with regional fossil remains dating to the Bronze Age (1800–1000 BC)—the breed developed in virtual isolation high in the mountains between France and Spain. In the fourteenth century Gaston Phoebus wrote of these mountain dogs, and in 1407 French records praised their service guarding the Château of Lourdes, where each dog was reckoned equal to two men. In 1662 Basque fishermen carried them to Newfoundland, where crosses with settlers' black retrievers helped create the Landseer Newfoundland, and in 1675 the Dauphin at the court of King Louis XIV adopted the breed as the Royal Dog of France. General Lafayette brought the first pair to the United States in 1824 for J. S. Skinner, Queen Victoria owned one in 1850, and in 1870 the breed contributed to rebuilding the depleted St. Bernard in Switzerland. After Count de Bylandt published the first detailed description in 1897, French enthusiasts formed the first breed clubs at Argelès-Gazost and Lourdes in 1907, and Bernard Sénac-Lagrange united fanciers in 1923 to establish the modern conformation standard. In 1931 Francis and Mary Crane founded Basquaerie Kennels in Massachusetts, importing key European stock prior to the Second World War.
overview.originalPurpose: Autonomous guarding of sheep and other livestock against wolves, bears, and thieves on the steep slopes of the Pyrenees, as well as guarding mountain châteaux and estates
currentRoles: Open-range livestock guardian and all-purpose farm or ranch guardian
Therapy dog visiting hospitals, schools, and assisted-living facilities
Cart-pulling (draft work), obedience, rally, tracking, scent work, barn hunt, and versatility participant

physical.coatType: Weather-resistant, dirt-repellent double coat with a long, flat, thick, coarse outer coat (straight or slightly wavy) over a dense, fine, woolly undercoat
physical.coatLength: Medium to long: flat and crisp on the shoulders and back, shorter and finer on the face and ears, and more profuse around the neck and shoulders (forming a mane or ruff, especially in males), along the backs of the thighs ('pantaloons'), and on the plumed tail
coatColors: White with badger or wolf-grey markings
White with varying shades of tan, pale yellow (lemon), or orange (arrouye) markings
physical.sheddingLevel: very high
distinctiveFeatures: Well-formed double dewclaws on each hind leg (a defining breed trait whose absence or atrophy is a serious or eliminating fault) and single (or occasionally double) dewclaws on the forelegs

Long, bushy plumed tail reaching at least the point of the hock, preferably hooked at the tip ('shepherd's crook') at rest and curling in a circle over the loin ('making the wheel' or arroundera) when alert

Blunt V-shaped head not heavy for the dog's size, with skull width equal to skull length, flat cheeks, a gentle slope rather than an apparent stop, and a line formed where upper and lower facial hair meet from the outer eye corner to the ear base
Almond-shaped, slightly oblique dark amber-brown eyes with close-fitting black-rimmed lids and an intelligent, contemplative, dreamy expression
Completely black nose and close-fitting black or heavily black-marked lips and roof of the mouth, with minimal dewlap
Slightly rectangular body (longer from point of shoulder to buttocks than height at the withers) with chest depth reaching the elbows
Rear feet that structurally toe out slightly while the hind legs remain straight and parallel

Shoulder height of 70–80 cm for males and 65–75 cm for females (with a +2 cm allowance up to 82 cm and 77 cm for superior type internationally; 68.6–81.3 cm [27–32 in] for males and 63.5–73.7 cm [25–29 in] for females in North America), and minimum weights of about 45–50 kg (100–110 lbs) for minimum-height males and 39–40 kg (85–88 lbs) for minimum-height females (typically ranging up to 64 kg / 140 lbs in proportion to frame)

traits: Calm and composed indoors
Confident and fearless when protecting charges
Gentle and affectionate with family
Patient and nurturing toward children and young or vulnerable animals
Independent decision-maker with strong initiative
Vigilant and territorial
Reserved and discerning with unfamiliar visitors
Strong-willed and indifferent to repetitive obedience drills
Naturally nocturnal and vocal when alerting to perceived threats

exercise.level: moderate
activities: Daily leashed walks at a steady, unhurried pace
Supervised patrolling and exploration in a securely fenced yard or pasture
Cart-pulling (draft work), hiking, and backpacking once skeletally mature
Nose work, tracking, barn hunt, and versatility activities
Short, varied obedience, rally, or therapy-dog visits

grooming.brushing: Thorough brushing once or twice a week (about 30 minutes per week) with a pin brush or slicker brush; use a 1 to 1.5-inch undercoat rake or wide-toothed comb during heavy seasonal coat blows
grooming.bathing: Infrequent, only as needed; the coarse outer coat is naturally dirt- and tangle-resistant, though a warm bath during shedding season helps loosen and lift dead undercoat
notes: Despite its abundance, the double coat is naturally self-cleaning and resists matting when brushed once or twice weekly; avoid over-brushing the outer guard hairs, which can break hair ends.
Focus weekly brushing on the thick neck ruff, rump, hind-leg pantaloons, foreleg feathering, and behind the ears.
Trim all toenails and both front single and rear double dewclaws regularly with clippers or a grinder; dewclaws do not touch the ground and will curl back into the leg if neglected.
Never remove the characteristic rear double dewclaws and never shave or clip the double coat in summer, as the coat insulates against both cold and solar heat.
Check the long eyebrow hairs at least once a month and trim carefully if they curl downward into the eyes.
Inspect the ears weekly for dampness, wax buildup, or foul odour, and check beneath the dense coat and between the toes for trapped moisture, fungus, or hot spots.

training.difficulty: moderate to challenging
tips: Begin gentle leash conditioning, house-training, and socialization immediately in puppyhood, keeping sessions brief (a few minutes once or twice a day) and varied.

Understand the breed's heritage: bred to think independently and conserve energy while guarding flocks, these dogs quickly grow bored with repetitive drills and often respond to sit, heel, or recall cues at a deliberate, unhurried pace.
Never allow a Great Pyrenees off-leash in an unfenced area, as its instinct to establish and patrol a wide territory overrides recall.
Never tie or chain a dog outside unsupervised, which encourages frustration, territorial aggression, and severe entanglement hazards.
Keep growing puppies and adolescents off slick or highly polished floors that lack traction and can cause orthopedic injury or 'sea-legs'.
Manage nocturnal barking in suburban or urban neighbourhoods by bringing the dog indoors at night.
Recognize that the breed has very little natural ball-chasing or retrieving drive; motivate learning with praise, affection, and varied real-world tasks.
training.socialization: Expose puppies after immunization to varied people, sights, sounds, surfaces, and calm dogs. A well-socialized adult should accept guests welcomed by its household while remaining composed, neither timid nor unprovokedly aggressive.

climates: Cold and snowy mountain climates
Cool climates
Temperate climates with shade and ventilation
Warm climates only with reliable shade, cool indoor resting areas, fresh cold water, and restricted midday activity
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Companion dogs thrive on daily human companionship and quiet indoor rest near their family; lonely, under-stimulated dogs left loose indoors can become destructive or vocal. Puppies should be safely confined in a crate or exercise pen with water and durable chew toys when unsupervised.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, nutritionally complete and balanced large- or giant-breed dog food with moderate protein and energy density suited to the dog's life stage
nutrition.guidelines: Because Great Pyrenees have a relatively slow metabolism, adults often eat less than expected for their giant frame. Feed a high-quality, balanced commercial diet at regular set times, and never add calcium or mineral supplements to an already balanced ration during growth. To help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), offer multiple smaller meals per day rather than one large meal and avoid vigorous exercise before and after eating.
considerations: Select a balanced large-breed formula with moderate protein to support steady skeletal growth without rapid weight gain.
Do not add extra calcium, vitamins, or mineral supplements to balanced commercial foods.
Divide daily food intake into multiple smaller meals at regular times and restrict strenuous activity around mealtimes to lower bloat (GDV) risk.
Provide hard dog biscuits for dental chewing, and never feed splintering bones.
Keep fresh, cold water available at all times.
nutrition.note: Authoritative breed standards and national breed-club guides recommend multiple small meals per day at set times rather than prescribing fixed numerical meal counts by life stage; tailor portion sizes with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Great Pyrenees is generally a resilient breed with a typical lifespan of 10 to 12 years, but its giant frame and several documented inherited conditions make health screening and preventive veterinary care essential. Parent-club health protocols require pre-breeding evaluations for hip dysplasia and patellar luxation alongside elective screening for elbow dysplasia, shoulder osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), cardiac disease (such as subaortic stenosis), autoimmune thyroiditis, eye anomalies, congenital deafness, Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 1 (CMR1), and Type I Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GT). Peer-reviewed genetic studies have also identified autosomal recessive neuronal degeneration (NDG, caused by a SACS gene deletion) and autosomal recessive chondrodysplasia (dwarfism), for which DNA tests are available. In breed health surveys, osteosarcoma and hemangiosarcoma are the two highest-incidence cancers, and gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) remains an important emergency risk. In addition, because the breed has a low basal metabolic rate, veterinarians should always weigh the dog accurately and administer anesthetics cautiously 'to effect'.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia and patellar luxation: the two mandatory orthopedic evaluations in parent-club pre-breeding health certification
Additional orthopedic and spinal conditions: elbow dysplasia, shoulder osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), panosteitis (self-limiting bone inflammation in growing dogs), and spondylosis

Osteosarcoma (bone cancer) and hemangiosarcoma: identified in national breed health surveys as the two cancers with the highest incidence in Great Pyrenees, alongside reported lymphosarcoma and mast cell tumors
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat): a sudden, life-threatening distension and twisting of the stomach in large, deep-chested dogs

Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 1 (CMR1): an autosomal recessive retinal disorder caused by a BEST1 stop-mutation (c.73C>T / p.R25X) that produces multifocal subretinal blisters between 11 and 16 weeks of age, typically stabilizing by 1 year without causing blindness
Other ophthalmic disorders: hereditary cataracts, persistent pupillary membranes (PPM), progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), and entropion or ectropion

Type I Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GT): a rare autosomal recessive platelet-function bleeding disorder caused by an ITGA2B gene mutation affecting platelet glycoprotein IIb-IIIa, resulting in mucosal bleeding and nosebleeds

Neuronal Degeneration (NDG): an autosomal recessive central and peripheral nervous system degeneration caused by a 4-bp frameshift deletion in the SACS gene (p.Val4244AlafsTer32), with onset around 4 to 12 months of age causing progressive hind-limb ataxia, slipping on smooth surfaces, and inability to climb stairs

Chondrodysplasia (dwarfism): an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia (distinct from FGF4 retrogene dwarfism) visible by 14 days of age, resulting in disproportionate short-limbed adults (33–46 cm tall, 15–23 kg) and often accompanied by deafness, dental crowding, and reduced fertility

Degenerative myelopathy (DM): a late-onset progressive spinal cord neuropathy reported in the breed; while a SOD1 risk allele exists, breed-club guidance notes that current DNA tests are not specific for clinical diagnosis in Great Pyrenees and compressive spinal disorders must be ruled out

Endocrine, immune-mediated, auditory, and skin conditions reported in breed surveys: autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), Addison's disease, subaortic stenosis, congenital deafness, sebaceous adenitis, and moisture-trapped hot spots or interdigital fungal infections
Low metabolic sensitivity to anesthesia: requires accurate pre-anesthetic weighing and titrating anesthetic agents carefully 'to effect'
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents hold clearances for hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, and relevant breed-specific DNA and clinical screenings (elbows, heart, thyroid, eyes, hearing, CMR1, GT, NDG, and chondrodysplasia).

Feed multiple smaller meals daily, avoid vigorous exercise around mealtimes, and learn the emergency warning signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (unproductive retching, distended abdomen, restlessness).
Remind your veterinarian of the breed's slow metabolism so the dog is weighed accurately before any sedation or anesthesia and dosed strictly 'to effect'.
Raise puppies on non-slip surfaces, maintain a lean body condition, and avoid over-supplementing growing dogs to protect developing joints.
Keep toenails and all front and double rear dewclaws trimmed short, check eyebrow hairs monthly so they do not curl into the eyes, and keep the ears dry.
Monitor adult and senior dogs closely for persistent lameness, bone swelling, pale gums, or unexplained weakness that could indicate orthopedic disease or cancer.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic screening or distraction-index evaluation; required for parent-club health certification)
Patellar luxation veterinary examination (required for parent-club health certification)
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation and shoulder osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) radiographic evaluation (elective parent-club screenings)
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (elective parent-club screening)
Cardiac evaluation and thyroid panel including autoimmune thyroiditis testing (elective parent-club screenings)
BAER (brainstem auditory evoked response) hearing test for congenital deafness (elective parent-club screening)
Targeted DNA tests for Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 1 (CMR1 / BEST1), Type I Glanzmann Thrombasthenia (GT / ITGA2B), Neuronal Degeneration (NDG / SACS), and Chondrodysplasia (dwarfism)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste, provide safe hard dog biscuits rather than splintering bones, and schedule routine veterinary dental checks for tartar buildup.
health.earCare: Inspect the triangular hanging ears weekly for mites, dampness, dark discharge, or odour. Keep the ear canals dry—using a cotton ball or drying ear powder as advised by a veterinarian—because trapped moisture predisposes the ear canal to fungal or mite infections.
health.skinCare: Part the thick double coat during weekly brushing to check for hot spots (acute moist dermatitis), parasites, and sebaceous adenitis, and inspect between the toes for fungal irritation. Never shave the coat in warm weather, as it protects the skin from sunburn and heat.

idealFor: Ranchers, farmers, and acreage owners needing a dependable livestock or property guardian
Families with a securely fenced yard seeking a calm, affectionate, protective household companion
Owners who appreciate an independent, self-directed dog and use patient, consistent guidance
Households comfortable with heavy seasonal shedding, white hair indoors, and weekly coat and dewclaw maintenance
Handlers interested in therapy dog work, cart-pulling (drafting), tracking, or nose work
notIdealFor: Small apartments or dense urban settings with little yard space and high neighbourhood noise sensitivity
Owners who want an off-leash hiking companion in unfenced areas or instant, rapid-fire obedience compliance
Households intolerant of territorial barking—especially at night—or heavy seasonal shedding
People who cannot physically manage a giant dog weighing 39 to 64+ kg or provide secure fencing

funFacts: In 1407, historical records at the Château of Lourdes noted the value of these mountain guardians, counting each dog as equal to two armed men on guard duty.
Adopted as the Royal Dog of France in 1675 by the Dauphin at the court of King Louis XIV, the breed is still affectionately called 'Patou' in French shepherd tradition.

In 1662, Basque fishermen brought Great Pyrenees to Newfoundland, where crosses with black curly-coated retrievers helped produce the black-and-white Landseer Newfoundland; in 1870, the breed also helped rebuild the St. Bernard in Switzerland after avalanches and distemper.
General Lafayette brought the first pair of Great Pyrenees to the United States in 1824 as a gift for agricultural writer J. S. Skinner, and Queen Victoria owned one in 1850.
Every Great Pyrenees has characteristic double dewclaws on each hind leg—traditionally believed to act like snowshoes in deep mountain snow—and their absence is a conformation fault.
When alert, a Great Pyrenees raises its long plumed tail in a circle over its back with the tip touching the loin, a traditional Pyrenean gesture called 'making the wheel' (arroundera).
Despite its snowy white coat, the coarse outer hair is naturally dirt-resistant and self-cleaning: dried mud brushes right out, requiring only about 30 minutes of brushing once or twice a week.

faq.question: What is a Great Pyrenees?
faq.answer: The Great Pyrenees—known across Europe and the United Kingdom as the Pyrenean Mountain Dog and in France as the Chien de Montagne des Pyrénées or Patou—is a giant livestock guardian breed from the Pyrenees mountains between France and Spain, prized for its weatherproof white coat, calm indoor nature, and fearless devotion to its flock or family.

faq.question: How big does a Great Pyrenees get?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 70 to 80 cm for males and 65 to 75 cm for females (with a +2 cm allowance up to 82 cm and 77 cm for dogs of exceptional type). North American standards specify 27 to 32 inches (68.6–81.3 cm) for males and 25 to 29 inches (63.5–73.7 cm) for females. Minimum adult weights start around 45 to 50 kg (100–110 lbs) for males and 39 to 40 kg (85–88 lbs) for females of minimum height, with working and companion dogs commonly ranging from 39 to 64 kg (85–140 lbs) in proportion to their frame.

faq.question: How long does a Great Pyrenees live?
faq.answer: The typical lifespan is 10 to 12 years.

faq.question: Why do Great Pyrenees have double dewclaws on their back legs?
faq.answer: Each hind leg carries a pair of well-formed dewclaws (while each front leg carries a single, or occasionally double, dewclaw). This ancient anatomical hallmark of the breed was traditionally thought to provide extra stability—like snowshoes—on steep, snowy mountain slopes, and its absence is a disqualifying or serious fault in breed standards. Because dewclaws do not wear down on the ground, they must be trimmed regularly so they do not curl into the leg.

faq.question: Is the white coat difficult to keep clean?
faq.answer: Surprisingly no. The coarse outer guard coat is naturally dirt-, tangle-, and mat-resistant, so dried mud falls or brushes off easily. A 30-minute brushing session once or twice a week is usually sufficient outside of seasonal coat blows, when an undercoat rake helps remove the heavy shedding undercoat. The double coat should never be shaved in summer, as it protects the dog from both heat and sunburn.

faq.question: Why should a Great Pyrenees never be let off-leash in an unfenced area?
faq.answer: Because the breed was selected for thousands of years to patrol vast mountain pastures independently, an unconfined Great Pyrenees will instinctively roam to establish and expand its territory, ignoring recall commands and risking traffic accidents.

faq.question: Do Great Pyrenees bark a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. As nocturnal flock guardians that use a deep, resonant bark to deter predators before a confrontation occurs, Great Pyrenees are naturally vocal—especially at night. In suburban or urban neighbourhoods, owners generally need to keep their dogs indoors overnight.

faq.question: Why are Great Pyrenees slow to obey standard obedience commands?
faq.answer: Unlike herding dogs or retrievers bred to watch a handler and execute rapid commands, Great Pyrenees were bred to make decisions on their own and conserve energy between threats. They learn quickly, but they have almost no natural ball-retrieving drive, dislike repetitive drills, and often perform sits, heels, and recalls at a calm, unhurried pace.

faq.question: What health screenings and genetic tests are recommended for Great Pyrenees?
faq.answer: Pre-breeding health certification requires hip dysplasia and patellar luxation evaluations plus at least one elective clearance from elbow dysplasia, shoulder OCD, cardiac exam, thyroid panel, ophthalmologist exam, BAER hearing test, Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 1 (CMR1) DNA testing, or Type I Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GT) DNA testing. DNA tests are also available for SACS-associated neuronal degeneration (NDG) and breed-specific chondrodysplasia (dwarfism).

faq.question: What special anesthesia precaution should Great Pyrenees owners know about?
faq.answer: Great Pyrenees have a slow basal metabolism compared with many other breeds. Before any surgery or sedation, owners should remind their veterinarian to weigh the dog accurately and administer anesthetic drugs cautiously 'to effect'.

overview.summary: A medium-sized native Japanese hunting Spitz renowned for its endurance, bold courage, acute judgment, deep family loyalty, and weatherproof double coat built for severe winter cold.
overview.description: The Hokkaido Ken is a sturdy, medium-sized Japanese Spitz-type dog with strongly marked sexual dimorphism, small forward-inclining prick ears, dark triangular eyes, a high-set curled or sickle tail, and a harsh straight outer coat over a dense, insulating undercoat. Slightly longer in body than tall in a 11:10 ratio, the breed combines tough, clean-cut muscling with light, resilient movement and remarkable stamina in mountainous, snowy terrain. Devoted and affectionate with its household—often following family members from room to room and greeting them with expressive vocalizations—it is naturally watchful, bold, and independent. Because of its strong hunting drive and potential reactivity toward unfamiliar dogs and small animals, it thrives with an experienced, active handler who provides early socialization, positive structure, and purposeful daily outlets.
overview.history: One of Japan's six native Spitz breeds, the Hokkaido traces its heritage to ancient indigenous dogs of the Japanese archipelago and to medium-sized hunting dogs that accompanied migrants from the Tohoku region of Honshu to the northern island of Hokkaido during the Kamakura era in the 1140s. For centuries, the indigenous Ainu people bred these courageous dogs—which they called Seta—to track and hold brown bear, deer, and other game in rugged forests and heavy snow. When British zoologist Thomas Blakiston studied Hokkaido's fauna in 1869, he referred to the dogs as 'Ainu Ken'. In 1902, dogs of the breed assisted in searching for survivors after an Imperial Japanese Army regiment was caught in a catastrophic blizzard crossing the Hakkōda Mountains. In 1937, Japan designated the breed a Living Natural Monument under the name of its northern home region, and dedicated preservation societies formed in the mid-twentieth century to safeguard its working instincts and traditional type. In 2007, a white Hokkaido portraying the talking patriarch 'Otōsan' in a long-running Japanese television commercial series brought renewed public attention to this rare breed.
overview.originalPurpose: Hunting and holding large game—particularly brown bear and deer—as well as working in harsh, snowy mountain terrain
currentRoles: Agility, obedience, rally, and trick-dog participant

physical.coatType: Dense weatherproof double coat with a harsh, straight outer guard coat and a soft, thick insulating undercoat

Tight, black-edged lips and a tongue that frequently displays blue-black pigmentation or spotting
Broad, slightly flat skull equal in length to cheek width, with a 3:2 skull-to-muzzle ratio and a powerful scissor bite
Sturdily boned body slightly longer than tall (height-to-length ratio of 10:11, with females slightly longer)
High-set, thick tail carried vigorously curled over the back or curved like a sickle, nearly reaching the hocks when lowered
Well-arched, tightly closed toes with thick, elastic pads and hard dark nails adapted for deep snow

traits: Devoted and deeply loyal to family
Bold and courageous

Dignified with natural simplicity
Enduring with high stamina
Intelligent problem solver
Independent and strong-willed
Vocal and expressive with household members

exercise.level: High. Requires vigorous daily physical exercise combined with structured mental work—a working 'job'—to prevent boredom, anxiety, and destructive habits.
activities: Brisk daily walks and long hikes on secure trails
Agility, rally, obedience, and trick-dog training
Tracking, nosework, and scent-detection games
Supervised outdoor play in mud, snow, or shallow creeks
Problem-solving puzzle toys and interactive games

grooming.level: Low to moderate for most of the year; high daily maintenance for several weeks roughly twice a year when blowing the undercoat.
grooming.brushing: Brush weekly during normal periods to remove dead hair and debris; increase to thorough daily brushing for several weeks twice a year during seasonal coat blows.
grooming.bathing: Infrequent, only as needed; natural skin and coat oils repel water and dirt, and the coat has virtually no doggy odour when fed a sound diet.
notes: Unlike some other native Japanese breeds that avoid puddles, many Hokkaido dogs love splashing in creeks, mud, and snow, though dried dirt brushes or falls off easily once dry.
Never shave or clip the double coat; shaving permanently damages the guard hairs and does not keep the dog cooler in summer.
Expect a heavy twice-yearly seasonal shed ('coat blow') lasting several weeks when the entire dense undercoat is released.
Keep nails trimmed short—ideally rounded with a rotary nail grinder—so they do not click on hard flooring.
Inspect the ears, teeth, and skin beneath the dense undercoat during routine grooming.

training.difficulty: Challenging for novice handlers; highly intelligent and quick to learn, yet independent, strong-willed, and vocal when given repetitive or unconvincing cues.
tips: Build a cooperative bond through reward-based positive reinforcement, clear boundaries, and mutual respect rather than heavy-handed punishment.
Channel the breed's problem-solving intelligence by giving the dog a structured job such as agility, tracking, or trick training.
Keep the dog on leash or within a securely fenced area featuring at least a 6-foot (1.8 m) fence, as the breed has a strong prey drive and is an agile jumper and climber.
Be prepared for expressive vocalizations—including howling, 'singing' greetings, rooing, and grumbling protests—and teach calm indoor manners early.

Allow roughly nine months for full housebreaking, using crate training and scheduled potty breaks at least every four hours during puppyhood while avoiding harsh reactions that could trigger submissive urination.
Supervise play closely and keep socks, rocks, sticks, and small household objects out of reach, as pica (chewing and swallowing non-food items) occurs in the breed.
training.socialization: Begin structured, positive socialization early in puppyhood and maintain it throughout adulthood. Introduce unfamiliar people, sights, sounds, and calm, well-mannered dogs gradually. Because dog reactivity—especially between intact males—and strong small-animal prey drive are common, supervise inter-dog interactions carefully and never force greetings.

climates: Cold and snowy climates
Cool climates
Temperate climates
Warm climates only with strict heat precautions, air conditioning or cool tiled floors, shade, fresh water, and exercise restricted to cool hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Hokkaido dogs bond closely with their families, follow their owners from room to room, and want to participate in daily household life. Prolonged isolation or lack of stimulation frequently leads to separation anxiety, vocalizing, destructive chewing, pica, or compulsive water drinking.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced canine diet formulated for the dog's life stage, activity level, and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a high-quality, nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and working or exercise demands, adjusting portions to maintain a lean, muscular body condition. Work with a veterinarian or breeder to establish an appropriate puppy and adult feeding schedule. Keep fresh water available while monitoring for compulsive overdrinking in anxious or bored individuals.
considerations: Adjust calorie intake to match seasonal activity levels and keep the dog lean to reduce stress on hips, elbows, and patellas.
Limit treats and table scraps to prevent obesity.
Supervise feeding and play environments carefully because familial pica (ingesting rocks, socks, sticks, or toys) is documented in the breed.
Monitor water consumption; compulsive drinking of large volumes of water followed by regurgitation (psychogenic polydipsia) has been observed in under-stimulated or anxious dogs.
Consult a veterinarian before introducing supplements or specialized therapeutic diets.
nutrition.note: Authoritative breed references do not prescribe a fixed daily meal count for puppies, adults, or seniors; meal frequency and portion sizes should be planned with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Hokkaido Ken is generally a hardy, cold-adapted breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 15 years, but its small global gene pool makes pre-breeding health screening essential. The most prevalent scientifically established hereditary condition in the breed is Collie eye anomaly (CEA), an autosomal recessive developmental eye defect associated with a 7.8-kb deletion in the NHEJ1 gene. Genotyping surveys indicate that roughly one-third of tested Hokkaido dogs are genetically affected and two-thirds are carriers, although the defect is non-progressive after eight weeks of age and nearly 90% of genetically affected dogs exhibit no clinical vision loss or only mild choroidal hypoplasia. Conversely, genetic screening has shown that tested Hokkaido dogs do not carry the MDR1 (ABCB1) ivermectin-sensitivity mutation. Other documented concerns tracked by preservation and breed clubs include hip dysplasia, cardiac murmurs, patellar luxation, idiopathic seizures, and stress- or drive-related behavioral syndromes such as pica and psychogenic polydipsia.
commonConditions: Collie eye anomaly (CEA / NHEJ1-related choroidal hypoplasia), the most prevalent hereditary disorder in the breed (autosomal recessive 7.8-kb deletion in the NHEJ1 gene on chromosome 37, with genotyping studies reporting roughly one-third affected and two-thirds carriers, though ~90% of genetically affected dogs have normal functional vision or only mild non-progressive fundus changes)
Hip dysplasia, a multifactorial orthopedic malformation identified in North American and European dogs and targeted by mandatory pre-breeding radiographic screening
Heart murmurs and cardiac abnormalities (systolic, diastolic, or continuous murmurs graded I–VI), reported in Japanese and international lines and subject to mandatory pre-breeding cardiac evaluation
Idiopathic seizures (epilepsy of unknown cause), reported in some dogs in North America and overseas with typical onset between 6 months and 6 years of age
Additional orthopedic and ophthalmic screening targets: patellar luxation, elbow dysplasia, and progressive retinal atrophy (PRA)

Behavioral and ingestive conditions observed in the breed: familial pica (chewing and swallowing non-food items such as rocks, socks, and sticks, sometimes requiring emergency surgery), psychogenic polydipsia (compulsive water drinking followed by vomiting excess liquid), and separation anxiety
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have completed mandatory pre-breeding clearances for hips, cardiac health, ophthalmic examination, and the Collie eye anomaly (NHEJ1) DNA test.
Schedule veterinary ophthalmic examinations early in puppyhood and periodically throughout adulthood to evaluate ocular health.
Maintain a lean body weight and age-appropriate exercise routine to protect developing and adult joints.
Provide abundant daily physical exercise, mental enrichment, and companionship to reduce the risk of anxiety, psychogenic polydipsia, and destructive behaviour.
Keep floors and yards clear of swallowable objects (rocks, socks, stick fragments, small balls) and supervise chewing closely to prevent pica-related gastrointestinal obstructions.
Protect the dog from heat stress in warm weather by providing shade, cool indoor floors or air conditioning, and fresh water, and never shave the insulating double coat.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic screening at 12 months of age or older for preliminary evaluation or 24 months for final certification, or distraction-index evaluation)
Cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (at 12 months of age or older for breeding stock, plus puppy eye screening)
Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA) DNA test (NHEJ1 7.8-kb intronic deletion)
Optional additional clearances: patellar luxation evaluation, elbow dysplasia evaluation, thyroid evaluation, progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) DNA test, and degenerative myelopathy (DM) DNA test
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary dental examinations. The breed standard requires strong jaws with a complete, evenly spaced scissor bite.
health.earCare: Inspect the small, erect triangular ears weekly for debris, wax buildup, redness, or odour, and clean gently only when needed using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleaner.
health.skinCare: Part the dense undercoat regularly to check the skin for ticks, burrs, hot spots, or irritation, keep nails trimmed short with a grinder or clippers, and inspect the thick paw pads after hikes on rough or icy terrain.

idealFor: Experienced handlers who understand independent, strong-willed primitive and hunting Spitz breeds
Active individuals and families who enjoy daily hiking, trail exploring, tracking, agility, or trick training
Households where the dog is included indoors as a constant companion rather than left isolated for long workdays
Homes with a securely fenced yard (at least 6 feet / 1.8 m high) and cool or temperate weather
Owners prepared for expressive vocalizations ('singing', howling, rooing) and heavy twice-yearly coat blows
notIdealFor: First-time or passive dog owners seeking an effortlessly biddable, low-energy pet
Apartment dwellers or noise-sensitive households where loud vocal greetings and howling would cause conflict
Households that leave dogs alone for long hours each day
Multi-dog homes expecting automatic compatibility with unfamiliar dogs (especially intact males) or small pets
Owners in hot climates who cannot provide indoor cooling and careful heat management

funFacts: In 1902, Hokkaido dogs assisted search parties looking for survivors of an Imperial Japanese Army regiment stranded in a catastrophic blizzard in the Hakkōda Mountains.
The indigenous Ainu people of northern Japan called these dogs 'Seta' and relied on them to track and hold brown bears and deer in deep mountain snow.
British zoologist Thomas Blakiston coined the name 'Ainu Ken' in 1869 before the breed was designated a Living Natural Monument of Japan in 1937 and named after the island of Hokkaido.
Like several other native Japanese breeds, the Hokkaido frequently has blue-black spots or pigmentation on its tongue, which is explicitly permitted by the breed standard.
Unlike the fastidious Shiba Inu that often avoids puddles, many Hokkaido dogs love splashing in creeks, swimming, and rolling in mud, though dried mud falls quickly off their harsh guard coat.
Since 2007, a white Hokkaido portraying the talking family father 'Otōsan' in a famous Japanese mobile-phone commercial campaign has made the breed a household icon in Japan.

faq.question: What is a Hokkaido Ken?
faq.answer: The Hokkaido Ken (also called the Hokkaido Inu or Ainu Ken) is a medium-sized native Japanese Spitz breed historically developed on the northern island of Hokkaido to hunt bear and deer in snowy mountain terrain. Today it is kept primarily as a devoted household companion, watchdog, and outdoor sporting partner.

faq.question: How big does a Hokkaido Ken get?
faq.answer: It is a sturdy medium-sized dog, though height ranges differ slightly between standards. Japanese preservation and North American breed-club standards specify 48.5 cm ± 3 cm (45.5–51.5 cm, or 18–20 inches) for males and 45.5 cm ± 3 cm (42.5–48.5 cm, or 17–19 inches) for females, whereas international conformation standards list 48.5–51.5 cm for males and 45.5–48.5 cm for females. Typical adult weight is 20–30 kg (44–66 lbs), though some preservation lines weigh roughly 13.6–25 kg (30–55 lbs).

faq.question: How long does a Hokkaido Ken live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 12 to 15 years when supported by responsible genetic screening, a lean diet, and routine veterinary care.

faq.question: What is Collie eye anomaly (CEA) in the Hokkaido Ken?
faq.answer: Collie eye anomaly is an autosomal recessive developmental eye condition associated with a 7.8-kb deletion in the NHEJ1 gene. Genotyping studies in Hokkaido dogs have found that roughly one-third are genetically affected and two-thirds are carriers. However, the condition is non-progressive after eight weeks of age, and nearly 90% of genetically affected Hokkaido dogs show either no vision loss or only mild choroidal hypoplasia. Responsible breeders use DNA testing and ophthalmic exams to avoid producing clinically impaired puppies while preserving genetic diversity.

faq.question: Is the Hokkaido Ken good for first-time dog owners?
faq.answer: Generally no. While deeply loyal and intelligent, the Hokkaido has a bold, independent working character, a strong prey drive, expressive vocal habits, and a tendency toward dog reactivity (particularly in intact males). It does best with an experienced handler committed to early socialization and daily mental and physical engagement.

faq.question: Does the Hokkaido Ken get along with other dogs and pets?
faq.answer: Because of its hunting heritage, the breed has a strong prey drive toward small animals and can display dog aggression or selectivity, especially between intact males. Early, carefully managed socialization helps, but compatibility with unfamiliar dogs or small pets should never be assumed.

faq.question: Is the Hokkaido Ken a quiet breed or a vocal breed?
faq.answer: It is a very vocal, expressive breed. Hokkaido dogs are famous for bursting into loud, multi-minute 'songs' when their owners return home, rooing at visiting friends, and howling or grumbling in protest when given a cue they would rather ignore.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should owners expect?
faq.answer: Outside of shedding season, grooming is straightforward: weekly brushing keeps the weatherproof coat clean, and the breed has almost no doggy odour even when it swims or plays in mud. Roughly twice a year, however, the dog blows its entire dense undercoat over several weeks, requiring daily brushing. The double coat must never be shaved.

faq.question: What are pica and psychogenic polydipsia in Hokkaido dogs?
faq.answer: Pica—chewing and swallowing non-food items such as rocks, socks, sticks, or toys—appears to have a familial tendency in the breed and has caused veterinary emergencies in multiple dogs. Psychogenic polydipsia (compulsive drinking of large quantities of water followed by regurgitating the excess) has also been observed, often linked to high drive, boredom, or anxiety. Keeping non-edible objects out of reach and providing ample daily exercise and enrichment are essential precautions.

faq.question: Is the Hokkaido Ken suitable for apartments or hot climates?
faq.answer: Apartment living is generally unsuitable because the breed is vocal, energetic, and thrives with a securely fenced yard (at least 6 feet high). Because its thick double coat is built for subzero snow, living in a hot climate requires indoor air conditioning or cool tiled floors, shade, plenty of water, and restricting outdoor exercise to the coolest hours of the day.

breeds.name: Hovawart
breeds.group: FCI Group 2 — Pinscher and Schnauzer, Molossoid breeds, Swiss Mountain and Cattledogs; Section 2.2 — Molossoid breeds, Mountain type; working trial required.

origin.region: Historically associated with German farms and estates, including the Harz and Black Forest regions; the modern breed was reconstructed from 1922.

overview.summary: A powerful German working dog bred to guard homes and property, the Hovawart is loyal to its family, self-confident, alert and happiest when given purposeful activity.
overview.description: The Hovawart is a substantial, long-haired working companion with a guarding instinct and a close bond with its household. Developed to watch over farms and property, it is capable of making decisions without constant direction. A well-raised Hovawart can be affectionate, composed and versatile, but its confidence, size and independent judgement call for consistent training, careful socialisation and daily engagement. It is not simply a yard dog: it needs to live as part of the family and have regular opportunities to use its body and mind.
overview.history: The Hovawart's name comes from older German words associated with a farm or estate and a watchman. Dogs of this type guarded homes, farms and livestock in Germany. The modern reconstruction of the breed began in 1922 using suitable farm dogs and carefully managed outcrosses, including German Shepherd Dogs, Newfoundlands and Leonbergers. The FCI records recognition as a breed in 1937 and working-dog status in 1964. Selection for hip health has been an important feature of the breed's modern development.
overview.originalPurpose: Guarding farms, estates, property and livestock, with the independence needed to watch over an area.
currentRoles: Search-and-rescue or other structured working activities when training and aptitude are suitable
Dog-sport partner for obedience, agility and working trials

physical.coatType: Long, thick, slightly wavy hair that lies close to the body, with relatively little undercoat and feathering on the neck, underside, backs of the legs and tail.
physical.coatLength: Long-haired, with shorter hair on the head and fronts of the legs.
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate, with loose hair during seasonal shedding; the coat needs regular thorough brushing.
distinctiveFeatures: Powerful, medium-large build with a slightly elongated body
Males and females differ in head shape and body build
Long, slightly wavy coat with feathering on the legs and tail
Black-and-tan dogs have defined tan markings on the face, chest and legs
Black dogs have a shiny black coat; blond dogs have a medium-blond coat that lightens toward the legs and belly
Triangular, hanging ears with gently rounded tips
Oval, dark- to medium-brown eyes
A bushy tail that reaches below the hock and changes carriage with the dog's mood

traits: Loyal and strongly devoted to familiar people
Self-confident and composed
Alert and naturally protective of home and family
Intelligent, with a strong sense of smell
Versatile and capable of learning varied working tasks
Independent enough to assess a situation without constant direction
May be strong-willed and intense in play, making training and socialisation important
Benefits from positive, consistent guidance rather than intimidation

exercise.level: High. Plan substantial daily exercise and mental work. The Royal Kennel Club lists more than two hours per day as a breed-profile guideline; adapt the routine to the dog's age, health and conditioning.
activities: Brisk walks and age-appropriate hikes
Scent work, tracking games and nose-led exploration
Reward-based obedience and everyday skills
Agility, mantrailing or working trials after physical maturity and appropriate conditioning
Puzzle feeders and supervised problem-solving games
Controlled play with compatible dogs

grooming.level: Moderate. Coat length and feathering can tangle if neglected.
grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly several times a week, combing through the whole coat rather than only its surface. Check behind the ears, around the elbows and the feathering on the backs of the legs for knots; increase brushing during shedding.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty or needed, using a dog-safe shampoo and rinsing thoroughly. Dry the coat and paws after wet outdoor activity.
notes: Introduce brushing, paw handling, ear checks and tooth brushing early.
Check ears and paws for grass seeds, debris, redness or soreness after outdoor activity.
Inspect the skin while brushing, especially under feathering and around tangles.
Keep nails trimmed to a comfortable length.
Avoid clipping the coat close to the skin unless a veterinarian recommends it for a medical reason.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for inexperienced owners. The breed is intelligent and versatile but also confident, protective and capable of independent decisions.
tips: Begin reward-based training and calm, positive exposure to everyday life in puppyhood.
Teach loose-leash walking, recall, settling and reliable responses around visitors before the dog reaches full size.
Use short, varied sessions that give the dog a clear purpose.
Reward calm behaviour at doors, fences and when meeting unfamiliar people.
Avoid harsh or confrontational handling; build cooperation through consistency and trust.
Provide structured mental work as well as physical activity.
Choose dog sports or working activities that fit the dog's temperament and physical development.
training.socialization: Start in puppyhood and continue throughout life. Introduce people, dogs, places, sounds and handling in safe, positive, controlled situations. Socialisation should build calm judgement and confidence, not force the dog to welcome every stranger. Maintain supervision and secure management because the breed has a guarding background.

climates: Cool and temperate conditions
Variable weather when the dog has shelter, water and a suitable resting place
Warm weather with shade, ventilation, fresh water and exercise during cooler hours

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate for the dog's life stage, body condition, activity level and veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.adult: Use a predictable daily schedule, but choose meal count and portion size according to age, activity, body condition and the food being fed. Ask a veterinarian for an individual plan.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet in measured portions and monitor body condition as well as weight. Large-breed puppies grow in spurts, so adjust intake with veterinary guidance and avoid excessive exercise while joints are developing. Include training treats in the daily calorie allowance, keep fresh water available and make diet changes gradually.
considerations: Discuss an appropriate growth diet and healthy growth rate with a veterinarian when feeding a puppy.
Reassess portions when activity, age or body condition changes.
Do not add calcium, vitamins or supplements unless a veterinarian recommends them.
Use training treats sparingly and include them in the daily ration.
Ask the veterinarian whether individual health findings call for a specific diet.
nutrition.note: No authoritative Hovawart-specific puppy or senior meal frequency was established in the reviewed sources. Nutrition guidance here is general advice, not a prescription for an individual dog.

health.overview: Hovawarts have benefited from deliberate selection for hip health, but that does not remove inherited risk in an individual dog. Breed-club guidance recommends hip scoring, thyroid testing and degenerative myelopathy DNA testing for breeding animals. These recommendations are most directly relevant when choosing a puppy or planning a breeding; they are not a diagnosis, and results vary by country, population and screening programme.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — a developmental hip-joint condition that can affect mobility; the breed has long-running screening and selection programmes.
Hypothyroidism or thyroid dysfunction — thyroid testing is included in one Hovawart club's breeding-health guidance.
Degenerative myelopathy (DM) susceptibility — DNA testing can identify the SOD1 variant associated with risk, but a result does not guarantee clinical signs will develop.

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) — a life-threatening emergency possible in dogs, particularly large or deep-chested dogs. Sudden abdominal swelling, unproductive retching, restlessness or collapse require emergency veterinary care.
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary examinations and follow an appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention plan.
Maintain a lean body condition and discuss lameness, stiffness or reluctance to exercise promptly.
Ask breeders for documented hip scores and relevant thyroid and DM screening results for breeding dogs.
Discuss the meaning and limitations of a DM DNA result with a veterinarian or knowledgeable breeder.
Learn the warning signs of bloat and identify an emergency veterinary service before one is needed.
Brush teeth regularly and include ears, skin, paws and nails in routine checks.
recommendedScreenings: Hip scoring or hip-dysplasia assessment for breeding dogs, using an accepted national scheme.
Thyroid-function testing for breeding dogs as advised by the relevant breed club and veterinarian.
Degenerative myelopathy (SOD1 variant) DNA testing for breeding dogs, interpreted alongside the intended mating and applicable breed-club rules.
When buying a puppy, request written copies of the parents' screening results rather than relying only on verbal assurances.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly, ideally daily, with a dog-specific toothbrush and toothpaste. Arrange veterinary oral examinations and professional cleaning when recommended.
health.earCare: Check the ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge, debris or repeated head-shaking. Clean only when needed with a veterinarian-approved product; seek advice if irritation persists.
health.skinCare: Check the skin during brushing, paying attention to tangles, damp areas, parasites and irritation beneath the feathering. Dry wet coat and paws, and ask a veterinarian about persistent itching, hair loss or skin changes.

notIdealFor: People seeking a low-exercise or low-involvement dog
Owners unable to provide consistent training, socialisation and purposeful activities

funFacts: The breed's name combines older German words associated with a farm or estate and a watchman.
The modern breed reconstruction began in 1922 and included managed outcrosses before a consistent working type was re-established.
The Hovawart is recognised in three standard colours: black and tan, black, and blond.
The breed standard describes a body slightly longer than the dog's height at the withers.
The Hovawart's nose and versatile working background suit activities such as tracking and scent work.

faq.question: Is the Hovawart a good dog for first-time owners?
faq.answer: It is usually a better match for owners prepared for a large, intelligent and protective working breed. The Hovawart needs regular exercise, early socialisation and consistent training, so a first-time owner should seek experienced support and plan for a substantial daily commitment.

faq.question: How big does a Hovawart get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 63–70 cm for males and 58–65 cm for females. A UK breed-club profile reports typical weight ranges of 30–40 kg for males and 25–35 kg for females; individual dogs vary.

faq.question: What colours do Hovawarts come in?
faq.answer: The three standard colours are black and tan, black, and blond. Black-and-tan dogs have clearly defined lighter markings, while blond dogs have a medium-blond coat that lightens toward the legs and belly.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Hovawart need?
faq.answer: It is an active working breed. The Royal Kennel Club's profile recommends more than two hours of exercise per day as a guide. Adapt the routine to the dog's age, health and fitness, and keep exercise controlled while a puppy is growing.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a Hovawart breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip scores, thyroid-function results and degenerative myelopathy DNA test results for the breeding dogs. Screening recommendations vary between countries and clubs, so ask how the results were assessed and discuss them with a veterinarian.

faq.question: Is a Hovawart good with children and other dogs?
faq.answer: There is no guarantee based on breed alone. Individual temperament, early positive socialisation, training and adult supervision matter, especially because Hovawarts are strong dogs with guarding instincts and can play intensely with other dogs.

faq.question: Does a Hovawart need a lot of grooming?
faq.answer: The long coat needs regular thorough brushing, especially behind the ears and around the feathering on the legs. Check the coat more carefully during seasonal shedding and dry the coat and paws after wet outdoor activity.

overview.summary: A miniature sighthound of exceptional grace and slender elegance, combining the speed and visual chasing instinct of a coursing hound with the affectionate, warmth-seeking devotion of a close indoor companion.
overview.description: The Italian Greyhound is the smallest of the sighthounds—a true Greyhound in miniature, built with even more slender proportions and refined bone. Its body fits into a square outline where body length is equal to or barely less than height at the withers, with a deep, narrow chest let down to the elbows, an arched loin, a pronounced abdominal tuck-up, and long, lean legs. The head is narrow and elongated with large, expressive dark eyes and small, fine-textured rose ears that fold back against the nape when relaxed and stand out horizontally ('flying' or 'propeller' ears) when alert. Lively, docile, and deeply affectionate with its immediate family—preferring to snuggle under blankets or on a lap rather than sit on the floor—it retains a true sighthound's flash-and-dash speed and strong instinct to bolt after small moving animals. Because of its fine leg bones, short satin-like coat, and minimal body fat, it requires protection from cold weather and careful management to prevent jumping injuries.
overview.history: Descended from small sighthounds kept in ancient Egypt at the court of the Pharaohs and across Greece (Laconia) and Anatolia more than 2,000 years ago, the breed reached Italy by the beginning of the fifth century BC, where it was depicted on vases, bowls, and Roman sculptures. It flourished in Renaissance Italy among aristocratic households and was immortalized in works by masters such as Giotto, Carpaccio, Sassetta, Memling, Van der Weyden, Hieronymus Bosch, and Tiepolo. Across Europe, monarchs and nobles—including Anne of Denmark, Mary Beatrice d'Este, Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, and Queen Victoria—kept these miniature hounds as treasured companions, and the African king Lobengula once traded 200 head of cattle for a single dog. Organized studbook registrations began in Britain in 1874 and in the United States in 1886. After the First and Second World Wars nearly extinguished European bloodlines, surviving North American and Austrian stock helped rebuild the modern population.
overview.originalPurpose: Noble companion and small-game sighthound used to course hare, rabbit, and other small, fast-moving quarry
currentRoles: Agility, rally, and reward-based obedience competitor

distinctiveFeatures: Square body outline in which body length is equal to or barely less than height at the withers (32–38 cm)
Elongated, narrow head reaching up to 40% of withers height, with parallel skull and muzzle axes and skull length equal to half the total head length
Large, roundish, expressive dark eyes with pigmented rims
Very high-set, small rose ears folded back on the nape at rest and held out laterally ('flying' or 'propeller' ears) when attentive
Deep, narrow chest reaching the elbows, arched dorsal-lumbar topline, very sloping muscled croup, and accentuated sternal tuck-up
Long, straight, finely boned legs with oval hare feet where the two middle toes and nails are slightly longer than the outer ones
Low-set, fine tail tapering to the tip, carried low and straight in its first half and curved in its second half, reaching the hock
Springy, harmonious, high-stepping trot with good forward reach and a fast, sharp-springing gallop capable of bursts up to 60 km/h (35 mph)
Weight up to 5 kg maximum in international standards (ideal 3.6–4.5 kg in British standards; 3.2–6.4 kg / 7–14 lbs in North American profiles)

Coat colour rules differ by standard: international conformation standards allow only solid black, grey, and isabella (with white limited to chest and feet), whereas British and North American standards also allow red, cream, white, and parti-colour (while all standards disqualify brindle and black-and-tan markings)

traits: Deeply affectionate and cuddliness-loving with family
Lively and vivacious
Docile and gentle
Playful well into adulthood
Emotionally sensitive
Alert and watchful
Clever problem solver
Can appear aloof or reserved with strangers
Independent and occasionally stubborn about routine commands
Strong visual chasing and prey instinct

exercise.level: Moderate to active. Combines energetic bursts of running and play with long periods of indoor lounging and cuddling.
activities: Daily walks using a secure martingale collar or properly fitted harness and leash
Supervised sprinting and play in a safely enclosed, fenced area
Indoor interactive play (especially in multi-Italian Greyhound households)
Lure coursing and amateur racing
Age-appropriate agility, rally, and positive-reinforcement trick training

grooming.level: Low for the coat, but high priority for daily dental hygiene and frequent nail grinding.
grooming.brushing: Wipe or brush occasionally with a soft bristle brush, hound glove, or damp cloth to remove loose hair and keep the satin coat gleaming; bathe only when necessary.
grooming.bathing: Rarely required unless the dog gets dirty; use a gentle dog shampoo and dry thoroughly so the dog does not become chilled.
notes: Daily tooth brushing with canine toothpaste and yearly veterinary dental examinations/cleanings are essential because the breed is highly prone to periodontal disease.

Grind or file nails 1 to 3 times per week using an electric rotary grinder; this breed's nails and inner quicks grow rapidly, and maintaining short nails that clear the floor when standing helps preserve foot conformation and reduce leg-fracture risk.
Because the breed has a hare foot, the two middle nails naturally remain slightly longer than the outer two nails.
Dress the dog in warm sweaters, coats, or boots during cold or wet weather, as its thin coat and low body fat offer little insulation.
Inspect the fine skin regularly for scrapes, abrasions, or irritation.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Quick to solve problems and responsive to gentle praise and treats, yet sensitive to harsh corrections, independent-minded, and notoriously slow to house-train reliably.
tips: Use reward-based training with small, immediate food rewards and enthusiastic praise; harsh verbal or physical corrections will cause these sensitive dogs to shut down.

Commit to diligent house-training for the first 1 to 2 years: puppies only begin developing true bladder control around 14 to 16 weeks of age and need very frequent outdoor trips or a dedicated indoor paper/litter area.

Never crate a puppy for more than 2 to 3 hours at a time; for longer absences, use a secure, covered exercise pen with paper/pad area, bedding, and safe chew toys so the puppy does not learn to soil its crate.

Teach puppies how to step or jump safely off low surfaces first; young puppies often leap fearlessly off high beds, sofas, or tables before their bones mature, which is a leading cause of radius and ulna fractures.
Always use a martingale lead or escape-proof harness outdoors and never allow the dog off-leash in unfenced areas, as even obedience-trained dogs will bolt into traffic after a cat or squirrel.
Avoid unsupervised all-size dog parks; limit off-leash group play to secure areas with dogs of similar small size and gentle play style.
training.socialization: Because Italian Greyhounds bond intensely with their owners and can be aloof or timid toward unfamiliar people and children, introduce puppies early and consistently to gentle people, well-mannered children, calm dogs, and neighbourhood sights and sounds.

climates: Temperate climates
Warm climates
Cold or northern climates only as a strictly indoor dog provided with warm clothing outdoors and heated indoor living spaces
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Italian Greyhounds are indoor companion dogs—never kennel, backyard, or basement dogs—that thrive on physical closeness and often do best in pairs or in households where someone is home during the day.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, energy-dense, complete and balanced small-breed dog food formulated for puppy, adult, or senior life stages, or a veterinarian-supervised home-prepared diet.

feedingFrequency.puppy: 3 meals daily until at least 6 months of age (some puppies continue needing 3 daily meals for several additional months due to their small stomach capacity and high energy demands).
feedingFrequency.adult: 2 meals daily, with clean, fresh water available at all times.

nutrition.guidelines: Because an Italian Greyhound's stomach capacity is small relative to its metabolic rate, feed a nutrient-dense, high-quality diet in measured portions. Watch calorie intake and training treats carefully to prevent excess weight, which places dangerous strain on slender legs and joints. On an Italian Greyhound in proper body condition, the tips of the hip bones should just be visible, while the ribs should not be visible but should be easily felt beneath a thin layer of flesh.
considerations: Feed puppies three times a day until at least 6 months of age so their small stomachs can meet growth and energy needs.
Keep training treats tiny and account for them in daily calories to prevent obesity.
Monitor body condition using the breed-specific visual benchmark: hip bones barely visible and ribs easily palpable but not protruding.
Combine appropriate nutrition with daily tooth brushing to manage the breed's susceptibility to gum and periodontal disease.
Consult a veterinarian promptly if digestive sensitivities, food allergies, or unexplained weight changes occur.
nutrition.note: Puppy (3 meals/day until at least 6 months) and adult (2 meals/day) schedules reflect national breed-club guidance; senior meal frequency should be individualized with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Italian Greyhound is generally a hardy, long-lived toy sighthound that routinely reaches 14 to 15 years of age or more (and shows a 0% incidence of hip dysplasia in orthopedic registry data), but several hereditary, immune-mediated, dental, and traumatic conditions require proactive management. Peer-reviewed genetic research has established breed-specific DNA tests for three inherited disorders: autosomal recessive familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH / amelogenesis imperfecta, caused by an ENAM gene deletion with an estimated 14% affected and 30% carrier prevalence), progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-IG1, affecting 2%–4% of the breed across 5 susceptibility loci), and primary closed angle glaucoma (PCAG, associated with two linked susceptibility variants). In addition, historical population bottlenecks and homozygosity in the dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class I and II regions predispose the breed—especially females—to autoimmune disorders including autoimmune thyroiditis, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, and immune-mediated polyarthritis. Clinically, periodontal disease and radius/ulna leg fractures in young dogs jumping from furniture are among the most frequent everyday veterinary concerns.
commonConditions: Periodontal disease, gingivitis, and premature tooth loss (common in dogs that do not receive daily tooth brushing and regular veterinary dental cleanings)

Familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH / autosomal recessive amelogenesis imperfecta), caused by a 5-bp deletion (c.1991_1995delTTTCC) in exon 10 of the ENAM gene on chromosome 13 (estimated 14% affected and 30% carriers; causes rough, thin, brownish-mottled enamel and small pointed teeth, though not linked to periodontal disease)

Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-IG1), a progressive photoreceptor degeneration leading to blindness that affects 2%–4% of Italian Greyhounds (average diagnosis age 6.5 years; 5-locus genetic panel identifies 90% of breed susceptibility, with aa or dd genotypes carrying a 30x risk)

Primary closed angle glaucoma (PCAG), an acute, painful intraocular pressure spike causing optic nerve damage and blindness (average diagnosis age 3.9 years, range 0.5–6 years; dogs homozygous for two linked susceptibility variants have a 60x higher risk)

Autoimmune disorders and autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), linked in peer-reviewed studies to genome-wide and DLA class I/II homozygosity (females are 2–5 times more likely to be affected; manifestations include immune-mediated hemolytic anemia [IMHA], immune-mediated polyarthritis [IMPA], immune-mediated thrombocytopenia [IMTP], thyroiditis, pemphigus, Addison's disease, and steroid-responsive meningitis)
Traumatic forelimb fractures (particularly radius and ulna fractures), most common in puppies and young adolescents leaping off beds, sofas, stairs, or during rough play
Patellar luxation and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head)
Less frequent or sporadic reported conditions: idiopathic seizures/epilepsy, allergies, digestive sensitivities, congenital deafness, and cervical intervertebral disc disease
preventiveCare: Brush teeth daily with canine toothpaste starting as soon as adult teeth erupt, and schedule annual professional veterinary dental examinations and cleanings.
Grind nails 1 to 3 times weekly so they do not touch the floor when standing, supporting proper foot posture and reducing slip-and-fracture hazards.
Prevent puppies and young dogs from jumping off beds, couches, tables, or out of arms, and supervise play strictly around stairs, large dogs, and young children.

Verify that breeding stock has completed mandatory pre-breeding clinical evaluations (patellas, thyroid, and annual ophthalmologist exams) and recommended breed-specific DNA panels (PRA-IG1, PCAG glaucoma, FEH enamel hypoplasia, and genetic diversity).
Keep the dog on a martingale collar or secure harness and leash whenever outdoors in unfenced areas to prevent high-speed traffic accidents triggered by prey drive.
Protect the dog from cold and wet weather with sweaters or coats, and provide warm indoor bedding.
recommendedScreenings: Patella evaluation by a veterinarian (once after 12 months of age)
Thyroid blood evaluation (annually from ages 2 to 4 years, then biennially until age 8 years)
Ophthalmologist evaluation by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (annually until age 10 years)
Susceptibility to Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA-IG1) DNA test (5-locus panel; once at any age)
Susceptibility to Primary Closed Angle Glaucoma (PCAG) DNA test (once at any age)
Familial Enamel Hypoplasia (FEH / ENAM) DNA test (once at any age)
Canine Genetic Diversity DNA test (STR and DLA class I/II haplotype assessment to reduce homozygosity and autoimmune risk)
Brucellosis (Brucella canis) screening for breeding pairs prior to each mating
health.dentalCare: Daily tooth brushing with an unflavoured canine toothpaste and a soft canine toothbrush is the single most critical routine care habit for an Italian Greyhound, paired with yearly veterinary dental examinations and cleanings. Distinguish between preventable periodontal gum disease and inherited familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH), which causes congenital mottled, thin enamel and can be identified by DNA testing.
health.earCare: Inspect the delicate, folded rose ears weekly for wax buildup, redness, or odour, and clean gently only as needed with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser.
health.skinCare: Because the skin is fine, tight, and covered only by a very short single coat with minimal subcutaneous fat, inspect regularly for scrapes, bruises, or dryness, provide soft padded bedding to protect bony prominences, and use warm clothing in cold weather.

idealFor: Adults, couples, or families with older, gentle, considerate children who respect a finely boned toy sighthound
Apartment and city dwellers as well as country homeowners who want an affectionate, clean indoor lap companion
Households where someone is home much of the day or where a second small sighthound provides companionship
Owners committed to daily tooth brushing, weekly nail grinding, patient house-training, and cold-weather clothing
People who enjoy daily leashed walks, enclosed running play, agility, or lure coursing
notIdealFor: Households with very young, boisterous, or unsupervised children, or homes with large, rough-playing dogs
Owners who expect reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas around wildlife or traffic
People who work long hours away from home every day and would leave a single dog crated or isolated
Anyone unwilling to manage a prolonged house-training process or perform daily dental and weekly nail care
Households seeking an outdoor, kennel, or cold-hardy dog

funFacts: The Italian Greyhound is the smallest member of the sighthound (gazehound) family, yet it can sprint in bursts of up to 60 km/h (35 mph).
When the dog is alert, its high-set folded ears lift at the base and stand out horizontally to the sides—a distinctive posture known in the breed standard as 'flying ears' or 'propeller ears'.

Italian Greyhounds appear in paintings by Renaissance and early modern masters including Giotto, Vittore Carpaccio, Sassetta, Hans Memling, Rogier van der Weyden, Hieronymus Bosch, and Giambattista Tiepolo.

Royal admirers across history included Anne of Denmark, Mary Beatrice d'Este, Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, and Queen Victoria, while the southern African king Lobengula once traded 200 head of cattle for a single Italian Greyhound.
The breed has 'hare feet', meaning the two middle toes and their nails are naturally longer than the outer toes, creating an oval, arched foot built for sprinting.
In orthopedic registry statistics evaluating 157 dog breeds for hip dysplasia, the Italian Greyhound ranked as the least affected breed with an incidence of 0%.

faq.question: What is an Italian Greyhound?
faq.answer: The Italian Greyhound (also called the Piccolo Levriero Italiano or Italian Sighthound) is the smallest of the sighthound breeds—a true Greyhound in miniature bred for more than two millennia both as an aristocratic lap companion and as a swift courser of small game.

faq.question: How big does an Italian Greyhound get?
faq.answer: Both males and females stand 32 to 38 cm (about 12.5 to 15 inches) at the withers, with a square body outline whose length equals or is barely less than its height. International conformation standards specify a maximum weight of 5 kg (11 lbs) for both sexes, British standards list an ideal weight of 3.6 to 4.5 kg (8–10 lbs), and North American profiles describe a typical range of 3.2 to 6.4 kg (7–14 lbs).

faq.question: Why do coat colour rules differ for Italian Greyhounds in different countries?
faq.answer: European and international conformation standards allow only solid black, grey (blue/slate), and isabella (fawn/beige) in any shade, tolerating white markings solely on the chest and feet and disqualifying multi-coloured coats. By contrast, British and North American standards also accept red, cream, white, and parti-colour (white broken with coloured markings). Across all major standards, brindle markings and black-and-tan patterns are disqualifications.

faq.question: Are Italian Greyhounds good for families with young children?
faq.answer: Generally no. Because of their fine bone structure and sensitive, sometimes timid nature, national breed-club guidance advises against placing Italian Greyhounds in homes with very young or rambunctious children or large, boisterous dogs where accidental falls or rough play can easily break a leg. They do best with adults or older, gentle children.

faq.question: Why are leg fractures a concern in Italian Greyhound puppies?
faq.answer: Until skeletal maturity, an Italian Greyhound's long, slender radius and ulna bones are vulnerable to snapping from awkward landings. Young puppies often leap fearlessly from high beds, sofas, tables, or a handler's arms ('thinking they can fly'), so owners must supervise furniture access, teach controlled low steps, and keep nails ground short for traction.

faq.question: Are Italian Greyhounds difficult to house-train?
faq.answer: Yes, house-training requires patience and consistency over the first one to two years. Puppies only begin developing reliable bladder control between 14 and 16 weeks of age, cannot hold their bladder for long workdays, and dislike cold rain. Successful owners use frequent scheduled outdoor trips, positive rewards, or a dedicated indoor paper/litter area, and never crate a puppy for more than 2 to 3 hours at a stretch.

faq.question: Can an Italian Greyhound be trusted off-leash in an unfenced area?
faq.answer: No. Despite being cuddly lapdogs indoors, Italian Greyhounds retain a powerful visual sighthound prey drive and will bolt instantly after a squirrel, cat, or rabbit—ignoring recall cues and running into traffic. Outside of a securely fenced yard, they should always wear a properly fitted martingale collar or escape-proof harness and leash.

faq.question: How often should an Italian Greyhound's teeth and nails be cared for?
faq.answer: Teeth should be brushed daily with canine toothpaste and examined annually by a veterinarian, as periodontal disease is very common in the breed. Nails should be ground 1 to 3 times a week with an electric grinder so they clear the floor when the dog stands; the breed's nails and inner quicks grow rapidly, and long nails distort the hare foot and increase injury risk.

faq.question: What genetic and clinical health tests are recommended for Italian Greyhounds?
faq.answer: National breed-club guidelines recommend three clinical screenings—veterinary patella evaluation (after 12 months of age), thyroid blood testing (annually from ages 2 to 4, then biennially to age 8), and annual board-certified ophthalmologist exams (until age 10)—along with DNA tests for progressive retinal atrophy susceptibility (PRA-IG1), primary closed angle glaucoma susceptibility (PCAG), familial enamel hypoplasia (FEH / ENAM), and canine genetic diversity.

faq.question: How can you tell if an Italian Greyhound is at a healthy weight?
faq.answer: Because excess weight stresses their slender limbs, Italian Greyhounds should be kept lean. On a dog in ideal body condition, the tips of the hip bones should just be visible, and the ribs should not be visible but should be easily felt under a thin covering of flesh.
