overview.summary: A medium-sized, loyal, and adaptable German companion and house dog, celebrated for its spirited personality, deep devotion to its family, agile jumping ability, and two distinct coat varieties: rough-haired with a signature beard and smooth-haired with flowing furnishings.
overview.description: The Kromfohrländer is an athletic, medium-sized companion dog originating in Germany, characterized by a slightly rectangular silhouette in which body length slightly exceeds height at the withers. The breed is bred in two distinct coat varieties: a rough-haired (wirehaired) variety defined by a characteristic beard, longer facial hair, and a harsh, wiry outer coat across the back and limbs; and a smooth-haired variety distinguished by a clean-shaven face without a beard, close-lying body hair, longer feathering on the ears, chest, and legs, and a well-plumed tail. Both varieties display a white ground colour adorned with light brown to very dark brown patches or saddle markings, centered around a distinctive head mask split by a symmetrical, uninterrupted white blaze reaching the forehead or nape. Spirited, docile, and highly adaptable, the breed combines lively indoor affection with a sensitive, thoughtful nature. It forms an exceptionally intense bond with its household—often choosing a favourite person—while maintaining a natural, polite reserve around unfamiliar people and strange dogs. Its keen intelligence and desire for companionship make patient, reward-based training essential.
overview.history: The Kromfohrländer is one of the youngest recognized German dog breeds, originating in 1945 in the aftermath of the Second World War near the town of Siegen in southern North Rhine-Westphalia. The breed was established by Ilse Schleifenbaum, who took in a scruffy, wirehaired stray terrier-type dog named Peter that had been found in northern France by American soldiers and served as their military troop mascot. When Peter mated with a local black-and-white female terrier named Fiffi, the resulting puppies exhibited a remarkably uniform, appealing appearance and loving character. Recognized ancestors in the breed's foundation include the wirehaired Fox Terrier and the Grand Griffon Vendéen. The breed takes its name from the local geographical district 'krom Fohr' (Low German for 'crooked furrow') near Hilchenbach and Siegen where Schleifenbaum lived. Formal breed club stewardship began with the establishment of the national breed club in 1955, the same year the breed gained definitive international recognition. The breed subsequently expanded to North America, where dedicated fanciers established national club representation and studbook recording in the early twenty-first century.

In the rough-haired variety, the coat is harsh and thick with longer hair on the face forming a beard, and harsher hair along the back and limbs. In the smooth-haired variety, the coat lies close to the body without a beard, featuring short facial hair, longer hair on the ears, lower neck, and chest, distinct feathering along the backs of the legs and thighs, and a plumed tail.

grooming.level: Low to moderate. Straightforward routine upkeep for both coat types, though the rough-haired variety requires periodic hand-stripping to maintain its proper harsh texture.
grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a firm bristle brush or pin brush to remove loose hair and prevent tangles in the feathering. The rough-haired coat requires regular hand-stripping or plucking with a stripping knife several times a year to remove dead wire hair and preserve coat texture; electric clipping or shaving should be avoided as it destroys the wiry texture.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally as needed. The coat naturally repels dirt, dries quickly, and carries virtually no typical doggy odour, even after outdoor play or when damp.
notes: The rough-haired coat should be hand-stripped periodically rather than clipped or shaved, which softens the wire and alters colour.
The smooth-haired variety requires routine brushing through the longer feathering on the ears, neck, chest, tail, and back of the legs to prevent knots.
The coat naturally repels mud and dirt and has little to no doggy odour even when wet.
Begin gentle nail trimming in early puppyhood and maintain it consistently, as the breed's natural sensitivity can make foot handling challenging if neglected.
Inspect the semi-drop ears weekly for dirt, wax, or redness, and brush teeth regularly to support oral hygiene.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Highly intelligent, intuitive, and quick to learn commands, but its emotional sensitivity requires gentle, patient guidance rather than heavy-handed pressure.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement with treats, gentle praise, and play.
Avoid harsh verbal scolding or physical corrections, as sensitive dogs easily become inhibited or timid under pressure.
Keep training sessions engaging, short, and varied to channel the breed's problem-solving intelligence.
Gradually build confidence for independent activities such as competitive agility.
Introduce novel people, animals, and environments slowly at the dog's own pace, keeping in mind that the breed prefers familiar companions over crowded dog parks.
Provide plenty of mental enrichment through trick training, puzzle solving, and agility games.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, comprehensive socialization during early puppyhood and continue throughout adolescence. Expose the puppy positively to varied people, calm dogs, novel surfaces, and household sounds. Because the breed is naturally reserved with strangers and selective with unfamiliar dogs, allow the dog to assess new acquaintances at its own pace rather than forcing immediate physical interactions.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Strongly attached to its household and particularly to its primary caregiver, the breed thrives on constant family inclusion. It does not tolerate prolonged isolation or outdoor kennel living well, and can become anxious or unhappy if left alone for extended periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality dog food formulated for active medium-sized dogs, tailored to the individual's life stage, body condition, and energy output.
nutrition.guidelines: Provide a high-quality, balanced diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. Individual appetites vary considerably: some individuals are finicky or selective eaters, while others consume meals with enthusiasm. Because the breed is naturally active and rarely overeats, portions should be measured to maintain lean muscle mass and an ideal body condition. Consult a veterinarian or breeder to determine customized puppy and adult feeding amounts, and ensure clean, fresh water is available at all times.
considerations: Appetite varies between individuals, ranging from selective eaters to enthusiastic feeders.
High-quality, nutrient-dense nutrition supports steady energy for this active breed.

health.overview: The Kromfohrländer is a relatively rare breed developed from a small foundation stock, making genetic surveillance and responsible breeding practices essential. Scientifically validated DNA screening has identified an autosomal recessive missense mutation in the FAM83G gene (c.155G>C, p.R52P) on canine chromosome 5 responsible for hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (HFH), also known as digital hyperkeratosis or 'corny feet'. An inherited bleeding disorder, von Willebrand disease (vWD Type I), is also recognized in the breed, and pre-breeding DNA testing allows breeders to identify carriers and prevent affected litters. Other conditions reported within breed populations include autoimmune disorders, idiopathic epilepsy, cystinuria, patellar luxation, and spondylosis. Pre-breeding health protocols in its country of origin require general veterinary fitness certification, dental charting, and mandatory genetic testing for digital hyperkeratosis alongside DNA archival for ongoing scientific research.
commonConditions: Hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (HFH / digital hyperkeratosis), an autosomal recessive dermatological disorder caused by a missense mutation in the FAM83G gene (c.155G>C, p.R52P) leading to severely thickened, hardened paw pads with painful fissures, abnormal nail growth, and coat texture changes beginning around 4 to 5 months of age
Von Willebrand disease (vWD Type I), an inherited blood-clotting deficiency causing prolonged bleeding from mucosal surfaces or surgical wounds, manageable through pre-breeding DNA testing
Autoimmune disorders, documented as an immune-mediated health concern in the breed population
Idiopathic epilepsy, a neurological seizure disorder reported in breed health surveillance
Cystinuria, an inherited metabolic condition predisposing dogs to the formation of cystine urinary bladder stones
Patellar luxation, an orthopedic condition involving kneecap instability or dislocation
Spondylosis, a degenerative spinal condition characterized by bony spurs along the vertebrae in maturing dogs
preventiveCare: Ensure breeding stock undergoes DNA testing for hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (FAM83G) and von Willebrand disease to avoid carrier-to-carrier matings and prevent affected offspring.
Review family health histories with a veterinarian, paying close attention to autoimmune, neurological, urinary, and orthopedic backgrounds.
Inspect paw pads, interdigital spaces, and nails regularly for signs of thickening, hardening, painful cracks, or lameness, seeking prompt veterinary care if lesions develop.
Maintain routine veterinary wellness visits, dental cleanings, parasite preventives, and core vaccinations.
Support joint health and longevity with regular moderate exercise, gradual positive nail care, and maintaining a lean, athletic body condition.
recommendedScreenings: Canine Footpad Hyperkeratosis (HFH) DNA Test (FAM83G c.155G>C variant)
Von Willebrand Disease Type I (vWD Type I) DNA Test
Pre-breeding general veterinary clinical examination and dental charting
Patellar luxation clinical veterinary evaluation
health.dentalCare: Establish a routine dental care program early in life, including regular tooth brushing with dog-safe toothpaste and periodic professional veterinary cleanings. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth (a pincer bite is permitted, and absence of more than two molars or more than three premolars is disqualified). Adults generally maintain sound dentition, though occasional tooth loss can occur with advancing age.
health.earCare: Inspect the semi-drop ears weekly during regular grooming for signs of wax buildup, redness, debris, or foul odour. Clean the outer ear gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleaner when necessary, and seek veterinary advice if persistent head shaking or discharge occurs.
health.skinCare: Examine the paw pads and skin regularly for signs of excessive keratinization, cracking, or tenderness. In dogs affected by hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis, clinical signs typically emerge between 4 and 5 months of age with hardened, cracked footpads, rapid-growing hard nails, and duller coat texture. Routine inspection and genetic testing provide the most reliable safeguards.

funFacts: The breed was established in 1945 and is one of Germany's youngest recognized companion breeds.

The entire breed descends from a stray wirehaired terrier mix named Peter, who was discovered by American troops in northern France during the Second World War and served as their beloved troop mascot before being adopted by the breed's founder.
The breed name honors the historical geographical district 'krom Fohr' (Low German for 'crooked furrow') near Siegen in North Rhine-Westphalia, where the original kennel was located.
A distinctive breed trait is the famous greeting grin, where happy dogs curl their lips into a toothy 'smile' and may sneeze when enthusiastically welcoming their owners.
Puppies are born in two distinct coat types—rough-haired with a charming beard and smooth-haired without a beard—both of which share the same clean, dirt-shedding qualities.
Despite its medium size and companion role, the breed possesses extraordinary jumping agility and springiness, often leaping effortlessly over obstacles.

faq.question: How big does an adult Kromfohrländer get?
faq.answer: Conformation standards specify a height at the withers of 38 to 46 cm (approximately 15 to 18 inches) for both males and females. Typical adult weight ranges between 11 and 16 kg (24 to 35 pounds) for males and 9 to 14 kg (20 to 31 pounds) for females.

faq.question: What are the two coat varieties of the Kromfohrländer?
faq.answer: The breed exists in rough-haired and smooth-haired varieties. The rough-haired variety features a harsh outer coat and a distinctive beard, while the smooth-haired variety has a smooth face without a beard, close-lying body hair, longer feathering on the ears, neck, chest, and legs, and a plumed tail.

faq.question: What colours and markings are standard for the breed?
faq.answer: The ground colour is white, marked with light brown, tan, to very dark brown patches or a saddle pattern. The head features symmetrical brown-to-tan markings across the cheeks, over the eyes, and on the ears, neatly divided by an unbroken central white blaze extending to the forehead or nape.

faq.question: What inherited health conditions affect the Kromfohrländer?
faq.answer: Key genetic concerns include hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (HFH / 'corny feet'), caused by a mutation in the FAM83G gene, and von Willebrand disease Type I. Both conditions can be identified through DNA screening. Additional health concerns monitored in the breed include autoimmune disorders, idiopathic epilepsy, cystinuria, patellar luxation, and spondylosis.

faq.question: What pre-breeding health screenings should prospective puppy owners look for?
faq.answer: Responsible breeding programs require DNA testing for hereditary footpad hyperkeratosis (FAM83G) and von Willebrand disease, along with general clinical veterinary examinations, dental evaluations, and patellar assessments to ensure sound breeding stock.

faq.question: How much exercise and mental stimulation does a Kromfohrländer need?
faq.answer: As an active and spirited companion, the breed requires daily outdoor exercise, such as long nature walks, interactive fetch, and scent games, paired with mental challenges like trick training or agility. High-impact jumping should be deferred until joints are fully mature around three years of age.

faq.question: How does a Kromfohrländer typically behave around strangers and other dogs?
faq.answer: The breed is naturally devoted to its immediate family but tends to be reserved and observant with unfamiliar people, preferring to make introductions at its own pace. It is generally polite with dogs it knows well, but it is not typically suited to bustling dog parks where strange dogs crowd its space.

overview.summary: The Löwchen, whose name means 'little lion' in German, is a small companion dog known for its lively expression, affectionate nature, and confident personality. It combines a sturdy build with an elegant outline and is often recognised by its traditional lion clip. It generally enjoys being involved in family life and benefits from positive training, play, and regular companionship.
overview.description: The Löwchen is a compact, well-proportioned dog with a proud head carriage, dark expressive eyes, and pendant ears with long fringes. Its long, silky, wavy coat has no undercoat and can appear in many colours and combinations. The traditional lion clip leaves a mane around the front of the body while the hindquarters are clipped short; the unclipped coat should remain natural rather than sculpted. Despite its decorative appearance, the breed is robust and lively, and enjoys walks, games, and learning with its people.
overview.history: The Löwchen has a long history as a European companion dog. Images resembling the breed appear in medieval and Renaissance art, including carvings and tapestries, and historical accounts describe its popularity among European court circles. Its early geographical origin has been debated, but the modern breed standard identifies France as its country of origin. By the twentieth century, numbers had become very low. Dedicated breeders, especially in Europe, worked to preserve and rebuild the breed population, and it later spread to the United Kingdom and North America.

grooming.level: Moderate to high, especially for a long coat or lion clip
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb the coat several times a week to reduce tangles and mats, paying attention to the ears, legs, tail, and longer coat around the neck. Dogs kept in a full coat may need more frequent grooming than dogs kept in a shorter pet trim.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo, rinse thoroughly, and gently dry and comb the coat to reduce tangling. A long coat or show-style lion clip may need more regular professional maintenance.
notes: Plan regular coat trimming or professional grooming if maintaining the lion clip.
Check the skin beneath long hair for tangles, irritation, or trapped debris.
Inspect the ears regularly and clean only when needed with a dog-safe product.
Trim nails as required and check paws routinely.
Brush teeth with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange routine dental checks.
Introduce brushing, bathing, and clipping gradually so grooming becomes a familiar routine.

training.difficulty: Usually responsive to positive training; consistency is important to prevent excessive barking and unwanted habits.
tips: Use rewards, play, and short training sessions.
Teach calm greetings and a reliable response to household sounds.
Reward quiet behaviour rather than repeatedly shouting at barking.
Practise recall and lead manners from an early age.
Provide mental enrichment as well as physical activity.
Use gentle handling and avoid harsh corrections.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy gradually and positively to different people, dogs, surfaces, sounds, handling, and everyday environments. Reward calm behaviour and allow the dog to approach new experiences at a comfortable pace. Continue practising polite greetings and settling skills throughout adulthood.

climates: Provide shade, fresh water, and ventilation in warm weather.
Protect the dog from temperature extremes and adjust activity to conditions.
A long coat requires regular maintenance to prevent tangles and trapped debris.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, activity, and individual health needs.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Puppies usually need several small, measured meals each day. Adjust the schedule to age, growth, the food's directions, and veterinary advice.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals per day can be a practical routine; portion size should reflect body condition, activity, and food energy density.
feedingFrequency.senior: Adjust the diet and portions to activity, body condition, dental health, appetite, and medical needs with veterinary guidance.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions and monitor body condition rather than relying only on package estimates. Small dogs can gain excess weight when treats are frequent or portions are not adjusted. Provide fresh water at all times, count training treats in the daily allowance, and ask a veterinarian for individual guidance if weight or digestion changes.
considerations: Use a complete diet appropriate for the dog's life stage.
Monitor body condition and adjust portions when activity changes.
Count treats and chews as part of daily food intake.
Avoid supplements or therapeutic diets unless there is a clear reason and veterinary guidance.
Discuss persistent dental, digestive, appetite, or weight concerns with a veterinarian.
nutrition.note: This is general canine nutrition guidance, not a breed-specific calorie prescription.

health.overview: The Löwchen is generally described by breed and kennel-club sources as a healthy companion breed, but responsible breeders are advised to screen for certain inherited concerns. These include hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, and eye disorders such as cataracts or progressive retinal atrophy. Screening recommendations identify risks worth managing; they do not mean that every dog will develop these conditions or establish their prevalence in the population.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia is a recognised screening concern.
Patellar luxation is included in breed-health screening recommendations.
Eye disorders, including cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy, are discussed in breed-health guidance.
preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and maintain vaccination and parasite prevention appropriate to local risk.
Maintain a healthy body condition and age-appropriate exercise.
Ask breeders for documented parental health-screening results.
Seek veterinary advice for persistent lameness, eye changes, repeated slipping of a hind limb, or sustained changes in appetite or behaviour.
Keep up with dental care and coat maintenance, which are important parts of routine care for a small, long-coated dog.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation
Patellar luxation evaluation
Eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist
Ask the breeder and veterinarian whether any additional testing is appropriate for the dog's family line
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste. Small dogs can develop dental problems, so have the mouth checked during veterinary visits and seek advice for persistent bad breath, pain, bleeding, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check the pendant ears and fringes regularly for tangles, dirt, redness, odour, or discharge. Clean only when needed with a dog-safe product, and consult a veterinarian if discomfort or persistent signs occur.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin while brushing, especially beneath long hair and around the ears, legs, and tail. Persistent itching, sores, unusual hair loss, or recurrent irritation should be assessed by a veterinarian rather than treated as a normal coat issue.

funFacts: The name Löwchen means 'little lion' in German.
The traditional lion clip is a defining part of the breed's show presentation.
The FCI standard describes the coat as long, silky, wavy, and without an undercoat.
Historical depictions of dogs resembling the Löwchen appear in European art dating back several centuries.
The breed is classified as a companion dog rather than a working dog.

faq.question: Where does the Löwchen come from?
faq.answer: The FCI lists France as the breed's country of origin. Its early history has been debated, and historical depictions of similar dogs appear in several parts of Europe.

faq.question: How big does a Löwchen get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 26–32 cm at the withers, with a tolerance of 1 cm above or below that range. The standard describes weight as approximately 6 kg rather than providing separate male and female ranges.

faq.question: Why is the Löwchen called a Little Lion Dog?
faq.answer: The name means 'little lion' in German and refers to the traditional lion clip, which leaves a mane-like coat around the front of the body while the hindquarters are clipped short.

faq.question: How long does a Löwchen live?
faq.answer: The American Kennel Club lists a life expectancy of 13–15 years. This is a population-level estimate, not a guarantee for an individual dog.

faq.question: Does a Löwchen shed?
faq.answer: The breed is often described as low-shedding, but loose hair can still occur. Regular brushing is important because the long coat can tangle or mat.

faq.question: Is the Löwchen easy to train?
faq.answer: It is intelligent and often responsive to positive training. Early work on recall, calm greetings, and barking helps establish good household habits.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip and patellar evaluations and an eye examination by a qualified veterinary ophthalmologist. Discuss family health history and any additional tests with the breeder and veterinarian.

faq.question: Does a Löwchen need the lion clip?
faq.answer: The FCI standard requires the lion clip for showing under that standard. A companion dog can be kept in a practical pet trim, provided its coat is cared for properly.

overview.summary: A large Italian livestock guardian known for its white coat, independent judgement and strong commitment to protecting its flock and territory.
overview.description: The Maremma Sheepdog is a substantial, sturdy working dog developed to stay with sheep and protect them from predators and other threats. It combines a dense, weather-resistant coat with an alert nature and the ability to make decisions without waiting for constant direction from a handler. With familiar people, a well-socialised Maremma can be deeply devoted, but it may assess unfamiliar visitors cautiously. Its size, guarding instincts, independence and vocal responses make secure space, careful management and early training especially important. It is generally best suited to an experienced owner who understands livestock guardian behaviour and can provide a meaningful role rather than expecting automatic obedience or a typical urban companion.
overview.history: The Maremma Sheepdog developed in Italy from traditional flock-guarding dogs associated with the Abruzzo region, the Tuscan Maremma and Latium. Seasonal livestock movement helped bring regional populations into contact, encouraging the development of a more unified breed type from the nineteenth century onward. Its long-standing working role shaped an independent guardian that could remain with sheep and respond to threats without continuous direction from people.
overview.originalPurpose: Protecting sheep flocks and guarding farms and rural property.
currentRoles: Livestock guardian for sheep and other farm animals
Rural working guardian where its temperament, environment and training are appropriate

physical.coatType: Dense coat with long, rather coarse outer hair and an abundant seasonal undercoat.
physical.coatLength: Long over the body, with a substantial neck collar and shorter hair around the muzzle, head, ears and front of the limbs.
coatColors: Ivory shades within the limits accepted by the breed standard
Pale orange shades within the limits accepted by the breed standard
Lemon shades within the limits accepted by the breed standard
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high, with noticeable seasonal shedding as the dense undercoat changes.
physical.droolingLevel: Some drooling is reported; the amount varies from dog to dog.
distinctiveFeatures: Large, sturdy and slightly rectangular body
Long white coat with a dense seasonal undercoat
Broad, conical head with a calm but attentive expression
Small, high-set, triangular ears that hang naturally
Dark-pigmented nose and eyelid rims
Thick neck with a noticeable coat collar, particularly in males
Low-set, well-furnished tail that hangs at rest and rises closer to the topline during activity
Build and coat suited to sustained outdoor flock-guarding work

traits: Perceptive and alert
Independent in decision-making
Devoted to familiar people
Protective of its flock and property
Naturally cautious or suspicious toward unfamiliar people
Capable of working at a distance from a handler
Intelligent but not always inclined to obey repetitive commands
Benefits from structured work, early socialisation and consistent handling

exercise.level: Moderate to high. A Maremma needs daily movement and mental work; livestock-guardian duties can involve substantially more movement than a companion-only routine.
activities: Daily walks adjusted to the individual dog's age, health and working responsibilities
Supervised movement and exploration in a securely fenced area
Purposeful livestock-guardian work when the dog is appropriately trained and managed
Short reward-based training sessions for recall, leash manners and visitor routines
Scent games and calm problem-solving activities for mental enrichment

grooming.level: Moderate to high, especially during seasonal shedding or when the dog spends much of its time indoors.
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly several times a week, working through the dense coat rather than only grooming the surface. Increase coat checks during seasonal shedding.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-safe shampoo, rinse thoroughly and dry the dense coat well. Bathing frequency should be based on the dog's cleanliness and skin condition.
notes: Inspect the coat regularly for tangles, trapped debris and areas that may conceal irritation.
Give extra attention to the dense undercoat during seasonal shedding.
Check paw pads and the hair between the toes; trim only when needed and safely.
Inspect the skin when brushing, especially if the coat stays damp or begins to mat.
Check ears, eyes and nails as part of the regular grooming routine.
Avoid shaving the double coat unless a veterinarian recommends clipping for a medical reason.

training.difficulty: Moderate to high for owners expecting automatic obedience. The breed is intelligent but was developed to make independent decisions while guarding.
tips: Begin reward-based training and safe exposure to everyday situations during puppyhood.
Teach reliable leash manners, recall and calm responses to household routines before the dog reaches full size.
Use short, purposeful sessions and reward the behaviours you want to maintain.
Avoid harsh or intimidating corrections; these can damage trust and complicate the management of a protective dog.
Introduce visitors gradually and use secure separation when a situation cannot be managed safely.
Provide an appropriate role and ongoing mental enrichment rather than relying on physical exercise alone.
training.socialization: Start early and continue throughout adulthood. Introduce different people, settings, sounds and animals in controlled, positive situations. Because the breed may independently assess unfamiliar people, teach calm, manageable routines instead of forcing close contact with visitors. Socialisation does not remove the need for secure containment or supervision.

climates: Cool and temperate climates
Warm climates when the dog has shade, fresh water, a cool resting area and exercise during cooler hours

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate for a large-breed dog, its life stage, body condition, activity and veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.adult: Divide the daily ration into smaller meals rather than offering one very large meal. The exact schedule and portions should be discussed with a veterinarian, particularly because bloat is a reported concern.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose a complete and balanced food that meets the dog's life-stage requirements. Measure portions, monitor body condition and adjust intake according to growth, activity and veterinary advice. Keep fresh water available at all times, and make food transitions gradually rather than switching diets abruptly.
considerations: Maintain a lean body condition to reduce unnecessary load on joints.
Discuss large-breed growth nutrition with a veterinarian when feeding a puppy.
Do not add calcium, vitamins or other supplements unless a veterinarian recommends them.
Because gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) is a reported concern, ask a veterinarian about feeding routines, individual risk factors and emergency warning signs.
A feeding routine may need to change with age, workload, body condition or medical needs.
Seek veterinary advice for persistent digestive problems or a sudden change in appetite.
nutrition.note: A reliable breed-specific meal count was not established for puppies or senior dogs in the reviewed references. The adult feeding guidance is general risk-management advice, not a guarantee against bloat.

health.overview: Health planning for a Maremma should account for its large size, active working background and the conditions reported in breed-care guidance. Hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia and gastric dilatation-volvulus are concerns to discuss with a veterinarian. The reviewed sources do not establish a single population-wide prevalence for these conditions, and a breed-level risk does not mean that an individual dog will develop them.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — a developmental disorder of the hip joint that can affect comfort and mobility.
Elbow dysplasia — a group of developmental elbow-joint problems that can contribute to lameness.
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat) — a life-threatening emergency involving stomach distension and possible twisting.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary examinations and follow an age-appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention plan.
Keep the dog at a healthy body condition and discuss any persistent lameness or reduced mobility promptly.
Discuss bloat risk and emergency warning signs with the veterinarian; suspected GDV requires urgent veterinary care.
Use responsible breeding practices and ask to see the parents' health-screening records before choosing a puppy.
Monitor appetite, weight, mobility, skin condition and behaviour so changes can be identified early.
recommendedScreenings: Hip-dysplasia evaluation for breeding dogs, using an accepted programme such as OFA certification or PennHIP assessment.
Discuss elbow evaluation and other appropriate orthopaedic checks with the veterinarian.
Ask a veterinarian to evaluate possible inherited or conformation-related concerns when relevant, including eyelid abnormalities, bite misalignment, umbilical hernia or cryptorchidism.
Confirm the appropriate tests and timing for the individual dog with a veterinarian and a responsible breeder.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly, ideally daily, using dog-specific toothpaste and a suitable toothbrush. Arrange veterinary oral examinations and professional cleaning when recommended.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge or repeated head-shaking. Clean only when necessary with a veterinarian-approved product, and seek veterinary advice if irritation persists.
health.skinCare: Regularly comb through the coat and inspect the skin beneath it, paying attention to tangles, damp areas, trapped debris and hot spots. During heavy shedding, increase grooming so loose undercoat does not conceal skin problems.

idealFor: Experienced owners who understand livestock-guardian behaviour
Rural households with adequate, securely managed land
Farms and livestock keepers who can provide appropriate guardian work
Owners who can invest in early socialisation, consistent training and visitor management
notIdealFor: Apartment living or cramped urban environments
Owners who require automatic obedience or a highly sociable dog with every visitor
Households unable to provide secure fencing, daily activity and meaningful engagement
Homes with frequent unsupervised visitors where the dog's protective responses cannot be managed safely
People looking for a low-maintenance first dog without experience managing large guardian breeds

funFacts: The breed's modern name brings together the names of two Italian regions associated with its development: Abruzzo and the Maremma.
Its traditional role is to remain with a flock and respond to threats, rather than wait for continuous commands from a handler.
The breed's characteristic white coat is closely associated with its traditional work among sheep.
Seasonal livestock movement helped bring regional flock-guardian populations into contact during the nineteenth century.

faq.question: Is the Maremma Sheepdog a good apartment dog?
faq.answer: Usually not. Its size, independent guardian instincts, need for purposeful activity and possible response to visitors make it better suited to a rural setting with secure space.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Maremma Sheepdog need?
faq.answer: A practical starting point is around 60–120 minutes of daily walking or equivalent activity, adjusted for the dog's age, health and workload. A working livestock guardian may move much more throughout the day.

faq.question: What colour is a Maremma Sheepdog?
faq.answer: The usual and preferred colour is solid white. Limited ivory, pale orange or lemon shades may be accepted within the breed standard's stated limits.

faq.question: Does a Maremma Sheepdog shed?
faq.answer: Yes. It has a dense coat and undercoat that requires regular brushing, with more attention during seasonal shedding.

faq.question: What health concerns should owners know about?
faq.answer: Hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia and gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) are reported concerns. These are not predictions for every dog; discuss screening, prevention and emergency signs with your veterinarian.

faq.question: Is a Maremma Sheepdog suitable for a family with children?
faq.answer: It depends on the individual dog, the household and the owner's experience. The breed can be devoted to familiar people, but its size and protective response to unfamiliar visitors require early socialisation, clear routines and adult supervision around children.

overview.summary: A compact, athletic, and intelligent Canadian retriever bred in southwestern Nova Scotia, celebrated for its red-to-orange water-repellent double coat, tireless love of swimming and retrieving, and fox-like shoreline play that lures curious waterfowl within gunshot range.
overview.description: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever—universally nicknamed the Toller—is the smallest of the retriever breeds, built with a muscular, compact, and well-boned frame that is slightly longer than tall (roughly a 10:9 ratio) without ever appearing heavy or clunky. Protected against icy maritime waters by a medium-length, water-repellent double coat in shades of golden red to dark coppery red (often accented by white markings on the tail tip, feet, chest, or blaze), it features a clean, wedge-shaped head, alert almond-shaped amber-to-brown eyes, high-set triangular drop ears, a heavily feathered tail that waves incessantly above the back when working, and strongly webbed feet. In the field, the Toller performs a dual job: darting, leaping, and retrieving sticks or balls silently along the shoreline so its flashing red coat and feathered tail arouse the curiosity of offshore ducks and geese, then plunging into frigid water to retrieve downed birds on command. At home, Tollers are deeply affectionate, playful, and attuned to their families, though they can be reserved with strangers, strong-willed if training becomes repetitive, and prone to an unmistakable high-pitched vocalisation ('the Toller scream') when brimming with excitement.
overview.history: Developed at the beginning of the nineteenth century in the coastal community of Little River Harbour in Yarmouth County, southwestern Nova Scotia, the breed was originally called the Little River Duck Dog or the Yarmouth Toller. Local hunters—drawing on Indigenous Mi'kmaq traditions and European observations of red foxes playing near the water's edge to entice rafting waterfowl toward shore—bred a small, fox-coloured dog that could both lure ('toll', from the Middle English tolian, meaning 'to entice or decoy') and retrieve waterfowl from icy tidal waters. Although exact early breeding records were not preserved, foundation stock is thought to have combined small European decoy spaniels (similar to the Nederlandse Kooikerhondje) with retrievers (including early Golden, Chesapeake Bay, or Flat-Coated Retriever stock and the extinct St. John's Water Dog), setters, spaniels, and local farm collies. After more than a century of regional breeding in Nova Scotia, the first 15 dogs were admitted to national studbook registration in Canada in 1945. When breed numbers dropped dangerously low in the 1970s, dedicated North American and European fanciers—including American pioneer Sue Van Sloun, who imported her first pair in 1978 and helped establish organized preservation in the United States in 1984—expanded preservation efforts. International recognition followed in 1987, the province of Nova Scotia proclaimed the Toller its official Provincial Dog in 1995, and full sporting-group recognition in the United States was granted in 2003.
overview.originalPurpose: Enticing ('tolling') offshore ducks and geese within gunshot range through silent, playful shoreline movement and retrieving downed waterfowl from icy water and land.
currentRoles: Field trial and retriever hunt-test competitor
Tracking, nose work, and scent-detection participant
Search-and-rescue or therapy dog where individually trained and temperament-suited

physical.coatType: Water-repellent double coat consisting of a medium-length, moderately soft straight outer coat (a slight wave along the back and a loose curl at the throat in winter coat are permissible) over a denser, even softer insulating undercoat, with soft feathering at the throat, behind the ears, on the backs of the thighs, and moderately on the forelegs and underside of the tail.
physical.coatLength: Medium
coatColors: Red (ranging from golden red to dark coppery red, with lighter shadings on the feathering and underside of the tail)
Orange (various shades of orange, with pigment on the nose, lips, and eye rims matching the coat in flesh/liver or black)

Red or orange with at least one white marking on the tip of the tail, feet (not extending above the pasterns), chest, or facial blaze (solid red/orange without any white is also acceptable, whereas buff/silver dilution, brown, black, pinto, tricolor, or white on the shoulders, around the ears, on the back of the neck, or across the back/flanks are disqualifying faults)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate year-round, with heavier seasonal shedding twice a year during spring and autumn coat changes.
distinctiveFeatures: Smallest of the retriever breeds, built on a compact, muscular, slightly rectangular outline (approximately 10:9 body length to withers height) with a deep chest reaching the elbows and a level topline

Clean-cut, slightly wedge-shaped head (measuring roughly 14 cm [5.5 in] between the ears tapering to 3.8 cm [1.5 in] at the nose bridge, and about 23 cm [9 in] from nose to occiput in a typical adult male, scaling with body size) with a flat-to-slightly-rounded skull and moderate stop
Almond-shaped, medium-sized eyes set well apart in amber to brown shades that harmonize with the coat, paired with flesh-coloured or black nose leather, tight-fitting lips, and eye rims
Triangular, medium-sized drop ears with rounded tips set high and well back on the skull, carried slightly raised at the base when alert and well feathered at the back of the fold

Broad-based, heavily feathered tail reaching at least to the hocks, carried below the level of the back only when standing at rest and curving high in continuous motion above the topline when alert or working (never touching the body)
Strong, round-to-oval, tightly webbed feet with thick pads and trimmed interdigital hair, functioning like paddles in cold water
Springy, effortless, ground-covering gait with strong rear drive and a level backline
Distinctive high-pitched, trembling vocalisation ('the Toller scream') expressed by many individuals when eager to retrieve or work

Ideal adult withers height of 48–51 cm (19–20 in) for males and 45–48 cm (18–19 in) for females over 18 months of age (with a ±2.5 to 3 cm [±1 in] allowance, or 18–21 in and 17–20 in in American standards), and substance-proportionate adult weight guidelines of 20–23 kg (45–51 lbs) for males and 17–20 kg (37–43 lbs; 35–50 lbs across both sexes in American profiles)

traits: Highly intelligent, observant, and quick to learn
Affectionate, loving, and playful with family members and familiar children
Outgoing, exuberant, and tireless when working or playing
Intensely driven to retrieve on land and in water
Alert, attentive, and determined
Patient with children when properly socialized and supervised
Often reserved or aloof (never aggressive or shy) toward unfamiliar people
Sensitive to handler tone yet persistent and capable of independent or strong-willed behaviour if bored
Expressive and vocal when excited (including the high-pitched 'Toller scream')

exercise.level: High
activities: Daily brisk walks, jogging, or trail hikes suited to the dog's age and conditioning
Structured retrieving games and field bumper work on land and in water
Swimming and dock diving in safe, supervised bodies of water
Canine sports such as agility, flyball, rally, and obedience
Tracking, nose work, and scent-detection games
Problem-solving puzzle toys and short, varied mental-enrichment drills

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly at least once a week with a pin brush, slicker brush, and metal comb to remove loose hair and prevent matting in the soft feathering behind the ears, around the throat, and on the hindquarters. Increase to daily brushing during seasonal spring and autumn coat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only as needed when dirty or after muddy or saltwater swims, using a mild dog-safe shampoo that preserves the natural oils of the water-repellent double coat, and rinse and dry thoroughly.
notes: The weatherproof double coat insulates against both icy water and summer heat; it should never be shaved, and show trimming is restricted to neatening the ears, feet, pasterns, and hocks.
Pay close attention to the fine, silky hair behind and under the ears, which tangles more easily than the body coat.
Trim excess hair between the paw pads and on the feet to maintain traction and prevent mud or ice buildup.
Rinse and dry the coat and inspect the drop ears after swimming in lakes, marshes, or the ocean.
Check toenails weekly and trim them regularly so they remain short and compact.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm grooming and handling.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Highly intelligent, eager to work, and quick to grasp new concepts, yet sensitive to heavy-handed methods and quick to invent its own rules if drills become monotonous.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement—combining food rewards with brief retrieving or tug play—and avoid harsh corrections.
Keep training sessions short, varied, and mentally challenging so this quick-thinking retriever does not become bored or self-employed.
Channel the breed's intense retrieving instinct as a high-value life reward for recall, impulse control, and obedience.
Teach calm steadiness and an 'off switch' indoors so the dog learns to settle quietly after high-arousal work or play.
Manage and redirect high-pitched excitement vocalisations ('the Toller scream') early by rewarding quiet focus before throwing a toy or releasing the dog to water.
Practise reliable recall in securely enclosed spaces and keep the dog on a leash or long line around wild waterfowl, small animals, and open water currents.
training.socialization: Begin positive, unhurried socialization early in puppyhood across diverse people, friendly dogs, children, surfaces, sounds, and environments. Because many Tollers are naturally reserved or discerning with strangers, allow the dog to observe and greet unfamiliar people without pressure so it matures into a confident, well-mannered adult. Supervise introductions to cats and small pets carefully due to the breed's innate bird- and small-game drive.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Tollers bond closely with their families and thrive on daily interaction, training, and outdoor activity. Leaving a Toller isolated for long workdays without adequate physical and mental outlets can lead to boredom, vocalising, or destructive chewing.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced dog food (commercial or veterinarian-formulated home-prepared diet) appropriate for the dog's life stage, workload, and health status.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age (puppy, adult, or senior) and daily activity level. Because Tollers are medium-sized athletic dogs whose caloric needs vary widely between active field/agility competitors and family companions, monitor body condition score regularly so the waist remains defined and the ribs are easily felt beneath a light layer of muscle. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Adjust daily calorie intake to match seasonal training, hunting, or sport workloads.
Count training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to prevent excess weight and unnecessary joint strain.
Transition between diets gradually over several days unless a veterinarian directs otherwise.

Consult a veterinarian promptly if unexplained weight loss, lethargy, intermittent vomiting, diarrhoea, or increased thirst/urination occur (which can also be early signs of endocrine or immune-mediated conditions).
Home-prepared diets should be formulated with a veterinarian or board-certified veterinary nutritionist to ensure complete micronutrient balance.
nutrition.note: No single daily meal count is prescribed across all puppies, adults, or seniors because optimal feeding schedules depend on age, caloric density, and individual metabolism; confirm meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever is an energetic, hardy sporting dog with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years, but its historical population bottlenecks have led to several well-characterized autosomal recessive genetic variants as well as an elevated predisposition to immune-mediated and endocrine disorders. Epidemiological research in insured Swedish Tollers (2015) documented significantly higher relative risks than in the general dog population for steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA; incidence 20 per 10,000 dog-years at risk, relative risk 12) and immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD; 6.8 per 10,000 dog-years at risk, relative risk 18), alongside a higher risk of lymphoma but lower overall rates of ear and heart disease. A follow-up 2024 Swedish owner-questionnaire survey (935 living and 177 deceased Tollers) estimated lifetime prevalence in living dogs at 3.0% for IMRD and 3.5% for SRMA, and reported neoplasia of any kind (benign or malignant, most commonly mammary and mast cell tumours) in 14% of living dogs and as the cause of death in 38.4% of deceased dogs—figures specific to that surveyed cohort rather than universal cancer rates. In 2026, a peer-reviewed genomic study identified an autosomal recessive missense variant in the RESF1 gene (c.3170C>T / p.Pro1057Leu on chromosome 27) associated with juvenile-onset Addison's disease (JADD) with incomplete (~75%–76%) penetrance by 1 year of age (average diagnosis 5 months) and multiple autoimmune syndrome (41.7%–70.8% of juvenile cases developing concurrent immune-mediated eye, blood, joint, gut, or thyroid disorders); this DNA test does not account for adult-onset Addison's disease. Earlier in 2023, researchers also identified an autosomal recessive frameshift variant in the LMNA gene (p.Asp576ThrfsTer124) causing fatal juvenile/young-adult cardiac laminopathy (CLAM, dilated and fibrosing cardiomyopathy). Validated DNA tests are likewise available for PRCD-progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd), Collie eye anomaly (CEA/CH), cleft palate 1 (CP1 / DLX6), cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS / ADAMTS20), cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC / SNX14), degenerative encephalopathy (DE), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), and FGF4 retrogene chondrodystrophy (CDDY/IVDD).
commonConditions: Hypoadrenocorticism (Addison's disease) and multiple autoimmune syndrome — occurs in both an adult-onset form (average onset ~2.6–4 years) and a juvenile-onset form (JADD, average onset 5 months, range 8 weeks to 12 months) associated with an autosomal recessive RESF1 missense variant (c.3170C>T / p.Pro1057Leu) showing ~75%–76% penetrance and frequent concurrent autoimmune manifestations (such as corneal edema, conjunctivitis, uveitis, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, polyarthritis, or inflammatory bowel disease).

Steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA, sometimes historically called 'Toller disease') — a non-infectious immune-mediated inflammation of the meninges and meningeal arteries affecting primarily young dogs (roughly 70% presenting before 18 months of age; 3.5% living prevalence in a 2024 Swedish survey), causing acute neck pain, stiffness, high fever, and depression that require prompt veterinary diagnosis and immunosuppressive therapy.

Immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD) — a systemic lupus erythematosus-related non-erosive polyarthritis (3.0% living prevalence and median onset 5 years in a 2024 Swedish survey, often ANA-positive) causing cyclic joint stiffness, shifting leg lameness, pain after rest, and sometimes skin lesions or fever.

Cardiac laminopathy (CLAM) — a fatal autosomal recessive dilated and fibrosing cardiomyopathy caused by a frameshift deletion in the LMNA gene (p.Asp576ThrfsTer124), typically resulting in myocarditis, arrhythmias, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death before 1.5 to 2 years of age (with myocardial fibrosis also reported in a 5-year-old heterozygous carrier); preventable via pre-breeding DNA screening.

Progressive retinal atrophy, photoreceptor rod-cone degeneration (PRA-prcd) and Collie eye anomaly / choroidal hypoplasia (CEA/CH) — autosomal recessive inherited retinal and choroidal eye disorders for which validated DNA tests and annual veterinary ophthalmologist examinations are core screening tools.

Cleft palate 1 (CP1, DLX6 insertion) and cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS, ADAMTS20 deletion) — two distinct autosomal recessive congenital craniofacial malformation syndromes in the breed, both preventable through pre-breeding DNA carrier testing.

Cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC) and degenerative encephalopathy (DE) — rare autosomal recessive neurological disorders in the breed; CDMC (caused by an SNX14 frameshift variant) produces cerebellar ataxia, tremors, and masticatory/generalized muscle inflammation between 10 weeks and 6 months of age, while DE causes progressive neurological dysfunction.
Hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and patellar luxation — developmental orthopaedic conditions monitored through pre-breeding radiographic and clinical evaluations.

Chondrodystrophy (CDDY) and intervertebral disc disease (IVDD) risk — associated with the semi-dominant chromosome 12 FGF4 retrogene insertion that predisposes discs to premature calcification and herniation.
Autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism) — an immune-mediated endocrine disorder monitored via periodic veterinary thyroid antibody panels.

Neoplasia (tumours) — population studies in Swedish Tollers have documented increased relative risk of lymphoma in insured dogs and reported benign or malignant tumours (most frequently mammary and mast cell tumours) in 14% of surveyed living dogs; tumour rates vary by age, sex, and spay/neuter status and do not represent a uniform breed-wide cancer probability.
preventiveCare: Verify documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents before acquiring a puppy, including hip radiographs, current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams, and breed-specific DNA test results.

Understand the scope of genetic testing: a Clear result on the RESF1 juvenile Addison's disease (JADD) DNA test rules out that specific juvenile-onset variant (which itself has ~75%–76% penetrance in homozygotes), but does not rule out adult-onset Addison's disease or other immune-mediated disorders.

Seek prompt veterinary evaluation if a young or adult dog develops acute neck pain, spinal stiffness, fever, shifting leg lameness after rest, waxing-and-waning lethargy, vomiting, diarrhoea, or increased drinking and urination, as early treatment is critical for SRMA, IMRD, and Addisonian crises.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and avoid excessive high-impact jumping in growing puppies to protect the hips, elbows, knees, and intervertebral discs.
Inspect, rinse, and dry the coat and drop ears after swimming to prevent moisture-related skin or ear irritation.

Keep routine veterinary wellness examinations, dental care, nail trimming, and regionally appropriate parasite prevention and vaccination schedules up to date (working with your veterinarian to tailor vaccination protocols for dogs with personal or family histories of immune-mediated disease).
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement).
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (core pre-breeding requirement).
Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd) DNA test (core pre-breeding requirement).
Juvenile Addison's disease (JADD / RESF1 c.3170C>T) DNA test — recommended to identify carriers and prevent homozygous matings while preserving genetic diversity.
Cardiac laminopathy (CLAM / LMNA p.Asp576ThrfsTer124) DNA test and clinical veterinary cardiac evaluation.
Cleft palate 1 (CP1 / DLX6) and cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS / ADAMTS20) DNA tests.

Cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC / SNX14), Collie eye anomaly (CEA/CH / NHEJ1), degenerative encephalopathy (DE), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), and chondrodystrophy (CDDY / FGF4) DNA tests.
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation, patellar luxation veterinary examination, and laboratory thyroid panel (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies).

Optional coat-colour dilution (Buff / D-locus MLPH) DNA test for breeding planning (identifies recessive buff coat dilution, which is a conformation disqualification rather than a medical disorder; note also that Tollers tested to date have not carried the MDR1 drug-sensitivity mutation).
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week—ideally daily—using dog-specific toothpaste, and schedule regular veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, tight scissor bite.
health.earCare: Check the high-set triangular drop ears weekly and after every swim or muddy outing. Gently clean and dry the outer ear and keep the feathering behind the ears free of mats, seeking veterinary advice if redness, foul odour, discharge, or head shaking occurs.
health.skinCare: Part the dense, water-repellent double coat during weekly brushing to check the skin for ticks, burrs, hot spots (acute moist dermatitis), or uncharacteristic hair loss. Rinse off salt or marsh water after swimming and dry the thick undercoat thoroughly.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who enjoy daily outdoor exercise, hiking, running, swimming, or canine sports
Handlers interested in retriever field work, agility, flyball, dock diving, obedience, rally, or scent work
Experienced or dedicated owners who use upbeat, varied, reward-based training and teach calm indoor settling
Families with children who supervise interactions and teach respectful handling
Households prepared for weekly brushing, twice-yearly seasonal coat sheds, and expressive excitement vocalisations
notIdealFor: Sedentary households or owners seeking a low-energy companion satisfied with brief casual walks
People who leave a dog isolated alone for long workdays without daily physical and mental engagement
Noise-sensitive households intolerant of a high-pitched, exuberant 'Toller scream' when the dog is excited
Handlers who use harsh, repetitive, or heavy-handed training methods
Owners expecting effortless off-leash reliability around waterfowl and wildlife without training and secure management

funFacts: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever is the smallest of all recognized retriever breeds, yet it has the strength and endurance to retrieve heavy geese from icy tidal waters.

The word 'toll' comes from the Middle English tolian ('to entice' or 'lure'): hunters patterned the breed's shoreline work after wild red foxes, which dart and play along the water's edge to lure curious ducks within range.

Developed in early nineteenth-century Little River Harbour in Yarmouth County, Nova Scotia, the breed was historically known as the Little River Duck Dog and the Yarmouth Toller before adopting its current name when registered in 1945.
In 1995, Nova Scotia declared the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever its official Provincial Dog—making it the first Canadian dog breed honoured as a provincial symbol.
At the thirty-three-letter mark (excluding spaces), 'Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever' is the longest official breed name in North American studbooks.
When eager to retrieve or work, many Tollers let out a famous high-pitched, trembling howl of pure anticipation known as the 'Toller scream' or 'Toller singing'.

Unlike most dogs whose tails hang or wag level with the spine, an alert or working Toller carries its heavily feathered tail curving high over its back like a waving flag so offshore ducks can spot it through shoreline reeds.
Tollers have strongly webbed, paddle-like feet and a water-repellent double coat so dense that icy water rarely reaches the skin.

faq.question: Where does the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever come from, and what were its early names?
faq.answer: The breed originated at the beginning of the nineteenth century in southwestern Nova Scotia, Canada—specifically around Little River Harbour in Yarmouth County. Before receiving its modern name upon national registration in 1945, it was known locally as the Little River Duck Dog and the Yarmouth Toller.

faq.question: What does 'tolling' mean, and how does a Toller hunt?
faq.answer: Tolling comes from a Middle English word meaning 'to entice' or 'lure'. Modeled on the behaviour of wild red foxes, the dog runs, leaps, and fetches sticks or balls thrown from a hunter's blind along the shoreline while remaining completely silent. Its flashing red coat and waving feathered tail arouse the curiosity of ducks and geese swimming offshore, drawing them within gunshot range; once the birds are downed, the dog swims out to retrieve them.

faq.question: How big is an adult Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever?
faq.answer: It is the smallest of the retrievers. International and Canadian standards specify an ideal withers height for dogs over 18 months of 48 to 51 cm (19–20 inches) for males and 45 to 48 cm (18–19 inches) for females, with a tolerance of ±2.5 to 3 cm (±1 inch), and weight guidelines of 20 to 23 kg (45–51 pounds) for males and 17 to 20 kg (37–43 pounds) for females. American standards specify 18 to 21 inches (ideal 19 inches) for males, 17 to 20 inches (ideal 18 inches) for females, and typical weights of 35 to 50 pounds (16–23 kg) in proportion to bone and substance.

faq.question: What coat colours and white markings are allowed?
faq.answer: The coat comes in shades of red and orange ranging from golden red to dark coppery red, with lighter shading on the feathering and the underside of the tail. Dogs commonly have at least one white marking on the tip of the tail, the feet (not extending above the pasterns), the chest, or as a facial blaze, though an otherwise sound dog without white markings is also accepted. Nose, lips, and eye rims must be flesh-coloured (blending with the coat) or black. Buff/silver dilution, solid brown/liver coat, black coat, pinto/tricolor patterning, or white on the shoulders, back, flanks, or around the ears are disqualifying faults.

faq.question: What is the 'Toller scream'?
faq.answer: The 'Toller scream' (sometimes called 'Toller singing') is a piercing, high-pitched, trembling vocalisation that many Tollers make when they are intensely excited—most often when they see water, birds, or a retrieving dummy. Not every Toller screams to the same degree, and handlers avoid reinforcing it in hunting blinds or quiet neighbourhoods by rewarding calm, quiet focus before releasing the dog.

faq.question: Is the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever a good family dog?
faq.answer: Yes, for active households. Tollers are deeply affectionate, playful, and patient with their own families and children when properly socialized and supervised. However, they are high-drive working dogs—not scaled-down Golden Retrievers—and can be reserved with unfamiliar people and restless if their daily physical and mental exercise needs are neglected.

faq.question: How much exercise and grooming does a Toller need?
faq.answer: Tollers have high energy and need daily brisk walks or runs paired with purposeful mental work such as retrieving drills, swimming, agility, flyball, or scent work. Their medium-length, water-repellent double coat is relatively easy to maintain with a thorough weekly brushing (paying extra attention to the fine hair behind the ears and feathering) and daily brushing during spring and autumn coat sheds. The double coat should never be shaved.

faq.question: Can a Toller live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment living can succeed if the owner provides substantial daily outdoor exercise, retrieving and mental enrichment, and training to manage the breed's excitement vocalisations. Without committed daily activity and companionship, however, an apartment lifestyle is a poor fit.

faq.question: What health conditions are researched or reported in the breed?
faq.answer: Key health concerns include hypoadrenocorticism (Addison's disease, both adult-onset and juvenile-onset), steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA), immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD), juvenile cardiac laminopathy (CLAM), inherited eye conditions (PRA-prcd and Collie eye anomaly), congenital cleft palate syndromes (CP1 and CLPS), cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC), hip dysplasia, intervertebral disc disease predisposition (CDDY), and autoimmune thyroiditis. Swedish population studies estimated living lifetime prevalence at 3.0% for IMRD and 3.5% for SRMA, and reported tumours of any type (benign or malignant) in 14% of surveyed living dogs.

faq.question: What does the juvenile Addison's disease (JADD / RESF1) DNA test tell breeders and owners?
faq.answer: In 2026, researchers identified an autosomal recessive missense variant in the RESF1 gene (c.3170C>T / p.Pro1057Leu) associated with juvenile-onset Addison's disease (average onset 5 months, range 8 weeks to 12 months) and concurrent multiple autoimmune disorders. The variant has incomplete penetrance—approximately 75% to 76% of dogs with two copies (N/N -> JADD/JADD) develop Addison's disease by 1 year of age—and a carrier frequency of roughly 20% to 23% in tested cohorts. The DNA test allows breeders to avoid mating two carriers, but a Clear result does not prevent adult-onset Addison's disease.

faq.question: What is cardiac laminopathy (CLAM) in Tollers?
faq.answer: Cardiac laminopathy (CLAM) is a fatal autosomal recessive dilated and fibrosing cardiomyopathy caused by a frameshift variant in the LMNA gene (identified in 2023). Affected puppies and young dogs typically suffer heart failure or sudden cardiac death before 1.5 to 2 years of age. A validated DNA test allows breeders to screen breeding stock and prevent affected litters.

faq.question: Which health screenings should I ask a breeder for?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results of core pre-breeding evaluations—hip radiographs, a current annual examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, and DNA testing for PRA-prcd—along with DNA panel results for juvenile Addison's disease (JADD / RESF1), cardiac laminopathy (CLAM / LMNA), cleft palate 1 (CP1), cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS), cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC), Collie eye anomaly (CEA/CH), degenerative encephalopathy (DE), degenerative myelopathy (DM), and chondrodystrophy (CDDY), as well as elbow, patellar, cardiac, and thyroid evaluations where appropriate.

breeds.name: Old Danish Pointer
breeds.group: FCI Group 7 — Pointing Dogs, Section 1.1 — Continental Pointing Dogs, Braque type (working trial required)

origin.region: Jutland; historically associated with Glenstrup near Randers and Hobro

overview.summary: A sturdy Danish pointing dog with a short white-and-brown coat, a steady temperament and a close-working style suited to bird hunting and scent-based field work.
overview.description: The Old Danish Pointer is a medium-sized, powerfully built gundog developed in Denmark for locating and pointing game birds. Its characteristic appearance combines a broad, substantial head, low-set hanging ears, a short dense coat and white colouring marked with brown patches or speckles. The breed is known for a calm, determined manner and a hunting style that keeps the dog in contact with its handler rather than ranging at extreme speed. At home, breed-club and Nordic kennel-club descriptions portray it as devoted to its family and generally steady around people and other dogs. It is best matched with people who can provide regular outdoor activity, scent work, retrieving or suitable field work, as well as close companionship. Its short coat is straightforward to maintain, but it does not provide strong weather insulation.
overview.history: The breed's documented history reaches back to around 1710 in Jutland, where Morten Bak is credited with developing a consistent white-and-brown pointing dog through repeated crossings of dogs kept by travelling Romani people with local farm dogs. The FCI history notes that the ancestry is not completely certain; St. Hubert-type scent hounds and Spanish pointing dogs are considered possible contributors. The resulting dogs became known as Bakhounds or Old Danish Pointing Dogs and were developed as practical, versatile bird-hunting companions.
overview.originalPurpose: Versatile gundog work, especially locating and pointing birds while maintaining contact with the hunter; the breed is also described as capable of tracking wounded game.

grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a rubber grooming brush or wipe with a damp chamois to remove loose hair and dirt; more frequent brushing can help manage visible white hairs around the home.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed, using a dog-appropriate shampoo and drying thoroughly after wet or cold-weather activity.

training.difficulty: Moderate; generally willing to cooperate, but needs consistent training that channels hunting and scenting instincts.
tips: Use reward-based methods, short sessions and clear, consistent cues.
Build reliable recall before allowing off-leash exercise in unsecured areas.
Provide structured scent games and retrieving tasks rather than relying only on repetitive physical exercise.
Introduce hunting-related distractions gradually and reward attention to the handler.
Keep training varied and motivating, with rewards delivered promptly.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog gradually and positively to different people, calm dogs, environments, handling and everyday sounds during puppyhood and continue social learning throughout life.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition and activity level
nutrition.guidelines: Choose a nutritionally complete food suitable for the dog's age, reproductive status and workload. Set portions using the food's calorie information, body condition and weight trend rather than a breed-only feeding estimate. Adjust intake as activity changes, keep fresh water available, and discuss major diet changes or special needs with a veterinarian.
considerations: Working dogs may need different energy intake across hunting, training and rest periods.
Monitor body condition and adjust portions to avoid excess weight.
Use treats as part of the daily energy allowance.
For puppies, older dogs or dogs with medical conditions, ask a veterinarian to tailor the feeding plan.
nutrition.note: No universal breed-specific ration or meal schedule is recorded. Individual calorie needs vary substantially with age, size, health and workload.

health.overview: The sources consulted for this record provide conformation and care descriptions but do not establish reliable breed-specific disease prevalence, a validated lifespan range or a definitive screening panel. Avoid treating generic canine risks or isolated reports as confirmed breed-wide predispositions. Ask breeders for veterinary records and family health history, and work with a veterinarian on preventive care.
preventiveCare: Arrange regular veterinary wellness examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local risk.
Maintain a healthy body condition and age-appropriate activity.
Check ears, skin folds, paws and coat after outdoor work.
Maintain routine dental care and nail trimming.
Seek veterinary advice promptly for persistent lameness, eye irritation, skin problems or changes in appetite or behaviour.
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary oral examinations. Dental chews or diets should complement, not replace, brushing and professional care.
health.earCare: Check the hanging ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge or discomfort. Keep them dry after wet activities and ask a veterinarian before using ear medication or cleaners if irritation is present.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin, throat folds, paws and coat after field work. Clean off debris gently and seek veterinary advice for persistent redness, itching, sores or unusual odour.

faq.question: What was the Old Danish Pointer bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a versatile gundog for bird hunting, especially locating and pointing game while staying in contact with the hunter. It can also take part in scent-based tracking work.

faq.question: How large does an Old Danish Pointer get?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives males a height of 54–60 cm and weight of 30–35 kg. Females are 50–56 cm tall and weigh 26–31 kg.

faq.question: What does its coat look like?
faq.answer: The coat is short, dense and somewhat hard to the touch. The standard describes a white base with brown patches or smaller brown speckles, with darker brown preferred.

faq.question: Is the Old Danish Pointer suitable for an active family?
faq.answer: It may suit an active household that can provide outdoor exercise, scent-based activities, training and companionship. Introductions and supervision should be appropriate for the ages and needs of the children and the individual dog.

faq.question: How much exercise does it need each day?
faq.answer: Breed sources describe it as a working dog that needs substantial daily activity, but the consulted references do not establish a reliable universal number of minutes. The plan should reflect age, health, conditioning and workload.

faq.question: What health problems is the breed known for?
faq.answer: The sources used here do not establish a reliable breed-specific list of common diseases or prevalence figures. Ask breeders about documented family health history and consult a veterinarian about appropriate screening and preventive care.

overview.summary: The Parson Russell Terrier is a small, athletic working terrier developed for fox hunting. It combines a lively, confident nature with stamina, agility, and a strong instinct to investigate and pursue moving animals. It generally suits people who can provide regular activity, training, supervision, and mental enrichment.
overview.description: This terrier has a balanced, flexible body, relatively long legs, a narrow chest, and an alert expression. Its coat can be smooth, broken, or rough, with a dense, weather-resistant texture. White is the dominant colour, usually with black, tan, or lemon markings depending on the standard being followed. The breed is energetic and clever, but its hunting instincts and independent problem-solving can make secure containment and consistent training especially important.
overview.history: The breed developed in southern England during the nineteenth century from fox-working terriers associated with Reverend John Russell. These dogs were expected to keep pace with hounds and horses, then enter underground dens to locate and flush foxes. The Parson Russell Terrier became a distinct recognised breed after a long period in which different working terriers were often grouped under overlapping Russell or Jack Russell names.
overview.originalPurpose: A working terrier bred to accompany foxhounds and pursue foxes both above ground and into underground dens.
currentRoles: Earthdog and other suitable terrier activities
Tracking and other structured canine sports

exercise.level: High. This active working terrier needs daily physical activity and purposeful mental enrichment. Adapt activity to age, fitness, health, weather, and the individual dog's behaviour.

Reward-based training and short learning sessions
Securely supervised fetch or interactive play
