grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a suitable dog brush or comb to remove loose hair and check the skin. Rough and broken coats may require hand-stripping or help from a groomer familiar with the breed.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when necessary with a dog-formulated shampoo. Frequent bathing is usually unnecessary unless the dog becomes dirty or a veterinarian recommends it.
notes: Keep the coat looking natural rather than excessively sculpted.
Check the ears regularly and clean only as needed with appropriate products.
Trim nails as needed to maintain comfortable movement.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste.
Inspect the skin and coat during routine grooming for irritation, parasites, or wounds.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for inexperienced handlers. The breed is intelligent and can learn quickly, but its energy, persistence, and hunting instincts require consistent management.
tips: Use short, varied, reward-based sessions to maintain engagement.
Train recall and loose-leash walking early, while recognising that prey drive can remain strong.
Reward calm behaviour and teach a reliable settle cue.
Provide safe outlets for sniffing, searching, and problem-solving.
Use secure fencing and a lead in open areas where wildlife or small animals may trigger chasing.
Introduce children, dogs, people, and new environments gradually and positively.
Avoid harsh or frightening methods; seek a qualified trainer if reactivity or chasing becomes difficult to manage.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog to people, dogs, household sounds, surfaces, transport, and new places gradually and positively. Supervise interactions with children and other animals, and do not assume that socialisation will eliminate the breed's natural hunting drive.

climates: A range of ordinary climates can be managed with suitable shelter and care.
In hot weather, provide shade, ventilation, fresh water, and cooler times for exercise.
In cold or wet conditions, provide a dry, comfortable resting area.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage, body condition, activity level, and health.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy diet in portions and at a frequency appropriate for the puppy's age, growth, and the food's feeding instructions. Ask a veterinarian for individual guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Use measured meals of a complete adult diet. Adjust portions to maintain a healthy body condition and account for treats used during training.
feedingFrequency.senior: Choose a complete diet suited to the dog's body condition, activity, dental health, and medical needs. Ask a veterinarian before making major dietary changes.

nutrition.guidelines: Choose a nutritionally complete diet and monitor body condition rather than relying on a universal portion size. Food requirements vary with age, activity, health, and the energy density of the food. Keep fresh water available, introduce dietary changes gradually, and discuss persistent weight changes, digestive problems, or supplement use with a veterinarian.
considerations: Measure portions and adjust them to maintain a healthy body condition.
Include training treats in the overall daily food allowance.
Provide fresh, clean water at all times.
Use a life-stage-appropriate complete diet.
Discuss suspected food intolerance, persistent digestive signs, or unexplained weight change with a veterinarian.
Do not add supplements unless there is a clear need and suitable veterinary advice.
nutrition.note: No universal calorie target or serving size is specified because individual requirements depend on body condition, activity, age, food composition, and health.

health.overview: The breed is generally described as robust, but breed-health resources identify concerns that responsible breeders may screen for, including patellar luxation, congenital deafness, certain inherited neurological conditions, and eye disorders. Primary lens luxation and inherited dental enamel disease also appear in breed-specific DNA-testing resources. These are potential concerns, not a prediction that an individual dog will develop them.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation, in which the kneecap moves out of its normal position

preventiveCare: Arrange routine veterinary examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention appropriate to local veterinary advice.
Ask the breeder for documented health-screening results for both parents.
Discuss breed-relevant eye, patella, hearing, and DNA tests with a veterinarian or knowledgeable breed specialist.
Seek veterinary advice promptly for sudden vision changes, unusual gait or balance, hearing concerns, or signs of pain.
Maintain dental hygiene, healthy body condition, and regular activity suited to the individual dog.

recommendedScreenings: Patella evaluation for breeding dogs.

health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Seek veterinary advice for persistent bad breath, oral pain, bleeding gums, damaged teeth, or difficulty eating.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, discharge, odour, or repeated scratching. Clean only when needed with a dog-safe product, and ask a veterinarian about persistent or painful signs.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin and coat during grooming. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, redness, sores, hair loss, or recurring skin problems rather than assuming the cause.

idealFor: People who enjoy regular outdoor activity and interactive training
Owners able to provide secure containment and supervised exercise

People prepared to manage a lively dog with strong hunting instincts
notIdealFor: People seeking a low-energy dog that needs little activity or engagement

People who cannot commit to ongoing training, enrichment, and daily interaction

funFacts: The breed was developed to work with foxhounds and horses and to pursue foxes underground.
The FCI standard describes male and female ideal heights separately: 36 cm for males and 33 cm for females.
The coat can be smooth, broken, or rough, and is intended to remain natural-looking rather than heavily sculpted.
The breed's hunting heritage helps explain why secure containment and recall training are important.

faq.question: How tall is a Parson Russell Terrier?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives ideal heights of 36 cm for males and 33 cm for females. The AKC standard gives ideal heights of 14 inches for males and 13 inches for females, and disqualifies dogs under 12 or over 15 inches. These are standard-specific measurements, not a guarantee of an individual dog's adult size.

faq.question: How much does a Parson Russell Terrier weigh?
faq.answer: The AKC standard describes 13–17 pounds as the usual weight for a terrier in hard working condition, approximately 5.9–7.7 kg. Healthy weight depends on the individual dog's frame, condition, and activity.

faq.question: What colours can a Parson Russell Terrier be?
faq.answer: The FCI standard describes a white or predominantly white coat with tan, lemon, or black markings, or a combination of these. Colour rules can differ between kennel-club standards.

faq.question: Does a Parson Russell Terrier need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: It is an active working terrier that generally needs regular exercise, training, and mental enrichment. No single daily minute target is provided here because needs vary by age, fitness, health, and the individual dog.

faq.question: Can a Parson Russell Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment suitability cannot be determined from breed alone. The dog's exercise, enrichment, noise, training, access to safe outdoor activity, and the household's circumstances all matter.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results relevant to the breed, including patella, eye, and hearing assessments, and discuss appropriate DNA tests for inherited conditions with a veterinarian or breed specialist. Testing recommendations can change and should be confirmed before breeding.

faq.question: How long does a Parson Russell Terrier live?
faq.answer: A reliable, consistently supported lifespan range was not established from the sources used for this record, so no numerical range is supplied. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, healthcare, environment, and chance.

overview.summary: An athletic, clean-lined Maltese warren hound (Kelb tal-Fenek) that hunts by sight, scent, and hearing across rocky limestone terrain, celebrated for its amber eyes, mobile erect ears, tan-to-chestnut coat, and habit of blushing rose-pink when happy or excited.
overview.description: The Pharaoh Hound—known natively in Malta as the Kelb tal-Fenek ('rabbit dog')—is a medium-sized, graceful yet powerful hound with hard, clean-cut lines and a noble bearing. Slightly longer in body from breastbone to haunch than tall at the withers, it combines a long, lean, blunt-wedge head with parallel skull and foreface planes, oval amber eyes, and large, broad-based erect ears that pivot attentively to pinpoint sounds when working close. Its short, glossy, odourless coat ranges from tan and rich tan to chestnut, harmonized with flesh-coloured nose, lip, and eye-rim pigment that flushes a deep rose colour ('blushing') when the dog is excited or pleased. Unlike pure sighthounds, it is a versatile triple-sense hunter that locates quarry by scent, tracks underground movement by hearing, and courses at high speed by sight. Indoors, a well-exercised Pharaoh Hound is affectionate, comical, and playful well into old age, while remaining vocal, independent-minded, and unsuitable for off-leash freedom in unenclosed areas.
overview.history: For centuries, rural hunters and farmers across the Maltese archipelago of Malta and Gozo bred the Kelb tal-Fenek to hunt wild rabbits at night among steep, rocky hills and dry-stone rubble walls, often working alongside belled ferrets. Popular accounts long proposed that Phoenician traders brought ancient Egyptian 'Tesem' hunting dogs to Malta, inspired by the breed's striking visual similarity to hounds depicted in Egyptian tomb chapels (such as those of Mereruka and Senbi) and to the jackal-headed god Anubis. However, the earliest written record in Malta dates to 1647, when Maltese historian Giovanni Francesco Abela wrote in 'Della Descrittione di Malta' of local rabbit-hunting hounds ('Cernechi') prized as far away as France for rocky mountain terrain. Modern canine genomic and phylogeographic studies (including microsatellite and mitochondrial analyses in 2004 and 2023) indicate that the Kelb tal-Fenek is not a direct unchanged survivor of ancient Egypt, but rather a member of the Mediterranean warren-hound family—closely related to the Sicilian Cirneco dell'Etna and Iberian Podencos—showing low inbreeding and high genetic divergence from modern Egyptian street dogs. First imported to Britain in the 1920s and early 1960s, the breed produced its first litter outside Malta in the United Kingdom in 1963 and its first litter in the United States in 1970. After British fanciers adopted the name 'Pharaoh Hound' (a name originally used on the continent in 1963 for Mediterranean prick-eared hounds), Britain approved a dedicated standard for the Maltese breed in 1974—the same year Malta honoured the Kelb tal-Fenek as its National Dog (commemorated on a 1977 one-Maltese-lira silver coin)—followed by updated international adoption in 1977 and North American recognition in 1983–1984.
overview.originalPurpose: Nighttime and daytime hunting and coursing of wild rabbits and small game across rocky limestone terrain and dry-stone rubble walls using scent, hearing, and sight (traditionally in tandem with ferrets)
currentRoles: Working rabbit-hunting warren hound in Malta
Lure coursing and amateur racing competitor
Agility, obedience, rally, nose work, and tracking participant
Therapy dog and alert household watchdog

physical.coatType: Short, glossy single coat ranging in texture from fine and close-lying to slightly harsh, with no feathering and no undercoat
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Tan (from yellowish-tan 'isfar' to rich golden tan)

Tan, rich tan, or chestnut with permitted white markings: white tail tip (strongly desired), white chest patch ('the Star'), white on the toes, and a slim white blaze or snip on the centre line of the face
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
distinctiveFeatures: Long, lean, well-chiselled head shaped like a blunt wedge from above and in profile, with a slight stop and parallel skull and foreface planes (foreface slightly longer than the skull)
Flesh-coloured nose, lips, and eye rims that blend with the coat colour (no other nose colour is permitted) and visibly 'blush' a deep rose-pink when the dog is happy or excited

Oval, moderately deep-set amber eyes that harmonize with the coat colour and give a keen, intelligent expression (puppies are born with blue eyes that transition through blue-grey to amber by 3 to 4 months of age)
Large, fine, broad-based ears set medium high, carried erect when alert, laid flat back for minimal wind resistance when sprinting, and remarkably mobile when listening for quarry

Lithe, slightly rectangular body (length from breastbone to haunch bone slightly greater than withers height) with an almost straight topline, deep brisket reaching the elbows, moderate tuck-up, and strong, well-knuckled feet that are neither cat nor hare feet
Medium-set, whip-like tail that is fairly thick at the base and tapers below the point of the hock in repose, carried high and curved like a rudder in action (a screw tail is a fault)

Strict coat-marking rules: a white tail tip is strongly desired, white on the chest ('the Star'), white toes, and a slim central facial snip/blaze are permitted, flecking is undesirable, and any solid white patch on the back of the neck, shoulder, back, or sides is a disqualification in North American standards

Withers height of 56–63.5 cm (22–25 in) for males and 53–61 cm (21–24 in) for females in international and British standards (58.42–63.5 cm [23–25 in] for males and 53.34–60.96 cm [21–24 in] for females in American standards) and typical adult weight of 20.4–24.9 kg (45–55 lbs)

traits: Alert, observant, and keen
Friendly, affectionate, and people-oriented with family
Playful and comical throughout adulthood and senior years
Intelligent and quick to learn, yet an independent thinker
Sensitive to harsh handling or heavy-handed corrections
Can be aloof or reserved with strangers, preferring to initiate greetings on its own terms
Vocal and expressive, using barks and a wide variety of pack-hound sounds
Intense hunting and chasing drive triggered by both sight and scent
Good alert watchdog that announces visitors, but non-aggressive and unsuited as a guard dog

exercise.level: High. Requires a consistent daily schedule: either 15 to 20 minutes twice daily of free sprinting for a 'self-runner' inside a minimum 50 × 50 foot (15 × 15 m) enclosure with a 6-foot-high (1.8 m) fence, or at least 20 minutes twice daily of brisk leashed walking and structured exercise.
activities: Free sprinting in a securely fenced enclosure (minimum 50 × 50 feet with a 6-foot fence)
Brisk daily leashed walks and jogging with an active handler
Lure coursing and amateur straight or oval racing
Agility, rally, and positive-reinforcement obedience
Tracking, nose work, and scent-detection games that engage the breed's keen nose
Interactive toy play (which most Pharaoh Hounds enjoy well into their senior years)

grooming.brushing: Light daily brushing or a thorough weekly going-over with a hound glove, rubber curry brush, or damp cloth to remove loose hair and keep the short coat gleaming.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only as needed with a gentle dog-safe shampoo; the breed naturally lacks a 'doggy odour' even when wet, so any noticeable body odour warrants a veterinary check.
notes: Keep toenails trimmed or ground short enough that they do not make a tapping sound when the dog walks across a hard floor.
Pay particular attention to keeping the large, erect ears clean and free of dust or debris after outdoor runs.
Inspect the thin skin and short coat after field runs for minor bramble or rock scratches (which are never penalized as conformation faults).
Provide a warm dog coat outdoors in cold, wet, or snowy weather and a soft, warm indoor bed.
Brush teeth regularly at home and have them checked at annual veterinary exams.

training.difficulty: Moderate
tips: Use creative, upbeat positive reinforcement ('praise, patience, and provisions'); Pharaoh Hounds are quick learners when convinced that the task is their own idea, but shut down or balk under harsh corrections.

Never trust any amount of obedience training to override the breed's hunting instinct in an unenclosed area: off-leash Pharaoh Hounds that catch a sight or scent trail will bolt oblivious to traffic and can be lost for days or struck by vehicles.
Enclose yards with a stout, minimum 6-foot-high (1.8 m) physical fence, and always use a strong leash and secure martingale collar or harness on walks.
Gently redirect or distract alert barking from puppyhood onward; the breed is naturally vocal and a household with a Pharaoh Hound is rarely completely bark-free.
Provide daily mental enrichment—such as tracking, nose work, agility, or puzzle toys—because a bored Pharaoh Hound quickly invents destructive entertainment.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to varied people, gentle children, friendly dogs, and novel sights. Because Pharaoh Hounds can be aloof with strangers, allow them the courtesy of making the first overture when meeting new people rather than forcing contact, and supervise carefully around cats and small furry pets.

climates: Warm and sunny Mediterranean climates (for which the short coat and large heat-dissipating ears are naturally adapted)
Temperate climates
Cool or cold climates only as a strictly indoor family dog provided with warm outdoor coats during exercise and cosy indoor bedding
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Because of its lack of insulating undercoat and strong need for human companionship, the Pharaoh Hound must be an indoor family dog rather than a backyard or outdoor kennel dog, and needs ample exercise before being left alone.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced commercial dog food or veterinarian-supervised and approved home-prepared diet appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior) and activity level
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age and workload, monitoring calorie intake and body condition so the dog stays lithe and lean without excess weight on its joints. Deduct training treats from the daily food allowance to prevent obesity, and keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Watch calorie consumption and treat intake closely, as some individuals are prone to gaining excess weight when not actively coursing or running.
Prepare home-cooked diets only under the supervision and approval of a veterinarian.
Avoid vigorous sprinting immediately before or after meals.
Consult your breeder or veterinarian to establish individualized daily meal schedules for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Consulted kennel-club and parent-club sources do not prescribe fixed numerical meal counts per day for puppies, adults, or seniors; tailor meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Pharaoh Hound is widely regarded by veterinary and breed-club health committees as a hardy, long-lived breed (typical lifespan 12 to 14 years) with low inbreeding and no widespread breed-specific genetic syndromes. Parent-club breeding ethics require all breeding dogs to be at least 24 months of age and to complete pre-breeding health certification screenings for hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, autoimmune thyroiditis (thyroid function), and inheritable eye diseases (via a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist), with elbow dysplasia also evaluated in health registries; the vast majority of screened dogs test normal. Like other lean coursing hounds, Pharaoh Hounds can be sensitive to certain anesthetics (such as barbiturates) and chemical insecticides due to their low body-fat percentage. In senior dogs, the most commonly reported cancers are hemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumours, and mammary tumours in unspayed females, which reflect general age-related canine risks rather than breed-specific defects.
commonConditions: Orthopedic screening targets: hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, and elbow dysplasia (screened prior to breeding under parent-club health protocols, with the majority of tested dogs scoring normal)
Autoimmune thyroiditis / hypothyroidism: monitored via mandatory pre-breeding thyroid blood panels in parent-club health programs
Hereditary ocular disorders: screened via periodic examinations by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Age-related cancers in older dogs: hemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumours, and mammary gland tumours in intact females (spaying companion females reduces mammary cancer risk)
Sighthound-type sensitivity to certain anaesthetic agents (such as thiobarbiturates) and chemical compounds/insecticides, linked to the breed's lean, low-body-fat build
Traumatic skin lacerations, torn nails, or sprains incurred while sprinting across rough or rocky terrain
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of any prospective puppy are at least 24 months of age at breeding and hold documented health clearances for hips, patellas, thyroid function, and veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams (as well as elbow evaluations where performed).

Ensure every puppy is permanently identified via microchip before placement, and keep secure 6-foot fencing and leashes in place to prevent traffic trauma—one of the greatest real-world threats to the breed.
Inform your veterinarian about coursing-hound anaesthetic and chemical sensitivities prior to dental cleanings or surgery.
Keep nails trimmed short enough that they never tap on hard floors to prevent toe and foot splaying or high-speed running injuries.
Maintain a lean, athletic body weight and inspect the skin, ears, and paw pads after outdoor runs.

health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly at home with dog-safe toothpaste and have the teeth and gums examined at every annual veterinary checkup. Conformation standards require powerful jaws with a complete, strong scissor bite set square to the jaws.
health.earCare: Pay close attention to keeping the large, upright, mobile ears clean and free of dust, seeds, or wax buildup, wiping gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleaner when needed.
health.skinCare: Because the short, fine single coat lacks an undercoat, inspect the skin regularly for scrapes after runs, provide a warm coat during cold or wet weather, and note that a healthy Pharaoh Hound has virtually no doggy odour (any strong skin or coat odour should be investigated by a veterinarian).

funFacts: Known natively in Malta as the Kelb tal-Fenek ('rabbit dog'), the breed was declared the National Dog of Malta in 1974 and featured on the reverse of the 1977 one-Maltese-lira silver coin.

When a Pharaoh Hound is happy or excited, increased blood flow causes its flesh-coloured nose, ears, and eye rims to 'blush' a deep rose-pink, and many dogs also curl their lips into a toothy 'smile'.
Puppies are born with bright blue eyes that gradually turn blue-grey and deepen to the adult golden-amber colour at around 3 to 4 months of age.

In traditional Maltese rabbit hunting ('kaċċa tal-fenek') at night among limestone rubble walls, hunters use a belled ferret ('nemes') to flush rabbits from deep burrows; the Kelb tal-Fenek can hear the ferret's tiny bell up to 3 metres (10 feet) underground through solid rock crevices.

Although the breed bears a striking visual resemblance to ancient Egyptian tomb reliefs and the jackal-headed god Anubis, modern DNA studies show that it is an indigenous Mediterranean warren hound closely related to the Sicilian Cirneco dell'Etna rather than a direct survivor from pharaonic Egypt.

The first documented historical mention of Malta's rabbit-hunting hounds appears in 1647, when Maltese historian Giovanni Francesco Abela wrote that the island's 'Cernechi' were sought after as far away as France for hunting in steep, stony terrain.
A healthy Pharaoh Hound has virtually no 'doggy odour'—even when soaking wet.

faq.question: What is a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The Pharaoh Hound—traditionally called the Kelb tal-Fenek ('rabbit dog') in its native Malta—is a medium-sized, athletic Mediterranean hunting hound that pursues quarry using scent, hearing, and sight. It is famous for its amber eyes, large erect ears, short tan-to-chestnut coat, and ability to 'blush' rose-pink on its nose and ears when excited.

faq.question: Did the Pharaoh Hound really come from ancient Egypt?
faq.answer: Despite popular lore linking the breed to ancient Egyptian tomb art and Phoenician traders, genomic and mitochondrial studies published in 2004 and 2023 show that the modern Kelb tal-Fenek is not a direct unchanged descendant of ancient Egyptian dogs. Instead, it developed on the islands of Malta and Gozo (where rabbit-hunting hounds were recorded by Giovanni Francesco Abela in 1647) as part of the Mediterranean warren-hound group alongside Sicily's Cirneco dell'Etna and Spain's Podencos. The English name 'Pharaoh Hound' was applied in the twentieth century when the breed was exported to Britain.

faq.question: How big does a Pharaoh Hound get?
faq.answer: International and British conformation standards specify a withers height of 56 to 63.5 cm (22–25 inches) for males and 53 to 61 cm (21–24 inches) for females, while American standards specify 23 to 25 inches (58.42–63.5 cm) for males and 21 to 24 inches (53.34–60.96 cm) for females. Typical adult weight is 20.4 to 24.9 kg (45–55 pounds) for both sexes.

faq.question: What coat colours and white markings are allowed on a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The coat ranges from tan and rich tan to chestnut (with flesh-coloured nose, lip, and eye-rim pigment that blends with the coat). Permitted white markings are a strongly desired white tip on the tail, a white patch on the chest called 'the Star', white on the toes, and a slim white blaze or snip on the centre line of the face. Flecking is undesirable, and any solid white spot on the back of the neck, shoulder, back, or sides is a disqualification in North American standards.

faq.question: Why does a Pharaoh Hound blush and smile?
faq.answer: Because the breed carries recessive dilution pigment that gives it a flesh-coloured nose, eye rims, and inner ears rather than black pigment, increased blood flow when the dog is happy, affectionate, or excited turns its nose and ears a vivid rose-pink. Many Pharaoh Hounds also pull back their lips in a toothy 'smile' to greet their owners.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Pharaoh Hound need, and what fencing is required?
faq.answer: For a dog that naturally runs on its own ('a self-runner'), 15 to 20 minutes of free sprinting twice a day in a securely enclosed area of at least 50 by 50 feet surrounded by a 6-foot-high fence is ideal. If such an enclosure is unavailable or the dog does not self-exercise, owners should provide at least 20 minutes of brisk leashed walking twice daily alongside regular opportunities for lure coursing, agility, tracking, or enclosed running.

faq.question: Can a Pharaoh Hound ever be trusted off-leash in an unfenced area?
faq.answer: No. Unlike pure sighthounds that hunt only by vision, the Pharaoh Hound hunts by both sight and scent. Once it spots or scents a rabbit, squirrel, or cat in an open area, its hunting instinct overrides obedience training; off-leash dogs frequently run for miles oblivious to road traffic.

faq.question: Are Pharaoh Hounds quiet or vocal indoors?
faq.answer: Because they were bred to hunt in pairs or packs and bark to signal when quarry is located, Pharaoh Hounds are naturally vocal. They make excellent alert watchdogs that announce visitors and use a wide repertoire of barks and expressive sounds at home, though early gentle redirection helps keep barking manageable.

faq.question: What health tests are required or recommended for Pharaoh Hound breeding stock?
faq.answer: The breed is generally very healthy with low rates of hereditary disease. Parent-club breeding ethics require breeding dogs to be at least 24 months old and to complete screenings for hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, autoimmune thyroiditis (thyroid blood panel), and inheritable eye diseases (board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist exam), with elbow dysplasia also evaluated in health registries.

faq.question: Are there special veterinary precautions for Pharaoh Hounds?
faq.answer: Yes. Like other lean coursing hounds with very low body fat, Pharaoh Hounds can be sensitive to certain anaesthetic drugs (such as thiobarbiturates) and chemical insecticides, so owners should remind their veterinarian before any surgery or dental procedure.

breeds.group: FCI Group 2 — Pinscher and Schnauzer, Molossoid and Swiss Mountain and Cattledogs; UKC Guardian Dog Group

origin.region: Aragon and the Spanish Pyrenees

overview.summary: A giant Spanish livestock guardian known for its substantial build, thick white coat with distinct patches, calm manner and confident protective instincts.
overview.description: The Pyrenean Mastiff is a very large, powerful dog developed to protect livestock in the mountainous regions of Spain. Its dense coat is predominantly white with clearly defined patches, often including markings around the eyes and ears. Despite its imposing size, the breed is expected to move with strength and balance rather than sluggishness. It is commonly described as calm, intelligent and affectionate with familiar people, while remaining alert and confident when unfamiliar people or potential threats approach. Responsible ownership requires early socialisation, consistent reward-based training, secure boundaries, room to move, regular grooming and the budget and physical ability to manage a giant dog.
overview.history: The breed developed in the Spanish Pyrenees, particularly in Aragon, where shepherds relied on large guardian dogs to protect livestock during seasonal movement between pastures. These dogs were expected to deter predators such as wolves and bears while remaining with the flock and its handlers. As large predators became less common and traditional livestock practices changed, the breed's numbers declined. Dedicated Spanish breeders later worked to rebuild the population from a limited number of dogs. The Pyrenean Mastiff is now kept as a livestock and property guardian and as a companion in homes prepared for its size and guarding instincts.

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly at least weekly, with more frequent brushing during seasonal shedding. Pay particular attention to the feathering behind the forelegs, underside, rear, tail and areas where the coat can trap moisture or debris.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed using a dog-appropriate shampoo. Dry the dense coat thoroughly to the skin after bathing or getting wet.
notes: Expect more loose coat during seasonal shedding periods.
Check and clean the drool-prone neck and dewlap area as needed.
Inspect hanging ears regularly for dirt, odour, redness or discharge.
Trim nails regularly, including dewclaws where present.
Check the coat and skin for mats, parasites, grass seeds and moisture-related irritation.
Avoid shaving the double coat unless a veterinarian advises a medical reason.
In hot or humid weather, provide shade, water and a cool resting place, and ensure the undercoat dries properly.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for inexperienced handlers because of its size, independence and natural guarding instincts.
tips: Begin reward-based training and household manners early, while the dog is still manageable physically.
Teach loose-lead walking, recall, a reliable stop cue and calm visitor routines.
Use consistent rules and rewards rather than intimidation or harsh punishment.
Socialise the puppy gradually with different people, environments, surfaces and appropriate dogs.
Teach the dog to settle calmly when people enter or leave the property.
Use secure fencing and controlled introductions rather than expecting instinct alone to determine whether a visitor or animal is safe.
Get help from a qualified trainer experienced with livestock guardians or giant breeds if guarding behaviour becomes difficult to manage.
training.socialization: Early, ongoing and carefully managed socialisation is important. Introduce visitors, other dogs, handling and everyday environments in a way that supports calm, controlled behaviour without forcing interactions.

climates: Cool and temperate climates
Mountain environments with suitable shelter
Warm climates with shade, plentiful water and activity scheduled for cooler hours

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced diet appropriate for a giant-breed dog's life stage, growth rate, body condition and health.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete large- or giant-breed puppy diet in several measured meals according to age, product guidance and veterinary advice. Avoid uncontrolled rapid growth and overfeeding.
feedingFrequency.adult: Many adult dogs do well with two measured meals per day. Adjust portions to activity level and body condition.

nutrition.guidelines: Giant breeds need careful weight and growth management. Use a nutritionally complete diet, measure portions, keep fresh water available and adjust intake to maintain a lean body condition. Ask a veterinarian to guide growth feeding, especially during puppyhood and adolescence.
considerations: Avoid excess calories and rapid weight gain during growth.
Choose a diet formulated for the dog's life stage and expected adult size.
Monitor body condition and adjust portions as activity changes.
Discuss joint health, supplements and any diet changes with a veterinarian rather than adding supplements automatically.
Ask a veterinarian about feeding and exercise routines that may reduce risk factors associated with bloat.
Keep food and treats appropriate to the dog's overall daily energy needs.
nutrition.note: There is no single correct portion for every Pyrenean Mastiff. Food requirements depend on age, body condition, activity, neuter status and the specific diet.

health.overview: As a giant breed, the Pyrenean Mastiff needs careful attention to joint development, body condition and heart health. Breed-club guidance highlights hip and elbow screening and cardiac assessment, while degenerative myelopathy DNA testing is also recommended by the national breed club listed in the breed profile. Deep-chested dogs may develop gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), a life-threatening emergency. Screening can help inform breeding and care decisions but cannot guarantee that an individual dog will remain healthy.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: an abnormal development of the hip joint that can contribute to pain and reduced mobility.
Elbow dysplasia: a group of developmental elbow disorders relevant to large and giant dogs.
Degenerative myelopathy: an inherited progressive neurological disease; DNA testing can help assess genetic status but results require correct interpretation.
Cardiac disease: breed-club health information notes concerns about heart disease in the population and recommends cardiac evaluation for breeding dogs.
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat): a sudden, potentially fatal emergency involving stomach distension and sometimes twisting.
Moisture-associated skin irritation or hot spots: dense coat can make thorough drying important, particularly in humid conditions.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary examinations and maintain appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention plans.
Ask breeders for documented hip and elbow evaluation results and relevant genetic test results.
Discuss cardiac examination and whether further testing is appropriate with a veterinarian.
Maintain a lean body condition and avoid excessive impact during growth.
Seek emergency veterinary care immediately if bloat is suspected.
Keep the dense coat dry to the skin after bathing or getting wet, especially in humid weather.
Use secure fencing and controlled handling to reduce risks associated with a powerful guardian dog.

health.dentalCare: Brush regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks. Large size does not remove the need for routine oral care.
health.earCare: Check the hanging ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge or discomfort. Clean only with a suitable product and method recommended by a veterinarian.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin beneath the dense coat and around the neck folds. Dry the coat thoroughly after bathing or wet weather and seek veterinary advice for persistent redness, itching, sores or discharge.

It developed in Spain as a livestock guardian, not as a mountain-dog breed from France.
The coat is expected to have a white base with distinct patches rather than being solid white.
The breed standard specifies minimum heights rather than a maximum height limit.
Its traditional role required it to accompany livestock over seasonal grazing routes and deter large predators.

faq.question: Is the Pyrenean Mastiff the same as the Pyrenean Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: No. They are distinct breeds with different breed histories and standards. The Pyrenean Mastiff is the Spanish livestock guardian also known as Mastín del Pirineo.

faq.question: How large does a Pyrenean Mastiff get?
faq.answer: The cited breed standards specify minimum heights of 77 cm for males and 72 cm for females, with no upper height limit in the standard used here. Individual size varies.

faq.question: Is the Pyrenean Mastiff a good family dog?
faq.answer: It can be a calm and affectionate family companion in a well-prepared home. Its giant size and guarding instincts make early training, socialisation and supervision especially important.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Pyrenean Mastiff need?
faq.answer: Regular walks and controlled daily activity are important. The 45–90 minutes shown in this profile is an editorial estimate, not an official rule; age, health and working responsibilities affect individual needs.

faq.question: Does the Pyrenean Mastiff shed?
faq.answer: Yes. Its dense coat can shed heavily during seasonal coat changes. Regular brushing and thorough drying help keep the coat and skin in good condition.

faq.question: What colours are accepted for a Pyrenean Mastiff?
faq.answer: The coat has a white base with distinct patches. Recognised patch colours vary slightly by registry, and some standards specify a facial mask and markings around the ears and eyes.

faq.question: Is the Pyrenean Mastiff easy to train?
faq.answer: It is intelligent but may be independent. Begin early with reward-based training, clear boundaries and gradual socialisation. Professional guidance can be useful for inexperienced owners.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip and elbow evaluations, a cardiac examination and degenerative myelopathy DNA test results. Discuss the results with a veterinarian and ask how they were considered in breeding decisions.

faq.question: Can a Pyrenean Mastiff live in a hot climate?
faq.answer: It can need extra care in warm weather because of its dense coat and large body. Provide shade, fresh water and a cool resting area, and avoid strenuous exercise during the hottest hours.

faq.question: What is bloat, and why should owners know about it?
faq.answer: Bloat is a potentially life-threatening stomach emergency. A swollen abdomen, repeated unproductive retching, restlessness, weakness or collapse requires immediate emergency veterinary attention.

overview.summary: A diminutive, long-legged, finely boned Russian companion breed developed in smooth-haired and long-haired varieties, combining lively intelligence and cheerful athleticism with intense devotion to its household.
overview.description: The Russian Toy (Russkiy Toy) is one of the world's smallest dog breeds—an elegant, lively, high-stationed toy dog with fine bone, lean musculature, and a square body outline in which height at the withers equals body length. Its chest reaches the elbows, the height at the elbows is slightly more than half the withers height, and sexual dimorphism is only slightly defined. The breed exists in two coat varieties that can appear in the same litter: a sleek, shiny, close-lying smooth coat without undercoat, and a long-haired variety featuring a 3 to 5 cm body coat, feathered limbs and tail, and dramatic, butterfly-like ear fringes covering large, high-set triangular ears. Active, cheerful, curious, and keenly intelligent, the Russian Toy bonds closely with its family, loves both energetic play and lap snuggling, and may be slightly reserved with strangers while remaining neither timid nor aggressive.
overview.history: The Russian Toy traces its ancestry to English Toy Terriers imported into Russia as early as the eighteenth century—evidenced by a preserved short-haired terrier dated 1716–1725 in the Zoological Museum in Saint Petersburg that belonged to Emperor Peter the Great—and became a fashionable companion of the Russian aristocracy by the early twentieth century. Following the 1917 revolution and between 1920 and 1950, breeding of purebred toy terriers nearly ceased and numbers fell to a critical level. When Soviet breeders began reviving the stock in the mid-1950s in isolation, most surviving dogs lacked pedigrees and were not purebred, resulting in a distinct Russian type with a higher, rounder skull, flatter cheeks, and rounder eyes than the English Toy Terrier. On 12 October 1958, two smooth-coated dogs (one with slightly longer hair) produced a male puppy named Chikki with striking fringes on his ears and limbs. Acquired and bred in Moscow by Yevgueniya Fominichna Zharova—who mated him to a slightly long-coated female named Irma—this line became known as the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier. A first Russian standard for the two varieties was approved in 1966, and in 1988 both the smooth-haired Russian Toy Terrier and the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier were unified under a single breed standard, later dropping the word 'Terrier' to become the Russian Toy.
overview.originalPurpose: Aristocratic companion dog (historically also used as an alert household watchdog and ratter)
currentRoles: Agility, obedience, rally, and trick-dog competitor

physical.coatType: Two coat varieties: smooth-haired (short, close-lying, glossy single coat without undercoat) and long-haired (straight or slightly wavy close-lying coat with ear fringes and limb/tail feathering)
physical.coatLength: Smooth-haired: short and close-lying all over. Long-haired: moderately long (3–5 cm / 1–3 in) on the body and neck, short and close-lying on the head and front of the legs, with long silky hair on the feet hiding the nails, distinct feathering on the backs of the legs and tail, and thick ear fringes that completely cover the outer edges and tips of the ears by three years of age
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
distinctiveFeatures: Diminutive, high-legged, square-proportioned build with fine bone and lean muscle, where height at the elbows is slightly more than half the height at the withers
Small, light, wedge-shaped head with a high, slightly rounded skull, clearly pronounced stop, and lean pointed muzzle measuring one-third to two-fifths of head length
Large, thin, high-set erect ears shaped like a high isosceles triangle—dramatically fringed in the long-haired variety once mature (by about 3 years of age)
Large, rounded, dark, expressive eyes set well apart and looking straight ahead, with pigment matching the coat colour
Two interbreedable coat varieties (smooth-haired and long-haired) that can be born in the same litter when smooth-coated parents carry the recessive long-coat allele
Moderately high-set sickle or sabre tail carried at or above back level when moving (or docked to 2–4 vertebrae where legal)
Light, straightforward, fast, energetic gait with the head held proudly high and no change in the topline

Preferred height of 25 cm (range 22–27 cm internationally, 20–28 cm ± 1 cm in Britain, and 8–11 in / 20.3–27.9 cm in North America) and preferred weight of 2.3 kg (up to 3 kg internationally, with weight under 1.5 kg or over 3 kg disqualifying; up to 6–6.5 lbs in North America)

traits: Active and lively
Very cheerful
Curious and alert
Strongly devoted to its owner
Keenly intelligent and eager to please
Affectionate and fond of snuggling
Playful and spirited
Sometimes slightly aloof or reserved with strangers
Neither cowardly nor aggressive

exercise.level: Moderate (up to 1 hour per day). Energetic and playful indoors and outdoors, yet small enough that daily walks, yard runs, and interactive indoor play readily meet its physical needs.
activities: Daily walks on a harness and leash with its owner
Romping and chasing toys in a safely enclosed yard or indoor space
Agility, obedience, rally, and trick-dog training
Nose-work and scent-detection games
Lure coursing for toy breeds

grooming.level: Low to moderate. Simple routine upkeep for both varieties, with extra brushing required for the long-haired variety's ear fringes and feathering.
grooming.brushing: Long-haired variety: brush or comb 2 to 3 times per week, paying special attention to the ear fringes and leg feathering. Smooth-haired variety: brush weekly with a soft bristle brush and wipe daily with a chamois cloth to maintain shine and minimize loose hair.
grooming.bathing: Bathe monthly (or every 1 to 2 weeks for show/companion maintenance) using a gentle, high-quality dog shampoo and conditioner or creme rinse; smooth-coated dogs can also be bathed occasionally as needed.
notes: Both varieties shed minimally, with noticeably less visible hair from the short smooth coat.
On long-haired dogs, comb out ear fringes and feathering gently to prevent tangles and keep them free of debris.
Long-coated puppies typically shed much of their puppy coat between 5 and 12 months of age; full adult coat develops after 1 year and full ear fringing may take until 2 to 3 years of age.
Keep nails clipped short and trim excess hair beneath the feet on long-coated dogs; no other coat trimming is needed (and trimmed coats are penalized in conformation).
Brush teeth regularly and inspect ears, eyes, and skin during routine grooming.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Keenly intelligent, agreeable, and eager to please, though capable of a terrier-like stubborn streak and trying to take charge if boundaries are inconsistent.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based training with tiny treats and praise; keep sessions fun and engaging.
Enrol in puppy kindergarten and obedience classes early to channel the breed's intelligence and prevent bossy behaviour.
Take advantage of the breed's athleticism and nose by introducing agility, trick training, rally, or nose work.
Always walk the dog on a well-fitted harness rather than attaching a leash to a collar, protecting the delicate neck and trachea.
Remove collars and harnesses while the dog is inside the home so they cannot snag on household objects and cause injury.
Because of the breed's fine bone structure, prevent jumping from heights above 40 cm (such as high sofas or beds) and supervise interactions around large dogs.
training.socialization: Begin early, positive socialization in puppyhood with varied people, gentle handling, puppy kindergarten classes, and calm, size-appropriate dogs so natural reserve toward strangers does not turn into timidity or reactivity.

climates: Temperate climates
Indoor living with cold-weather protection (coats/sweaters or indoor litter/pad options during severe winter weather)
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Deeply attached to its human companions, the Russian Toy thrives on closeness and will quickly vocalize or become stressed if left isolated or neglected for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced, high-quality small-breed dog food (with extra-small kibble) or a veterinarian-supervised and approved home-prepared diet appropriate to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior).
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age and activity level, selecting very small kibble that suits a miniature jaw. Because some Russian Toys have a poor sense of satiety and can easily become overweight—placing extra stress on delicate bones and patellas—measure daily portions carefully, limit training treats, avoid free-feeding, and keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Choose extra-small kibble sized for a toy breed weighing under 3 kg.
Monitor body condition and calorie intake closely, as excess weight strains slender legs and kneecaps.
Keep training treats tiny and deduct them from the daily food allowance.
Prepare home-cooked diets only with veterinary supervision and nutritional balancing.
Consult a veterinarian or breeder to set appropriate daily meal counts for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Consulted kennel-club and breed-club sources do not prescribe fixed daily meal counts for puppies, adults, or seniors; feeding schedules should be tailored with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Russian Toy is generally a healthy, long-lived toy breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years (and some individuals reaching 15 years or more). As in many diminutive breeds, dental issues are the most frequent everyday veterinary concern: most puppies retain deciduous (baby) teeth that require veterinary extraction by about nine months of age to prevent malocclusion, and tartar buildup with periodontal disease can begin by one year of age. Because of its fine bone structure, the breed is also vulnerable to limb fractures from falls or rough play and to tracheal injury if walked on a neck collar rather than a harness. For breeding stock, national breed-club and kennel-club health programs prioritize clinical screening for patellar luxation, inherited eye diseases (such as progressive retinal atrophy), and cardiac abnormalities, with optional evaluations for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip and elbow dysplasia, and congenital liver shunts.
commonConditions: Retained deciduous (puppy) teeth: most puppies fail to shed all baby teeth naturally as adult teeth erupt around 6 months of age, frequently requiring surgical extraction under anaesthesia by 9 months of age to prevent double rows of teeth, misalignment, and periodontal disease
Periodontal disease, plaque, and tartar buildup: can begin as early as 1 year of age without regular tooth brushing and routine veterinary dental care
Patellar luxation: a potentially inherited kneecap instability common to toy breeds and included in mandatory pre-breeding orthopedic screening

Inherited and traumatic eye conditions: progressive retinal atrophy (PRA, screened via ophthalmic exams and biobank research) as well as corneal ulcers and surface eye injuries due to large, prominent eyes
Cardiac conditions: monitored through pre-breeding veterinary cardiology evaluations

Traumatic bone fractures and open fontanel: fine limb bones can fracture from jumping off furniture or rough contact with large dogs, and an open fontanel (unclosed skull soft spot) past 9 months of age is a disqualifying developmental defect

Additional conditions monitored via optional breed-club screening: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head), hip and elbow dysplasia, and congenital portosystemic (liver) shunts
preventiveCare: Brush the teeth regularly and have a veterinarian monitor tooth eruption between 6 and 9 months of age so retained baby teeth can be removed before they cause misalignment or gum disease.
Schedule routine veterinary dental examinations and professional cleanings as needed starting in young adulthood.
Walk the dog using a well-fitted harness rather than a neck collar to protect the fragile neck and trachea, and remove collars and harnesses indoors to prevent snagging accidents.
Prevent jumps from furniture or heights over 40 cm and supervise all interactions with large dogs or young children to avoid bone fractures.
Verify that breeding dogs have completed recommended orthopedic (patellar luxation), ophthalmic, and cardiac evaluations.
recommendedScreenings: Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation for breeding dogs
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (or accredited national eye-scheme examiner) for breeding dogs
Basic cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist for breeding dogs

Optional additional breed-club evaluations: radiographic screening for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip dysplasia, and elbow dysplasia; paired serum bile acid testing for congenital liver shunts; and DNA biobank/panel participation
health.dentalCare: Most Russian Toy puppies retain deciduous (baby) teeth when their permanent teeth erupt, often requiring veterinary extraction by nine months of age so the jaw and bite develop normally. Because tartar and periodontal disease can start by one year of age, daily or frequent tooth brushing and regular veterinary dental checks are essential.
health.earCare: Inspect the thin, erect triangular ears during weekly grooming for wax, debris, or irritation. On long-haired dogs, comb the thick ear fringes two to three times a week to keep them tangle- and debris-free.
health.skinCare: The skin is thin and tight-fitting. On smooth-coated dogs, brush weekly with a soft brush and wipe daily with a chamois cloth to remove dead hair and prevent flaky skin; on both varieties, use a gentle dog shampoo and conditioner or creme rinse when bathing.

idealFor: Apartment, flat, or house dwellers seeking a tiny, clean, devoted indoor companion
Owners who spend plenty of time at home and enjoy both lap snuggling and lively daily play
Active handlers interested in small-dog agility, obedience, rally, trick training, or nose work
Careful, attentive households willing to brush teeth regularly, use a harness, and protect a finely boned toy dog from falls
notIdealFor: Households that leave a dog alone for long workdays without companionship
Homes with boisterous, loud, or unsupervised young children or large, rough-playing dogs
Owners unwilling to manage puppy dental care (including possible deciduous tooth extraction) and routine tooth brushing

funFacts: A preserved short-haired terrier named Lizetta dating from 1716–1725, which personally belonged to Russian Emperor Peter the Great, is displayed at the Zoological Museum in Saint Petersburg as early evidence of the breed's English-type ancestors in Russia.

The long-haired variety traces back to a single male puppy named Chikki, born on 12 October 1958 to two smooth-coated parents with slightly longer hair and developed in Moscow by breeder Yevgueniya Fominichna Zharova.
Both smooth-haired and long-haired puppies can be born in the same litter when two smooth-coated parents carry the recessive gene for long hair.
In long-haired Russian Toys, the signature butterfly-like ear fringes and full adult coat take two to three years to reach their full length.

Originally known separately as the Russian Toy Terrier (smooth-coated) and the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier (long-coated), the two varieties were united under one standard in 1988 and later had the word 'Terrier' dropped from the official breed name.

Despite standing only 22 to 27 cm tall (with 25 cm and 2.3 kg considered ideal in international standards), the Russian Toy competes enthusiastically in agility, rally, obedience, lure coursing, and nose work.

faq.question: How tall is a Russian Toy?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 22 to 27 cm for both males and females, with 25 cm preferred (and heights under 18 cm or over 29 cm disqualified). British standards list 20 to 28 cm (with a ±1 cm tolerance), and North American standards specify 8 to 11 inches (about 20.3 to 27.9 cm, with dogs under 7 inches or over 12 inches disqualified).

faq.question: How much does a Russian Toy weigh?
faq.answer: International standards specify a weight of up to 3 kg (6.6 lbs) for both sexes, with 2.3 kg (about 5 lbs) preferred, and disqualify dogs weighing under 1.5 kg or over 3 kg. North American standards specify a weight of up to 6 to 6.5 pounds (about 2.7 to 2.95 kg), with a preferred weight of 5 pounds and a disqualifying minimum of 2 pounds.

faq.question: What is the difference between the smooth-haired and long-haired Russian Toy?
faq.answer: The smooth-haired variety has a short, glossy, close-lying coat with no undercoat or feathering, and is often described as slightly more terrier-like in attitude. The long-haired variety has a 3 to 5 cm (1 to 3 inch) straight or slightly wavy body coat, distinct feathering on the legs and tail, and long, thick fringes on the ears that completely cover the ear edges and tips by three years of age. Both varieties share the same anatomy and can even be born in the same litter.

faq.question: Why do Russian Toy puppies often need baby teeth removed by a veterinarian?
faq.answer: Like several other tiny toy breeds, most Russian Toy puppies do not shed all of their deciduous (baby) teeth naturally when their permanent teeth erupt around six months of age. If retained baby teeth are not surgically extracted by about nine months of age, two teeth occupy the same socket, leading to bite misalignment, trapped food, rapid tartar buildup, and early periodontal disease.

faq.question: Why should a Russian Toy wear a harness instead of a collar on walks?
faq.answer: Because very small dogs have delicate necks and tracheas, pulling against a neck collar can cause throat or tracheal injury. Walking the dog on a well-fitted harness distributes pressure safely across the chest. Indoors, collars and harnesses should be removed so they cannot catch on furniture or vents.

faq.question: When does a long-haired Russian Toy get its full coat and ear fringes?
faq.answer: Puppies typically shed much of their puppy coat between 5 and 12 months of age. An adult coat does not develop until the dog is over a year old, and the full, dramatic ear fringing is often not complete until two to three years of age.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for Russian Toy breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Pre-breeding health programs recommend three core clinical evaluations—patellar luxation screening, an annual examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (or accredited eye-scheme examiner), and a basic cardiac evaluation—along with optional screenings for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip and elbow dysplasia, and paired serum bile acid testing for congenital liver shunts.

overview.summary: An ancient, noble medium-sized Swiss scent hound bred in four regional colour varieties—Bernese, Jura, Lucerne, and Schwyz—prized for its fine nose, resonant voice, and tireless stamina across rugged alpine and forest terrain.
overview.description: The Schweizer Laufhund (Swiss Hound) is a medium-sized, powerfully muscled yet lean scent hound whose conformation radiates strength, endurance, and nobility. All four regional varieties—the Bernese Hound, Jura Hound, Lucerne Hound, and Schwyz Hound—share an identical structural standard and differ only in coat colour and underlying skin pigmentation. Slightly longer in body than tall (about 1.15:1), the dog features a deep chest reaching at least to the elbows, a long, narrow, clean-cut head without forehead wrinkles, and narrow, folded, corkscrew-twisted pendulous ears reaching at least to the tip of the nose. Passionate, determined, and resonant when giving tongue on a cold or fresh trail with a low nose, the breed is gentle, docile, clean indoors, and deeply devoted to its handler—returning promptly to its owner whenever a scent trail is lost.
overview.history: The Swiss Hound has ancient origins in the Alpine region: a Roman-era mosaic discovered at Avenches (ancient Aventicum) in 1735—preserved in 1794 drawings by Ritter before French cavalry destroyed the original in 1798—depicts pack hounds closely matching the Swiss varieties. The earliest written records appear between 1475 and 1480 in the correspondence of Albrecht von Bonstetten, Dean of Einsiedeln Abbey, from whom dukes and church dignitaries in Milan requested hounds bred at the monastery. Prized by Italian sportsmen in the fifteenth century and by French nobility in the eighteenth century for its skill in pursuing hare, the native Swiss stock was also shaped by French scent hounds (including ancestors of the Petit Bleu de Gascogne, Petit Gascon-Saintongeois, Ariégeois, and Porcelaine) brought home by Swiss mercenaries. In 1882, separate standards were drafted for five Swiss varieties. By the 1909 revision, the wirehaired Thurgau Hound (Thurgauer Laufhund) had vanished, and on 22 January 1933 a single unified breed standard was established for the four surviving varieties—Bernese, Jura, Lucerne, and Schwyz—while the heavier St. Hubert type of the Jura Hound also disappeared.
overview.originalPurpose: Independent scent-trailing and vocal driving ('giving tongue') of hare, roe deer, fox, and occasionally wild boar across challenging mountain and forest terrain
currentRoles: Long-distance jogging, marathon-training, and hiking companion

physical.coatType: Short, smooth, dense, and close-lying single coat, very fine on the head and pendulous ears
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Bernese Hound (Berner Laufhund): White with black patches or a black saddle, pale to dark tan markings over the eyes, on the cheeks, inside the ears, and around the vent, sometimes with very slight black ticking

Jura Hound (Jura Laufhund / Bruno du Jura): Tan with a black blanket (sometimes with black overlay), or black with tan markings over the eyes, cheeks, around the vent, and on the legs, sometimes with a small white chest patch

Lucerne Hound (Luzerner Laufhund): 'Blue' roan/speckled coat formed by heavily speckled black and white hairs, with black patches or a black saddle (black blanket permitted) and pale to dark tan markings over the eyes, cheeks, chest, around the vent, and on the legs
Schwyz Hound (Schwyzer Laufhund): White with orange patches or an orange saddle or blanket, sometimes with very slight orange ticking
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
distinctiveFeatures: Four regional varieties—Bernese, Jura, Lucerne, and Schwyz—sharing one anatomical standard and distinguished by coat pattern and skin pigmentation

Elongated, narrow, lean skull equal in length to the finely chiselled muzzle (1:1 ratio), with slightly divergent cranial-facial axes, a visible occipital protuberance, and no frontal furrow or forehead wrinkles
Long, narrow, supple ears set below eye level toward the back of the skull, folded and twisted with rounded tips, reaching at least the tip of the nose
Harmonious rectangular build with body length to withers height of about 1.15:1 and withers height to chest depth of about 2:1
Medium-length tapering tail set in continuation of the croup, hanging at rest and carried in a gentle upward curve above the back line when moving, without a brush
Variety-specific skin pigmentation: black and white-marbled skin in the Bernese; black and lighter skin in the Jura and Lucerne; dark grey and marbled skin in the Schwyz
Resonant, melodious hunting voice ('giving tongue') used while working a trail with a low nose

traits: Lively and passionately keen when hunting
Sensitive and responsive to gentle handling
Docile and strongly attached to its handler
Calm, gentle, and very clean indoors
Friendly and peaceful with people and other dogs
Determined and tireless on a scent trail
Independent while tracking, yet returns promptly to its handler when a trail is lost
Resonant and vocal when working

exercise.level: High. Built as a long-distance endurance runner and scent tracker rather than a short-burst sprinter, requiring substantial daily outdoor exercise and structured nose work.
activities: Long daily walks and hikes across varied forest and mountain trails
Mantrailing (person search), blood-tracking (Schweissarbeit), and scent-discrimination courses
Long-distance jogging, marathon training, or cycling alongside an athletic owner
Structured tracking and recall games using food rewards
Supervised off-leash exercise in securely enclosed areas

grooming.level: Low for the short, smooth coat (no trimming or shaving required), with routine inspection of the long pendulous ears.
grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a rubber grooming mitt or soft bristle brush to remove loose hair and distribute natural skin oils.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when necessary using a mild dog-safe shampoo, drying the ears afterward.
notes: Never trim or shave the short, dense coat.

Inspect the long, drooping ears regularly to prevent inflammation of the outer ear canal, though ear infections are relatively uncommon because the breed is rarely used for water work and the inner ear pinnae are only sparsely haired.
Examine the hard, rough paw pads, interdigital spaces, and nails after trail work for thorns, ticks, or splits.
Check the tight-fitting eyelids and eyes for grass seeds, dust, or irritation after field outings.
Brush teeth regularly with canine toothpaste to maintain oral hygiene.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Easy to guide indoors and deeply bonded to its handler, yet independent and single-minded once its nose locks onto a scent trail.
tips: Begin playful, reward-based training in early puppyhood and always carry food treats to reward prompt return—even when recalling the hound from a trail with a hunting horn or whistle.

Never raise or keep puppies solely in an outdoor kennel; Swiss breed guidance stresses that hounds must spend at least several hours daily inside the home with their family to develop a sound, well-adjusted character.
Satisfy the dog's genetic scenting drive with formal mantrailing or blood-tracking (Schweissarbeit) courses if it is not used for hunting.
Favour endurance sports such as long-distance running and tracking over tight, rapid-turn sports like agility, for which this long-distance runner is poorly suited.
Keep the dog on a leash or long line in unfenced wildlife areas until recall is thoroughly established, and prevent young hounds from over-exerting themselves on long trails.
training.socialization: Introduce puppies early to household life, varied environments, children, and other dogs. Because of its pack-hound heritage, the breed is naturally sociable with other dogs and friendly toward people, but careful management around cats and small wild or domestic animals is essential.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool and alpine climates
Warm climates when endurance exercise is scheduled for cooler hours with shade and water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Strongly attached to its handler and family, the Swiss Hound must be integrated into daily household life rather than isolated in a kennel, and may bay or become restless if left alone for long periods without exercise.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality canine diet formulated for medium-sized active or working dogs, adjusted to the individual's age and workload.
nutrition.guidelines: Adjust daily caloric intake to match seasonal hunting, mantrailing, or endurance-running workload so the hound stays lean, muscular, and between its typical adult weight of 18 to 23 kg without developing hollow flanks. Provide constant access to fresh water and allow rest before and after meals.
considerations: Working hounds in active hunting or trailing seasons require higher energy density than companion dogs in lighter routines.
Avoid heavy meals immediately before or after vigorous running or field work.
Account for high-value training treats—used frequently during recall and scent work—in the daily calorie allowance.
Consult a veterinarian to tailor puppy, adult, and senior feeding schedules and portion sizes.
nutrition.note: Consulted breed standards and club publications do not specify fixed daily meal counts for puppies, adults, or seniors; feeding frequency should be established with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Schweizer Laufhund is generally a robust, healthy working hound with a life expectancy of 12 to 14 years and very few widespread breed-specific diseases. However, veterinary ophthalmology references document several known or presumed hereditary eye disorders in specific varieties—most notably in the Jura Hound (Bruno du Jura) and Bernese Hound (Berner Laufhund)—for which no commercial DNA tests yet exist, making clinical ophthalmic screening important. Because the breed is rarely used in water and the inner ear flaps are only sparsely haired, ear canal infections are an exception rather than the rule when basic ear hygiene is maintained. In Switzerland, every breeding dog must pass a mandatory conformation, temperament, and clinical health inspection (Ankörung) from 15 months of age.
commonConditions: Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA): documented by veterinary ophthalmologists in the Jura Hound (Bruno du Jura), presenting with night blindness at 3 to 5 years of age and progressing to complete blindness in dogs over 7 years of age (inheritance mode unknown; no DNA test available)
Pectinate ligament anomaly (PLA / goniodysgenesis): documented in the Jura Hound (Bruno du Jura), predisposing affected dogs to possible acute glaucoma at 6 to 8 years of age

Inferior lateral entropion and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS / dry eye): documented as presumed hereditary ocular conditions in both the Bernese Hound (Berner Laufhund) and Jura Hound (Bruno du Jura); entropion and ectropion (even if operated) are disqualifying faults in the breed standard

Nictitating membrane disorders: prolapse of the third-eyelid gland ('cherry eye', reported in the Jura Hound and Lucerne Hound) and eversion of the cartilage of the nictitating membrane (reported in the Jura Hound)

Otitis externa (outer ear canal inflammation): a potential risk due to the long, folded pendulous ears, though national kennel-club guidance notes that ear problems are relatively uncommon because the breed is not a water dog and the inner ear pinnae are sparsely haired
Hip and elbow dysplasia: general orthopedic considerations monitored in working hounds to preserve long-distance trailing soundness
preventiveCare: Arrange periodic clinical eye examinations by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, especially for breeding dogs and for Jura and Bernese Hounds.
Seek immediate veterinary care for signs of ocular pain, redness, cloudiness, squinting, tearing, or reduced night vision.
Check and gently clean the long pendulous ears to prevent outer ear canal inflammation, particularly after wet or muddy field work.

Verify that breeding parents have passed the mandatory breed-club breeding soundness and conformation inspection (Ankörung, minimum age 15 months; minimum mating age 18 months) and have no clinically relevant hereditary defects.
Maintain a lean body weight (typically 18–23 kg) and sound muscular conditioning to protect the joints during long-distance running and trailing.
recommendedScreenings: Clinical ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (including gonioscopy where indicated for Jura Hounds)
Mandatory pre-breeding conformation, behaviour, and health evaluation (Ankörung at 15 months of age or older under Swiss breed-club regulations)
Orthopedic evaluation of hips and elbows when warranted by breeding program standards, family history, or clinical signs
Routine veterinary physical and otoscopic ear examinations
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with canine toothpaste and schedule veterinary dental checks. The breed standard requires strong jaws with a complete, regular scissor bite (pincer bite accepted, and absence of one or two PM1 or PM2 premolars tolerated).
health.earCare: Although the inner ear flaps are sparsely haired and the breed is rarely used in water—making ear problems relatively uncommon—the long, folded ears should still be checked regularly for dirt, ticks, or moisture to prevent outer ear canal inflammation.
health.skinCare: After walks or tracking in forest and brush, inspect the short, dense coat, skin, and rough paw pads for ticks, thorns, cuts, or irritation.

idealFor: Hunters, blood-tracking handlers, and mantrailing or nose-work enthusiasts
Long-distance runners, marathon trainees, hikers, and cyclists seeking a tireless endurance partner
Families seeking a gentle, clean, friendly indoor companion who can meet its high outdoor exercise and scent-work demands
Homes with a securely fenced yard in a rural or quiet suburban environment where a resonant hound voice will not cause neighbour conflicts
notIdealFor: Apartment dwellers or densely packed urban neighbourhoods sensitive to loud, melodious baying
Owners seeking a dog for tight, rapid-turn sprint sports such as agility rather than endurance running and scent work
Anyone intending to keep a dog exclusively in an outdoor kennel without daily indoor family contact
Sedentary households or handlers who expect effortless off-leash recall around wildlife

funFacts: A Roman mosaic discovered in 1735 at Avenches (ancient Aventicum) in Switzerland depicted pack hounds matching the Swiss Hound varieties; although French cavalry destroyed the mosaic in 1798, 1794 drawings by Ritter preserved the image.

The earliest written records of the breed date from 1475 to 1480, when dukes and church dignitaries in Milan wrote to Albrecht von Bonstetten, Dean of Einsiedeln Abbey, requesting Swiss hounds from the monastery's kennels.

All four regional varieties—the Bernese, Jura, Lucerne, and Schwyz Hounds—share a single anatomical breed standard adopted on 22 January 1933 and differ only in coat colour and underlying skin pigmentation.

A fifth historical variety, the wirehaired Thurgau Hound (Thurgauer Laufhund), was included in the original 1882 Swiss standards but had vanished by 1909, along with the heavy St. Hubert type of the Jura Hound.

Even the skin beneath the coat is variety-specific: the Bernese Hound has black skin under its black hair and black-and-white marbled skin under its white hair, whereas the Schwyz Hound has dark grey skin under its orange patches.

Built as a long-distance marathon runner rather than a tight-turning sprinter, the Schweizer Laufhund excels at jogging and mantrailing rather than agility, and was selectively bred down around 1900 to create the separate, shorter-legged Schweizer Niederlaufhund (Small Swiss Hound).

faq.question: What is a Schweizer Laufhund?
faq.answer: The Schweizer Laufhund (known in English as the Swiss Hound and in French as the Chien Courant Suisse) is an ancient, medium-sized Swiss scent hound bred in four regional colour varieties to trail hare, roe deer, fox, and wild boar across rugged terrain while communicating its progress with a resonant voice.

faq.question: What are the four varieties of the Schweizer Laufhund?
faq.answer: The four recognized varieties are the Bernese Hound (tricolour white, black, and tan), the Jura Hound (black and tan, or tan with a black mantle), the Lucerne Hound ('blue' black-and-white speckled roan with black patches and tan points), and the Schwyz Hound (white with orange patches or saddle). Apart from coat colour and skin pigmentation, all four share the exact same conformation and working standard.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Schweizer Laufhund?
faq.answer: Males stand 49 to 59 cm (19 to 23 inches) at the withers and females stand 47 to 57 cm (18.5 to 22.5 inches), with no tolerance in the conformation standard for dogs over or under those heights. Adult weight is typically 18 to 23 kg (about 40 to 51 lbs), with males slightly larger and heavier than females.

faq.question: How does the Schweizer Laufhund differ from the Schweizer Niederlaufhund?
faq.answer: They are two distinct Swiss breeds that share the same four regional colour varieties (Bernese, Jura, Lucerne, and Schwyz). The Schweizer Laufhund is the original medium-sized hound standing 47 to 59 cm and weighing 18 to 23 kg, whereas the Schweizer Niederlaufhund (Small Swiss Hound) was selectively bred at the beginning of the twentieth century as a shorter-legged, slower hound standing 33 to 43 cm (and weighing up to 15–20 kg) for smaller hunting districts.

faq.question: What is the Schweizer Laufhund like inside the home?
faq.answer: Despite its passionate drive on a scent trail, indoors the Swiss Hound is calm, gentle, docile, and very clean. Swiss kennel-club guidance emphasizes that these hounds should never be raised solely in outdoor kennels and need daily indoor family life, where they get along well with children and other dogs.

faq.question: Can a Schweizer Laufhund be kept by a non-hunter, and what sports suit it best?
faq.answer: Yes, provided its nose and endurance are given another outlet. Because it is a long-distance runner rather than a tight-turning sprinter, it is poorly suited to agility, but it excels at mantrailing (person search), blood-tracking (Schweissarbeit), and accompanying owners on long jogging or marathon-training runs.

faq.question: What hereditary eye conditions are documented in the Schweizer Laufhund?
faq.answer: Veterinary ophthalmology manuals document progressive retinal atrophy (PRA, causing night blindness at 3–5 years and total blindness after 7 years) and pectinate ligament anomaly (predisposing to acute glaucoma at 6–8 years) in the Jura Hound, as well as inferior lateral entropion and dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) in the Bernese and Jura Hounds. Third-eyelid gland prolapse ('cherry eye') has also been reported in the Jura and Lucerne Hounds.

faq.question: Are ear infections common in the Schweizer Laufhund?
faq.answer: Although the long, folded ears require regular inspection to prevent outer ear canal inflammation, Swiss kennel-club guidance notes that ear problems are actually an exception rather than the rule because the breed is rarely used for water work and the inside of the ear flaps is only sparsely haired.
